# THE MORALISTS

## A PHILOSOPHICAL RHAPSODY

### PART I

#### SECTION I

->*Philocles to Palemon*<-

What person, if he had never happened to hear of your character, Palemon, could imagine that a talent suited for the most important matters, and shaped by royal courts and military camps, should have such a strong passion for philosophy and the academic schools? <note>original: "the schools"; refers to formal academic institutions and the traditional, often dense, philosophical methods taught there.</note> Who could possibly believe that someone of your social standing and reputation in the fashionable world should be so thoroughly familiar with the world of learning? Who would think you were so deeply interested in the concerns of a people who are so unappealing to most of mankind and so out of step with the mood of the age?

I truly believe you are the only gentleman who would have taken the whim to discuss philosophy in such a circle of fashionable company as we had around us yesterday, when we were in your carriage together in the Park. <note>original: "the Park"; likely refers to St. James’s Park in London, a primary social hub for the elite during this period.</note> How you could connect the sights there to such academic subjects was a mystery. I could only conclude that either you had an overwhelming passion for philosophy—enough to give up so many attractions for it—or that some of those beautiful attractions had such an intense effect on you that they drove you to philosophy for relief.

In either case, I pitied you. I thought it a kinder fate to be a more casual lover, as I truly was myself.

<summary>Philocles expresses his surprise that Palemon, a high-ranking man of the world, chooses to pursue philosophy despite its unpopularity in fashionable society. He playfully wonders if Palemon's intellectual interests are a distraction from the trials of romantic love.</summary>

<keywords>Shaftesbury, Philocles, Palemon, philosophy, social status, Enlightenment dialogue, the Park</keywords>

--- Page 16 ---
<meta>This page continues the address from Philocles to Palemon. Philocles is teasing Palemon for his obsessive interest in philosophy, comparing it to a romantic infatuation that is out of step with the fashionable world.</meta>

It was better, I told you, to admire beauty and wisdom a little more moderately. I maintained that it was better to engage so cautiously as to be sure of leaving with a whole heart, and an imagination as strong as ever for all the pretty entertainments and diversions of the world. For these, I thought, were things one would not willingly part with for the sake of a refined, romantic passion like those of the gentlemen called *virtuosi*. <note>original: "virtuosi"; in this period, the term referred to dedicated students of the arts and sciences, though it often carried a connotation of being an obsessive hobbyist or dilettante.</note>

I took that name to apply to both the lover and the philosopher; it didn't matter what the object of affection was, whether poetry, music, philosophy, or "the fair." <note>original: "the fair"; a common period expression referring to beautiful women.</note> All who were infatuated in any way were in the same condition. You could see it, I told you, by their expressions, their admiration, their deep thoughtfulness, their waking every now and then as if from a dream, their constant talking about one thing, and barely paying attention to what they said on any other subject—sad signs!

But all this warning did not deter you. For you, *Palemon*, are one of the adventurous type, whom danger inspires rather than discourages. And now, nothing less will satisfy you than to have our philosophical adventures recorded. Everything must be laid out for you and summarized in one complete account; to remain, it seems, as a monument to that ill-timed conversation, which was so contrary to the prevailing spirit of gallantry and pleasure.

I must admit, indeed, that it has become fashionable in our nation to talk about politics in every social gathering, and to mix discussions of State affairs with those of pleasure and entertainment. However, it is certain that we do not approve of such freedom in philosophy. Nor do we consider politics to be within her domain, or in the least related to her. We moderns have so degraded philosophy and stripped her of her primary rights.

You must allow me, *Palemon*, to mourn for philosophy in this way, since you have forced me to engage with her at a time when her reputation is so low. She is no longer active in the world, nor can she easily be brought onto the public stage with any success. We have locked her up, poor lady, in colleges <note>original: "colleges"; referring to the universities, where Shaftesbury felt philosophy had become dry, academic, and disconnected from the real world of social and political life.</note>

<summary>Philocles compares the obsessive pursuit of philosophy to a romantic infatuation and laments that philosophy has been "immured" in academic institutions, separated from the lively world of politics and social pleasure.</summary>
<keywords>virtuosi, philosophy vs. politics, Palemon, Philocles, social customs, academic vs. public life</keywords>

--- Page 17 ---
<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Philocles and Palemon. Philocles is describing the low state into which philosophy has fallen in modern society, arguing that it has been separated from public life and relegated to dry, academic study.</meta>

# THE MORALISTS

->5<-

...and cells, and have forced her to labor like a slave in the mines. Quacks <note>original: "Empirics"; in this period, it referred to those who practiced medicine or science based on trial and error rather than sound theory, often used as a derogatory term for frauds.</note> and pedantic pretenders <note>original: "sophists"; those who use clever but fallacious arguments.</note> are her primary students. Formal logic <note>original: "school-syllogism"</note> and alchemical potions <note>original: "elixir"</note> are the best things she produces. She is so far from training statesmen, as she did in ancient times, that hardly any prominent public figure dares to admit they owe her anything. If a few people still keep up an acquaintance with her and visit her retreats occasionally, they do so as the high-ranking disciple came to his Lord—"secretly, and by night." <note>A reference to Nicodemus in the Gospel of John, who visited Jesus at night to avoid being seen by his peers.</note>

However, as low as philosophy has sunk, if we admit that morality belongs to her, then politics must undeniably be hers as well. To understand the customs and nature of people in general, it is necessary to study the individual man first. We must know the human creature as he is in himself before we consider him in a group—how he functions in the State or as a member of a city or community. Nothing is more common than to debate about man in his organized state and national identity, or how he is tied to a specific society by birth or citizenship <note>original: "naturalisation"</note>. Yet to consider him as a citizen of the world—to trace his lineage one step higher and view his ultimate purpose and makeup within Nature itself—is apparently dismissed as some overly complicated or over-refined speculation.

Perhaps it could be argued that the reason for this general hesitation to explore moral questions is that the people responsible for these subjects have handled them in a way that makes sophisticated people embarrassed to be involved with them. By leaving these concerns entirely to academic specialists <note>original: "mere scholastics"</note>, their dry and formal style has infected the subject itself. We assume there are specific, formal places where enough is already said and taught about these serious topics. We cannot tolerate anything like it in polite company. The mere mention of such matters disgusts us and ruins our mood. If learning happens to come up, we dismiss it as being overly academic <note>original: "pedantry"</note>; if morality is discussed, we call it preaching.

One must admit, however, that this is a real disadvantage of our...

<summary>Philocles laments that philosophy has become a dry, academic pursuit shunned by polite society and statesmen, arguing that true politics must be rooted in an understanding of human nature and universal morality.</summary>
<keywords>philosophy, morality, politics, scholastics, human nature, citizenship, academic pedantry</keywords>

--- Page 18 ---
<meta>This page continues Philocles’s critique of modern intellectual life. He is arguing that philosophy has become too "delicate" and detached from the rigorous, "masculine" style of the ancients, leading to a decline in the quality of modern conversation and literature.</meta>

# SHAFTESBURY'S CHARACTERISTICS

...modern conversations, that by being so overly refined <note>original: "scrupulous nicety"</note> they lose those masculine supports of learning and sound reason. Even the fair sex—whom we claim to please with this lowering of our standards—may rightly despise us for it and laugh at us for mimicking their own particular softness. It is no compliment to them to imitate their manners and become effeminate. Our thoughts, language, and style, as well as our voice and appearance, should possess some of those masculine features and natural roughness that distinguish our sex. Whatever politeness we might claim, it is more a disfigurement than a real improvement of speech to make it so delicate.

No work of wit can be considered perfect without that strength and boldness of hand which gives it substance and proportion. A good piece of art, as painters say, must have good "muscling" <note>Shaftesbury uses an artistic metaphor here: just as a painting needs a strong underlying anatomical structure (muscling), a piece of writing needs strong logic.</note> as well as coloring and clothing <note>original: "drapery"</note>. Surely no writing or speech of any great importance can seem anything but weakened <note>original: "enervated"</note> when it is not accompanied by strong reason, antiquity, historical records, the natural history of man, or anything that can be called knowledge—unless it appears in some ridiculous disguise that gives it an air of playfulness and triviality <note>original: "dalliance"</note>.

This brings to mind a reason I have often looked for: why we moderns, who produce so many treatises and essays, are so reluctant to use the form of <term>dialogue</term>¹ <note>Dialogue: A literary form where philosophy is explored through conversation between characters, famously used by Plato.</note>. In the past, this was found to be the most polite and effective way of handling even the most serious subjects. The truth is, it would be a terrible lie and a misrepresentation of our era to put so much good sense together in any one conversation that it could hold up steadily and with clear coherence for an hour, until any single subject had been rationally examined.²

To apply colors, to draw, or to describe things in a way that goes against the appearance of nature and truth is a freedom permitted neither to the painter...

---

¹ *Advice to an Author*, part 1, section 3; *Miscellanies* 5, chapter 2.
² [*Compare Jonathan Swift's "Polite Conversation" and "Hints towards an Essay on Conversation."*] <note>Swift’s works on this topic were famous satires that mocked the empty, repetitive, and unintellectual nature of social chatter in the 18th century.</note>

<summary>Shaftesbury argues that modern discourse has become too "soft" and refined, losing the intellectual strength of the ancients. He suggests that the reason modern writers avoid the "dialogue" form is that real-life modern conversations are too shallow to sustain a serious, rational argument.</summary>
<keywords>masculinity in prose, effeminacy, dialogue, modern conversation, artistic proportion, Shaftesbury, Jonathan Swift</keywords>

--- Page 19 ---
<meta>This page continues the speaker's (Philocles) argument about why the dialogue form—once popular among ancient philosophers—has fallen into disuse in the modern era. He suggests that authors who portray themselves as victorious in debate appear arrogant and unrealistic.</meta>

...nor the poet. A philosopher has even less of a privilege to do this, especially when writing about himself. If he portrays his own philosophy as being impressive in conversation, if he claims victory in a debate and makes his own wisdom seem superior to everyone else's, he risks being mocked <note>original: "liable to sound raillery"</note> and perhaps even turned into a laughingstock <note>original: "made a fable of"</note>.

It is said of the lion that, while having a polite conversation with a man, he wisely refused to admit the man was stronger when, instead of providing facts, the man only showed him statues and paintings of human victories over lions. The beast realized these "masterpieces" of art were entirely human inventions <note>original: "human forgery"</note>, and he had every right to reject them. In fact, if he had ever seen a real fight like the ones the man showed him in art, perhaps the example would have convinced him. But old statues of *Hercules* or *Theseus* <note>Two of the most famous heroes of Greek mythology, known for slaying monstrous beasts like the Nemean Lion and the Minotaur.</note>—those famous slayers of beasts—could hardly intimidate him as long as he never saw or felt a living opponent capable of actually challenging him in the field.

We shouldn't be surprised, then, that this kind of "moral painting"—the philosophical dialogue—is so unfashionable, or that we see so few of these philosophical portraits today. After all, where are the real-life models? Even if you, *Palemon*, or I happened to meet such a person by chance and were impressed by their character, do you think it would make for a believable "picture"?

You also know that the <term>Academic philosophy</term> <note>This refers to the tradition of the Platonic Academy, which practiced a "Socratic" method of constant questioning and skepticism rather than providing rigid, dogmatic answers.</note> I am presenting to you involves a certain method of questioning and doubting that doesn't fit the spirit of our times at all. People today love to take sides immediately. They cannot bear being kept in suspense. The process of deep examination torments them, and they want to finish with it as quickly and easily as possible. It is as if people imagine they are drowning whenever they dare to trust the current of reason. They feel they are being swept away to some unknown place and are desperate to grab the first branch they see. They would rather hang there, no matter how precariously, rather than...

<summary>This page explains why the philosophical dialogue is no longer popular, arguing that readers find idealized depictions of wise philosophers to be unrealistic "fictions" and that modern audiences are too impatient for the slow, skeptical process of true reasoning.</summary>
<keywords>Shaftesbury, The Moralists, philosophical dialogue, Academic philosophy, skepticism, reason, Hercules, Theseus, lion fable, Palemon</keywords>

--- Page 20 ---
<meta>This page continues the speaker’s critique of modern philosophy. Having just mentioned the "Academics" (the skeptical school of ancient philosophy), he describes how people often cling to weak hypotheses to avoid the difficult work of true inquiry and instead prefer the easy answers provided by dogmatic systems.</meta>

# SHAFTESBURY'S CHARACTERISTICS

...trust their strength to keep them afloat <note>original: "bear them above water"</note>. Anyone who has grasped a hypothesis, no matter how flimsy, feels satisfied. He can immediately answer every objection and, using a few technical terms <note>original: "terms of art"</note>, explain everything without any effort.

It is no surprise that in this age the philosophy of the alchemists is so popular <note>original: "prevails so much"</note>,¹ since it promises such wonders and requires more physical labor than mental effort. We have a strange fantasy about being creators—at the very least, a powerful desire to know the "knack" or secret by which Nature accomplishes everything. The rest of our philosophers only aim to achieve through theory <note>original: "speculation"</note> what our alchemists hope to achieve in practice. Indeed, some alchemists have actually considered how to create a human being <note>original: "make Man"</note> through methods other than those Nature has provided until now. Every school of thought <note>original: "sect"</note> has its own "recipe." Once you know it, you become the master of Nature: you can explain all her phenomena <note>A phenomenon is an observable event or fact.</note>,² see all her designs, and account for all her operations. If it were necessary, you might even join her laboratory and work alongside her. At least, one would imagine that the followers of every modern school held this arrogant view <note>original: "conceit"</note>. In their own way, they are all like Archimedes <note>Archimedes was an ancient Greek mathematician who famously claimed that with a long enough lever and a place to stand, he could move the earth.</note>, and they claim they can create a world more easily than he offered to move one.

In short, there are good reasons why we are so superficial and, as a result, so arrogant <note>original: "dogmatical"</note> in our philosophy. We are too lazy, soft <note>original: "effeminate"</note>, and furthermore a bit too cowardly to dare to doubt. Making bold, final pronouncements is simply the style that best suits our current behavior.

<meta>This page continues the author’s critique of how people cling to dogmatic theories to avoid the discomfort of uncertainty. He now contrasts this modern avoidance of doubt with the ancient "Academic" tradition of skeptical inquiry and rigorous debate.</meta>

<page-num>9</page-num>

# THE MORALISTS

This mindset fits our vices just as well as it fits our superstition. Whichever one we prefer is protected by it. If we support religion and have adopted a hypothesis <note>A hypothesis is a proposed explanation or theory.</note> that we think our faith depends on, we are superstitiously careful not to let it be weakened. If our bad morals cause us to break away from religion, the situation is the same: we are just as afraid of doubting. We insist on saying, "It is impossible," or "It is proven." After all, who knows what would happen otherwise? To admit we do not know is to admit defeat!

So, we insist on knowing everything while refusing the hard work of examining anything. Therefore, of all types of philosophy, the most unpleasant must be the one that relies on no established theory <note>original: "hypothesis"</note> and offers no flattering system. Instead, it speaks only of probabilities, the suspension of judgment, inquiry, research, and the caution needed to avoid being misled or deceived. This is that Academic discipline <note>The "Academic" tradition refers to the skeptical school of ancient Greek philosophy associated with Plato’s Academy, which emphasized questioning and dialogue over fixed dogmas.</note> in which young people were formerly trained;¹ in an era when not only horsemanship and military arts had public practice grounds, but philosophy also had its famous "wrestlers." Reason and wit had their own academy and underwent this testing—not in a formal, isolated way away from the world, but openly among the upper classes as a refined exercise. The greatest men were not ashamed to practice this during breaks from public business, even while holding the highest offices and until the very end of their lives. This led to a style of dialogue and a patience for debate and reasoning that we hardly see anymore in any modern conversations.

Consider then, Palemon <note>Palemon is the fictional recipient of this letter/dialogue.</note>, what our description is likely to turn out to be, and how it will look—especially in the light you have unfortunately chosen for it. For who would try to compare philosophy with the lightheartedness, wit, and humor of the present age? However, if this reflects well on you, I am satisfied. The project is yours. You are the one who has paired philosophy so unevenly. Therefore, leaving you to take responsibility for its success, I begin this unlucky <note>original: "inauspicious"</note> work, which my bad luck <note>original: "ill stars"</note> and

I wondered most to find you suddenly so disillusioned <term>out of conceit: no longer in favor of or lacking an appreciation for something</term> with our modern poets and *gallant* <note>original: "galante" – referring to authors who write about courtly romance and refined social etiquette</note> writers. You acknowledged that it was true, as some recent thinkers <note>original: "late wits"</note> have observed, "that gallantry was a modern invention." And you thought this was likely the case, without any insult to the ancients, who understood **Truth** and **Nature** too well to allow such a ridiculous invention.

It was in vain, therefore, that I used this argument as a shield in my defense. I did my cause no favors when I pleaded on behalf of women using all the fine things usually said in this romantic style for their benefit. You attacked the very fortress of gallantry; you ridiculed the "point of honor," along with all the refined <note>original: "nice"</note> sentiments and ceremonies belonging to it. You even condemned our favorite novels—those dear, sweet, natural pieces, most of them written by women themselves. In short, you absolutely condemned this entire system of wit as false, monstrous, and **Gothic** <term>Gothic: used here to mean medieval, crude, or barbarous, rather than the later architectural or literary movement</term>. You saw it as completely unnatural and born from the mere leftovers of **chivalry** or **knight-errantry**—a system which you actually preferred over the style that rules today. 

For you thought that in a time when the "mystery of gallantry" involved the idea of **brave** <term>doughty: brave, strong, or determined</term> **knighthood**—when women were witnesses and, in a way, participants in feats of arms, involved in all the details of war and combat, and were won through the force of a lance and manly courage—it was not entirely absurd to pay them homage and adoration, make them the standard for wit and manners, and bring men under their rules. But in a country where no **female saints** <note>original: "she-saints" – a reference to the Protestant critique of the Catholic veneration of female saints</note> were worshipped by religious authority, you felt it was as inappropriate and senseless as it was disrespectful to **deify** <note>original: "deify" – to treat or worship someone like a god</note> the sex. You argued against raising them to a status beyond what **Nature** had allowed and treating them with a kind of respect that, in the natural course of love, women themselves were the most likely to complain about.

It was the same, I imagined, as in some of those expensive fabrics where the flowers and the background are combined oddly, with such irregular craftsmanship and clashing colors that they look bad in the sample pattern, but very natural and pleasing in the finished piece.

In your view, even storms and tempests had their own beauty—except for those that arose within human hearts. It was only because of this chaotic race of mortals that you were willing to criticize Nature. Now I understand why you were so excited by the story of Prometheus <note>In Greek mythology, the Titan Prometheus was said to have shaped the first humans out of clay.</note>. You wanted a creator like him for humanity, and you were tempted to wish that this story could be confirmed by modern theology <note>original: "divinity"</note>. By clearing the supreme powers of any involvement or hand in such poor workmanship, you would then have the freedom to attack those flaws without being blasphemous <note>original: "profaneness"</note>.

However, I told you that this was merely a clever excuse used by the religious poets of ancient times. It was easy to answer every objection by blaming Prometheus. If someone asked, "Why was humanity originally so full of folly and stubbornness? Why so much pride, ambition, and strange desires? Why are so many plagues and curses inherited by him and his descendants?" Prometheus was the cause. The "plastic artist" <note>original: "plastic artist"; from the Greek *plastikos*, meaning a creator who molds or shapes matter, like a sculptor</note>, with his clumsy hands, explained everything. "It was his invention," they said, "and he is responsible for it." They considered it a fair strategy if they could just push the cause of evil one step further away. If the public asked a question, the poets told them a story and sent them away satisfied. They assumed that, aside from a few philosophers, no one would be so nosy as to look further or ask a second question.

And in reality, I continued, it is amazing how useful a story is for distracting people—and not just children. Most men are much more easily paid with this "paper money" than with the "sterling silver" of solid reason. We should not be so quick to laugh at the Indian philosophers who, to satisfy their people's questions about how the massive frame of the world is supported, tell them it rests on an elephant. And what holds up the elephant? That is a sharp question! But it is a question that should never be answered. This is the only point where our Indian philosophers are to blame: they should be satisfied with the elephant and go no further. But instead, they keep a tortoise in reserve, whose back they believe is broad enough to hold everything. <note>This refers to the "World Turtle" myth, an ancient concept where the earth is supported by a giant turtle, which in turn stands on an elephant; it is often used as an example of "infinite regress" in logic.</note>

So the tortoise must bear the new load, and thus the situation stands worse than before.

The pagan story of Prometheus was, as I told you, much the same as this Indian one, only the pagan mythologists were wise enough not to go beyond the first step. A single Prometheus was enough to take the weight off Jove <note>The Roman name for the king of the gods, Jupiter.</note>. They essentially made Jove a bystander. He decided, it seems, to remain neutral and see what would come of this notable experiment—how the dangerous "man-molder" would proceed, and what the outcome of his tampering would be. This is an excellent account to satisfy the pagan commoners! But how, do you think, would a philosopher digest this? "For the Gods," he would say immediately, "either could have hindered Prometheus’s creation or they could not. If they could, they were responsible for the consequences; if they could not, they were no longer Gods, being thus limited and controlled. And whether 'Prometheus' was a name for chance, destiny, a formative nature <note>original: "plastic nature"; referring to a natural power that shapes matter</note>, or an evil spirit <note>original: "daemon"</note>, whatever was intended by it, it was still the same violation of omnipotence."

You admitted it was neither wise nor just that such a hazardous affair as creation should have been undertaken by those who did not have perfect foresight as well as total command. But you insisted on foresight. You allowed that the consequences were understood by the creating powers when they undertook their work, and you denied that it would have been better for them to have omitted it, even though they knew what the outcome would be. "It was still better that the project should be executed, whatever might become of mankind, or however hard such a creation was likely to fall upon the majority of this miserable race. For it was impossible," you thought, "that Heaven should have acted otherwise than for the best. So even from this misery and human evil, some good was undoubtedly arising—something which overbalanced everything else and made full amends."

This was a confession I truly wondered how I managed to draw from you, and soon afterward I found you somewhat uneasy about it. For here I took up your own side against

I admitted to you, Palemon, that there was truth enough in your charge. For above all things I loved ease, and of all philosophers, I preferred those who reasoned most at their ease and were never angry or disturbed—as you admitted those called Skeptics never were. I looked upon this kind of philosophy as the finest, most agreeable, and most wandering exercise of the mind imaginable. The other kind, I thought, was painful and laborious: “to keep always within the limits of one path, to aim always at one point, and to hold precisely to what men haphazardly call the Truth; a point that, by all appearances, is very unstable and hard to determine.” Besides, my way hurt nobody. I was always the first to comply on any occasion, and regarding matters of religion, I was further from profanity and erroneous doctrine than anyone. I could never have the presumption to shock my spiritual and learned superiors. I was the furthest from relying on my own understanding, nor was I one who exalted reason above faith, or insisted much upon what dogmatic men call demonstration, which they dare to oppose to the sacred mysteries of religion. And to show you, I continued, how impossible it is for men of our sort ever to stray from the universal and established faith, please consider that while others pretend to see with their own eyes what is most proper and best for them in religion, we, for our part, do not pretend to see with any eyes other than those of our spiritual guides. Neither do we presume to judge those guides ourselves, but submit to them as they are appointed for us by our rightful superiors. In short, you who are rationalists and walk by reason in everything pretend to know all things while you believe little or nothing. We, for our part, know nothing and believe everything.

Here I ended, and in return you only asked me coldly “whether with that fine skepticism of mine I made no more

It is merely of philosophy that I speak; and my desire is only to see what I can gather from it to counter the main arguments of atheism and re-establish what I have previously tried to loosen in the system of theism."

"Your project," you said, "is likely to reconcile me to your character, which I was beginning to distrust. For as much as I am against the cause of theism or the name of *Deist* when it is used to exclude revelation, I still consider that, strictly speaking, theism is the root of everything, and that to be a settled Christian, it is necessary to be first of all a good theist; for theism can only be opposed to polytheism or atheism.¹ Nor do I have the patience to hear the name of *Deist* (the highest of all names) denounced and set in opposition to Christianity. “As if our religion were a kind of magic that did not depend on the belief in a single supreme Being. Or as if the firm and rational belief in such a Being on philosophical grounds were an improper qualification for believing anything further.” An excellent excuse for those who are naturally inclined to disbelieve in revelation, or who, through vanity, pretend to have this kind of intellectual freedom! . . .

### SECTION III

"You shall find then," I said (assuming a grave air), "that it is possible for me to be serious, and that it is probable I am becoming so for good. Your excessive seriousness a while ago, at such an inconvenient time, may have driven me perhaps into the opposite extreme by resisting your melancholy mood. "Nor is the enjoyment of such a single beauty enough to satisfy such an aspiring soul. It seeks how to combine more beauties, and by what union of these to form a beautiful society. It views communities, friendships, relationships, and duties, and considers by what harmony of individual minds the general harmony is composed and the public good established.

"Not satisfied even with the public good in a single community of men, it creates for itself a nobler objective and, with expanded affection, seeks the good of mankind. It dwells with pleasure amidst the reason and the orders on which this fair connection and beneficial interest are established. Laws, constitutions, civil and religious rites; whatever civilizes or polishes unrefined mankind; the sciences and arts, philosophy, morals, virtue; the flourishing state of human affairs and the perfection of human nature—these are its delightful prospects, and this is the charm of beauty that attracts it.

"Still eager in this pursuit (such is its love of order and perfection), it does not rest here, nor satisfy itself with the beauty of a part, but, extending its shared bounty further, seeks the good of all and desires the interest and prosperity of the whole. True to its native world and higher country, it is here that it seeks order and perfection, wishing for the best and hoping still to find a just and wise administration.

"And since all hope of this would be vain and idle if no universal mind presided—since without such a supreme intelligence and providential care the fragmented universe would be condemned to suffer infinite calamities—it is here the noble mind labors to discover that healing cause by which the interest of the whole is securely established, and the beauty of things and the universal order are successfully sustained.

"This, Palemon, is the labor of your soul, and this is its melancholy when, unsuccessfully pursuing the supreme beauty, it encounters darkening clouds that block its sight."

22

Monsters arise, not those from Libyan deserts, but from the more fertile heart of man, and with their horrid appearance cast an unseemly reflection upon Nature. She—helpless (as she is thought) and working so absurdly—is condemned, the government of the world is called into question, and Deity is made void.

“Much is alleged in response to show why Nature errs, and how she became so powerless and erring from an unerring hand. But I deny she errs; and when she seems most ignorant or perverse in her productions, I assert that even then she is as wise and provident as in her finest works. For it is not when they see various interests mixed and interfering that men complain of the world’s order or abhor the face of things; nor when they see subordinate natures of different kinds, opposed to one another, and in their different operations the higher submitted to the lower. On the contrary, it is from this order of inferior and superior things that we admire the world’s beauty,¹ founded thus on opposites, while from such various and disagreeing principles a universal harmony is established.

“Thus, in the various orders of earthly forms, a resignation is required—a sacrifice and mutual yielding of natures to one another. Vegetables, by their death, sustain animals; and animal bodies, once dissolved, enrich the earth and raise up the vegetable world once again. The numerous insects are reduced by the superior kinds of birds and beasts, and these in turn are checked by man, who in his turn submits to other natures and resigns his form as a sacrifice shared with the rest of things. And if, in natures so little elevated or superior to one another, the sacrifice of interests can appear so just, how much more reasonably may all inferior natures be subjected to the superior nature of the world!—that world, Palemon, which even now transported you when the sun’s fading light gave way to these bright constellations and left you this wide system to contemplate.

The central powers, which keep the celestial bodies in their proper balance and movement, must not be disrupted to save a temporary form or to rescue a tiny animal from the precipice—a creature whose fragile body, no matter how well protected, must soon break down of its own accord. The surrounding air, the internal vapors, the hanging meteors, or whatever else nourishes or preserves this earth, must act according to a natural course; other individual structures must yield to the healthy state and constitution of the all-sustaining globe.

“Let us not, therefore, wonder if animal species are often afflicted by earthquakes, storms, plague-carrying winds, fires from below or above, or floods—and perhaps whole species are destroyed at once in a common ruin. Much less should we find it strange if, either by an external blow or some internal injury from hostile matter, individual animals are deformed even at their first conception, when disease attacks the reproductive organs and the seminal parts are harmed and blocked in their precise work. It is only then that monstrous shapes are seen: Nature is still working as she did before—not perversely or mistakenly, not weakly or with faint efforts—but overpowered by a superior rival and by the justly conquering force of another part of nature.

“Nor need we wonder if the internal form—the soul and temperament—shares in this occasional deformity and often sympathizes with its close partner. Who is there that can wonder at either the illnesses of the senses or the corruption of minds enclosed in such fragile bodies and dependent on such easily corrupted organs?

“Here, then, is the solution you require, and the explanation for those apparent flaws blamed on Nature. There is nothing in this besides what is natural and good. It is good that is dominant; and every perishable and mortal nature, through its mortality and decay, gives way only to something better—and all things together yield to that best and highest nature, which is incorruptible and immortal.”

Nothing I said made the slightest impression on you. ## PART II

### SECTION I

->*Philocles to Palemon*<-

AFTER such a day as yesterday, I might well have found it difficult, when I woke the next morning, to find myself under definite commitments to proceed in the same philosophical way without interruption, and upon harder terms than ever. For it was no longer the agreeable role of a companion that I now had to play. Your conversation, Palemon, which had supported me until now, was at an end. I was now alone, confined to my study, obliged to meditate by myself, and forced into the difficult position of an author and historian dealing with the most challenging subject.

But here, it seemed to me, favorable Heaven assisted me in some way. For if dreams were, as Homer teaches, sent from the throne of Jove, I might conclude I had a favorable one of the true sort toward the morning light; as I gathered my thoughts, it gave me a clear and perfect idea of what I desired so earnestly to bring back to my memory.

I found myself transported to a distant country, which presented a magnificent rural scene. It was a mountain not far from the sea, its crest adorned with ancient woods, and at its foot a river and a well-inhabited plain, beyond which the sea appeared, completing the view.

No sooner had I considered the place than I realized it was the very same spot where I had talked with Theocles on the second day I was with him in the country. I looked about to see if

What enjoyment, then, must the world provide (that common world of mixed and undistinguished company) without a little solitude; without stepping aside now and then, out of the road and beaten track of life—that tedious circle of noise and show which forces weary mankind to seek relief from every poor diversion?

By your rule, said I, Theocles, there should be no such thing as happiness or good in life, since every enjoyment wears out so soon; and becoming painful, is replaced by some other thing, and that again by some other, and so on. I am sure that if solitude serves as a remedy or diversion to anything in the world, there is nothing which may not serve as a diversion to solitude, which needs it more than anything else. And thus there can be no good which is regular or constant. Happiness is something elusive, and only to be found in wandering.

O Philocles, replied he, I rejoice to find you in the pursuit of happiness and good, however you may wander. Indeed, though you doubt whether such a thing exists, yet if you reason, it is enough; there is still hope. But see how you have unknowingly committed yourself! For if you have destroyed all good because in everything you can think of there is nothing that will remain constant, then you have established it as a maxim (and very justly in my opinion) “that nothing can be good except what is constant.”

the good itself, whatever it may be, depends no less on disposition than on fortune. For what chance may often spare, time will not. Age, a change of temperament, different thoughts, a new passion, new commitments, a new direction in life, or even a conversation—the least of these are fatal and sufficient on their own to destroy enjoyment. Though the object remains the same, the taste for it changes, and the short-lived good expires. But I would be very surprised if you could tell me of anything in life that was not of such a changeable nature, and subject to the same common fate of satiety and disgust.

I find then, he replied, that the current notion of good is not enough to satisfy you. You can afford to be skeptical where no one else would even hesitate; for almost everyone philosophizes dogmatically on this point. Everyone is certain of this: “that our real good is pleasure.”

If they would tell us “which” pleasure, I said, “or what kind,” and define once and for all the very species and distinct type—one that must constantly remain the same and be equally desirable at all times—then perhaps I would be better satisfied. But when “will” and “pleasure” are synonymous; when everything that pleases us is called pleasure,<sup>1</sup> and we never choose or prefer anything except as it pleases us; it is trivial to say “pleasure is our good.” For this has as little meaning as saying, “We choose what we think is worth choosing,” or “We are pleased with what delights or pleases us.” The question is, “Whether we are rightly pleased, and choose as we ought to?” For as highly pleased as children are with baubles, or with whatever affects their tender senses, we cannot in our hearts sincerely admire their enjoyment, or imagine them to be possessors of any extraordinary good. Yet we know their senses are as keen and as susceptible to pleasure as our own. The same reflection applies to mere animals, many of whom have the advantage over us in terms of the liveliness and delicacy of sensation. Would you then appeal, he said, against the immediate feeling and experience of someone who is pleased and satisfied with what they enjoy?

I most certainly would appeal, I said (continuing with the same zeal that <term>Theocles</term> had stirred in me against those who dogmatize about pleasure). Surely you would not ask me to list the various types of sensations that people of certain tastes have adopted and claimed as their chief pleasure and delight. For some men have even thought diseases valuable and worth cherishing, merely for the pleasure found in soothing the intensity of an irritating sensation. And those other people are closely related to these absurd <term>epicures</term>; they use studied stimulants to raise an unnatural thirst and appetite, and then, to make room for more food, prepare emetics <note>substances used to induce vomiting</note> as the final dessert, so they can restart the feast sooner. I know it is said proverbially that "tastes differ, and must not be disputed." And I remember seeing a motto like this once on an emblem, which was considered appropriate for this idea. It showed a fly feeding on a certain lump. The food, however vile, was natural for the animal. There was nothing absurd about it. But if you were to show me a brutish or barbarous man who is similarly occupied and comforted by his pleasure; if you showed me a drunkard in his solitary debauchery, or a tyrant exercising his cruelty, with this motto over him to forbid my appeal—I could hardly be convinced to think better of his enjoyment. Nor can I possibly suppose that a merely sordid wretch, with a base, miserable soul and the best fortune in the world, was ever capable of any real enjoyment.

If all, then every kind of sensuality must be precious and desirable. If only some, then we must seek what kind, and discover, if we can, what distinguishes one pleasure from another, making one indifferent, pitiful, or mean, and another valuable and worthy. Nor can anyone truly judge the value of any immediate sensation without first judging the state of their own mind. For what we consider a happiness in one state of mind is thought of differently in another. We must therefore consider which state is the most just: 'how to gain that perspective from which we may best discern, and how to place ourselves in that unbiased state in which we are most fit to judge.'"

They use this freedom to the fullest by following the first impulse of their will, and agreeing with the first dictate or report of any distracting whim,<note>*Advice to an Author*, part 3, section 2.</note> any immediate opinion or notion of what is good. For often, when they seriously reflect on their past pursuits and commitments, they freely admit "that for the rest of their lives they do not know whether they will remain consistent with themselves, or whether their whims, moods, or passions will later lead them to a completely different choice of pleasure, and to a disapproval of everything they ever enjoyed before." . . . A comforting thought!

"To bring mental satisfactions," he continued, "and the enjoyments of reason and judgment under the name of PLEASURE is merely a deception and a clear departure from the common understanding of the word. Those who, in their philosophical moments, admit something as pleasure which at an ordinary time and in the common practice of life is so little regarded as such, are not dealing fairly with us. The mathematician who labors over his problem, the scholar who toils, the artist who voluntarily endures the greatest hardships and exhaustion—none of these are said 'to follow pleasure.' Nor will 'men of pleasure' by any means accept them as part of their group. The satisfactions that are purely mental and depend only on the movement of a thought must likely be too refined for the understanding of our modern epicures, who are so preoccupied with pleasures of a more physical kind."

But it is this latter sort they promote and magnify when necessary, to avoid the shame that might fall on them from the former. Once this is done, the latter is left to its fate; its usefulness is immediately over. For it is observable that when people of this kind have recommended mental enjoyments under the name of "pleasure"—when they have thus dignified the word and included in it whatever is mentally good or excellent—they can afterwards contentedly let it slide back into its original and common meaning, from which they raised it only to serve a purpose. When pleasure is questioned and attacked, then reason and virtue are called to her aid and made the main parts of her nature. A complex form appears, immediately including everything that is noble, honest, and beautiful in human life. But when the attack is over and the objection is solved, the ghost vanishes; pleasure returns again to her former shape. She may still be called pleasure, and yet have as little to do with dry, sober reason as she really has in reality and according to common understanding. For if this rational kind of enjoyment is included in the concept of "good," how is it possible to also include that kind of sensation which, in effect, is the opposite of this enjoyment? It is certain that regarding the mind and its enjoyments, the eagerness and irritation of pure pleasure is as disturbing as the persistence and distress of pain. If either one throws the mind off its balance and deprives it of the satisfaction it finds in its natural activity and use, the mind in this case must suffer from one as much as the other. If neither does this, there is no harm on either side. . . .

"By the way," I said, interrupting him, "as sincere as I am in questioning 'whether pleasure is really good,' I am not such a skeptic as to doubt 'whether pain is really bad.'"

"Whatever is distressing," he replied, "can be nothing other than bad. But what is distressing to one is not even troublesome..."

In short then, I said, if pleasure and pain are thus interchangeable and mixed; if, according to your account, "that which is now pleasure, by being strained a little too far, turns into pain, and pain, when carried far, creates again the highest pleasure simply by stopping and through a kind of natural succession; if some pleasures are pains to some, and some pains are pleasures to others"; all this, if I am not mistaken, still supports my opinion and shows that there is nothing you can identify that can really be established as good. For if pleasure is not good, then nothing is. And if pain is bad (as I must necessarily assume), we have a strong chance of experiencing the bad side indeed, but no chance at all of the better. So we may reasonably doubt "whether life itself is not mere misery," since we can never be gainers by it; we can certainly be losers, and are likely to be so every hour of our lives. "It is enough," said Theocles, "I accept the terms; and if you promise to love, I will endeavor to show you that beauty which I count the most perfect and most deserving of love, and which will not fail to return that affection. . . . "...necessary to be first a friend to mankind." But how to qualify myself for such a friendship was, I thought, no small difficulty.

"Indeed," said Theocles, "you have given us a very poor account of yourself by saying so. If you had spoken this way about the friendship of any great man at court, or perhaps of a court itself, and had complained 'how hard it was for you to succeed, or gain influence with those who governed there,' we would have concluded on your behalf that there were conditions you had to meet that were unworthy of you. "How does it happen then," I asked, "that even these good terms themselves are so poorly accepted, and hardly ever taken (if I may put it that way) except on further conditions? "They are children indeed," replied Theocles, "and should be treated as such, if they need any force or persuasion to do what leads to their own health and well-being. “Gentlemen,” I said, “the descriptions you have been making are, no doubt, the finest in the world; but after all, when you have made virtue as glorious and triumphant as you please, I will bring you a true picture of another kind, where we shall see this triumph reversed: ‘Virtue herself a captive in her turn; triumphed over by a proud conqueror, degraded, stripped of all her honors, and defaced, so that she retains hardly a single feature of real beauty.’”

I offered to go further, but could not, being so violently denounced by my two fellow-guests, who protested they would never be brought to admit such a detestable picture. One of them (a formal sort of gentleman, somewhat advanced in years), looking intently at me, said in an angry tone that he had, until now, indeed held some hope for me, even though he observed my freedom of thought and heard me quoted as such a passionate lover of liberty. But he was sorry to find that my principle of liberty ultimately extended to a “liberty from all principles” (as he expressed himself), and he thought that “none except a libertine in principle would approve of such a picture of virtue, which only an atheist could have the audacity to create.”

*Theocles* meanwhile sat silent, though he saw I paid no attention to my opponents but kept my eye fixed steadily on him, waiting to hear what he would say. At last, letting out a deep sigh, “O *Philocles*,” he said, “how well you are master of that...”

How many religious authors, how many sacred orators, turn all their sharpest arguments this way and strike at moral virtue as a kind of stepmother or rival to religion! “Morality must not be mentioned; Nature has no claim; reason is an enemy; common justice is folly; and virtue is misery. Some of them hold zealously to virtue and are <term>realists</term> on this point. Others, one might say, are only <term>nominal moralists</term>, making virtue nothing in itself—a product of will alone, or a mere name dictated by fashion. It is the same in <term>natural philosophy</term>: some adopt one hypothesis and some another. I would be glad to finally discover the true foundation, and to distinguish those who effectively refute their other antagonists as well as the atheists, and who correctly uphold the shared cause of virtue and religion."

Here, Palemon, I got my wish. For by degrees, I prompted Theocles to reveal his views fully on these subjects, which served as a prelude to those we were to discuss the next morning—an arrival for which I longed impatiently. If his speculations proved to be of a rational kind, I knew this previous discourse would help me understand them; if they were only pleasant fancies, it would at least help me to enjoy them more.

Then began his critique of authors, which gradually grew into a continuous discourse. So much so that, had this taken place at a university, Theocles might very well have passed for some solemn professor of divinity or a teacher of <term>ethics</term>, reading an afternoon lecture to his students.

We all answered for ourselves, and he began thus:—

Of the many writers engaged in the defense of religion, it seems to me that the majority are employed either in supporting the truth of the Christian faith in general, or in refuting specific doctrines that are considered innovations in the Christian Church. It is thought that there are not many people in the world who are loose in the very foundations and principles of all religion; and we find that there are indeed not many writers who deliberately apply themselves to such people. They may think it a lowly task, and hardly becoming of them, to argue calmly with those who are almost universally treated with detestation and horror. But as we are required by our religion to have charity for all people, we surely cannot avoid having a real concern for those whom we believe to be under the worst of errors, and whom we find by experience to be the most difficult to reclaim. Nor, perhaps, should those whose numbers—however small—are thought to be increasing be treated with so little regard, especially since this is happening among people of no insignificant social rank. Thus, it may well deserve some consideration "whether the same remedies that have been tried until now can still serve in our age and country, or whether some others might be preferred as being more suitable to times of less strictness in religious matters and places less subject to authority."

He offers to conclude nothing positive himself, but leaves it to others to draw conclusions from his principles; having this one chief aim and intention: "how, in the first place, to reconcile these persons to the principles of virtue; that by this means a way might be laid open to religion, by removing those greatest, if not only obstacles to it, which arise from the vices and passions of men."

It is on this account that he endeavors chiefly to establish virtue on principles by which he is able to argue with those who are not yet induced to acknowledge a God or a future state. If he cannot do at least this much, he considers that he does nothing. For how can supreme goodness be intelligible to those who do not know what goodness itself is? Or how can virtue be understood to deserve reward, when its merit and excellence are as yet unknown? We surely begin at the wrong end when we would prove merit by favor, and order by a Deity. ...as a realist, he endeavors to show "that it is really something in itself, and in the nature of things; not arbitrary or factitious (if I may speak so); not constituted from without, or dependent on custom, fancy, or will; not even on the supreme will itself, which can in no way govern it; but being necessarily good, is governed by it and is ever uniform with it." I would not willingly propose it as a rule "that those who make only a name of virtue make no more of Deity, and cannot without affectation defend the principles of religion"; but this I will venture to assert, "that whoever sincerely defends virtue, and is a realist in morality, must of necessity, in a manner, by the same scheme of reasoning, prove to be just as much a realist in divinity."

All affectation, but especially in philosophy, I must own, I think is unpardonable. And you, *Philocles*, who can give no quarter to bad reasoning, nor endure any unsound or inconsistent hypothesis; you will be so frank, I dare say, as to reject our modern *Deism*, and challenge those who assume a name to which their philosophy can never in the least entitle them.

Commend me to honest *Epicurus*, who raises his deities aloft in the imaginary spaces, and setting them apart outside the universe and the nature of things, makes nothing of them beyond a word. This is frank and plain dealing; for this every one who philosophizes may easily understand.

The same frankness belongs to those philosophers whom you, *Philocles*, seem inclined to favor. When a skeptic questions "whether a real theology can be raised out of philosophy alone, without the help of revelation," he does no more than pay a handsome compliment to authority and the established religion. He can deceive no one who reasons deeply; since whoever does so will easily conceive that at this rate theology must have no foundation at all. For revelation itself, we know, is founded on the acknowledgment of a divine existence; and it is

the province of philosophy alone to prove what revelation only assumes.

I consider it, therefore, a very unfair approach for those who wish to be builders and undertake this task of proving, to lay such a foundation that is insufficient to support the structure. Overthrowing and undermining may be fair in other types of war, but in philosophical disputes, it is not permissible to work underground, or as in sieges, by tunneling. Nothing can be more unbecoming than to speak authoritatively and in solemn terms of "a supreme Nature, an infinite Being, and a Deity," when all the while a providence is never intended, nor is anything like order or the government of a mind acknowledged. For when these are understood and real divinity is acknowledged, the concept is not dry and barren; instead, such consequences are necessarily drawn from it that must move us to action and find employment for our strongest emotions. All the duties of religion clearly follow from this, and no objection remains against any of those great maxims which revelation has established.

Now, whether our friend is genuinely and sincerely one of these real theologians, you will learn best from the consequences of his hypothesis. You will observe whether, instead of ending in mere speculation, it leads to practice; and you will then surely be satisfied when you see such a structure built that, for the majority of the world, it must pass at least for high religion, and for some, in all likelihood, for nothing less than enthusiasm.

For I appeal to you, *Philocles*, whether there is anything in divinity that you think has more the appearance of enthusiasm than that notion of divine love which separates itself from everything worldly, sensual, or selfishly motivated? It is a love that is simple, pure, and unmixed, which has no other object than the excellence of that being itself, and admits of no other thought of happiness than in the enjoyment of that being alone. It is true that even if appearances hold ever so strongly against virtue and in favor of vice, the objection that arises from this against a Deity may be easily removed and everything set right again by the supposition of a future state. This is sufficient to clear every dark cloud of Providence for a *Christian*, or someone already convinced of such a great point. For he does not need to be excessively anxious about the fate of virtue in this world if he is secure about the *hereafter*. But the case is different for the people we must encounter here. They are at a loss regarding Providence and seek to find it in the world. Exaggerating the appearing disorders in worldly affairs, and presenting the darkest representation of society and human nature, will hardly help them toward this view. It will be difficult for them to read Providence in such signs. From such an unappealing face of things below, they will venture to think unfavorably of everything above. Based on the effects they see, they will be inclined to judge the *cause*, and judge *providence* by the *fate* of virtue. But once they are convinced of order and providence regarding present things, they may soon, perhaps, be satisfied even regarding a future state. The proper order in this world may lead us to conceive of a further structure. We grasp a larger scheme and easily understand why things were not completed in this state, but their fulfillment reserved instead for some later period. For if the good and virtuous of mankind had been entirely prosperous in this life; if goodness had never met with opposition, nor merit ever lain under a cloud; where would have been the trial, victory, or crown of virtue? Where would the virtues have had their stage, or from where would they get their names? Where would have been temperance or self-denial? Where would be patience, meekness, or magnanimity? From where do these have their being? What merit exists except from hardship? What virtue exists without a conflict, and the encounter with such enemies as arise both from within and from abroad?

But however many difficulties Virtue has to encounter in this world, her power is still superior. Exposed as she is here, she is not, however, abandoned or left miserable. She has enough to raise her above pity, though not above our desires, and as happy as we see her here, we have room for further hopes on her behalf. Her current portion is sufficient to show Providence is already engaged on her side. And since there is such provision for her here—such happiness and such advantages even in this life—how probable must it appear that this providential care is extended even further to a succeeding life, and perfected hereafter?

This is what, in our friend’s opinion, may be said in favor of a future state to those who question revelation. It is this that must make revelation probable and secure the first step toward it: the belief in a Deity and Providence. A providence must be proved from the order we see in present things. We must argue for order; and in this area especially, where virtue is concerned, not everything must be deferred to a hereafter. For a disordered state, in which all present care of things is abandoned, vice is uncontrolled, and virtue is neglected, represents a total chaos; it reduces us to the beloved atoms, chance, and confusion of the atheists. Those who intend to turn people toward thoughts of a better world by making them think so poorly of this one are greatly mistaken. For to speak against virtue in this way to those with less faith will make them believe in a Deity less, rather than believing more in a future state. Nor can it be sincerely thought that any person, by holding the highest opinion of virtue and the happiness it creates, was ever less inclined to believe in a future state. On the contrary, it will always be found that just as those who favor vice are always the least willing to hear of a future existence, those who love virtue are the most ready to embrace the opinion that makes it so glorious and ensures its cause is triumphant.

Thus, among the ancients, the great motive that inclined many of the wisest to believe this doctrine (though it was not revealed to them) was purely the love of virtue seen in those great men—the founders and protectors of societies, the legislators, patriots, liberators, and heroes—whose virtues they wished to see live on and be immortalized. Nor is there anything today more capable of making this belief attractive to the good and virtuous than the love of friendship, which creates in them a desire not to be completely separated by death, but rather to enjoy the same blessed company in the hereafter. How is it possible, then, that an author should be considered an enemy to a future state simply for exalting virtue? How can our friend be judged unfaithful to religion for defending a principle upon which the very concept of God and goodness depends? For he says only this, and this is the sum of it all:

> “That by building a future state upon the ruins of virtue, religion in general and the cause of a Deity are betrayed; and by making rewards and punishments the primary motives for duty, the Christian religion in particular is overthrown, and its greatest principle—that of love—is rejected and abandoned.”

Overall, then, we may justly as well as charitably conclude that the author's true design in addressing himself so fairly to those of loose principles is to lead them to such an understanding of the nature of mankind and of human affairs that it might form in them a notion of order in things. If I were to go further, I might be deeply engaged in spiritual matters and be forced to create some new model of a sermon based on his system of divinity. However, I hope that now, since matters have truly come very close to preaching, you will excuse me for what I have already performed."

## SECTION IV

Just as he had finished speaking, some visitors arrived, who occupied the rest of our afternoon with other conversations. But once these were over and our guests had gone (all except the old gentleman and his friend, who had dined with us), we began again with Theocles by claiming his "sermon" and begging him repeatedly to let us hear him at length in his theological way.

He complained that this was persecuting him. "As you have often seen a group," he said, "frequently persecute a reputed singer, not out of any love for the music, but to satisfy a malicious kind of curiosity, which usually ends in criticism and dislike."

However it might be, we told him we were resolved to persist. And I assured our companions that if they would support me heartily in the way I intended to press him, we should easily succeed.

"In revenge then," said he, "I will comply on this condition: that since I am to take the part of the theologian <note>The original uses "the divine."</note> and preacher, it shall be at Philocles’s expense, who shall play the part of the unbeliever and be the person preached to."

"Truly," said the old gentleman, "the part you have proposed for him is so natural and suitable that I do not doubt he will be able to act it without the least effort. I could instead wish that you had spared yourself the trouble of reminding him of his proper character. He would have been likely enough on his own to interrupt your discourse with his perpetual objections. Therefore, since we have now had enough entertainment through dialogue, I desire that the rules of a sermon be strictly observed: 'that there be no answering whatever is argued or advanced.'"

I consented to all the terms and told Theocles I would willingly be his target. Besides, if I really were that unbeliever he was to imagine me to be, I should consider it no misfortune, since I was sure of being thoroughly convinced by him if he would deign to take me on.

Theocles then proposed we should walk out, as the evening was fine and the open air suited such discussions better (as he thought) than a room.

Accordingly, we took our evening walk in the fields, from where the hardworking laborers <note>The original uses "hinds."</note> were now retiring. We naturally began to praise country life and talked for a while about <term>husbandry</term> and the nature of the soil. Our friends began to admire some of the plants which grew there to great perfection. And it being my luck (having acquired a little insight into the nature of <term>simples</term>) to say something they greatly approved of on this subject, Theocles immediately turning to me, said, “O my ingenious friend!”

“Now, in this mighty union, if there are such relations between parts as are not easily discovered—if, for this reason, the purpose and use of things do not appear everywhere—it is no wonder, since it is indeed nothing more than what must necessarily happen; nor could supreme wisdom have ordered it otherwise. For in an infinity of related things, a mind that does not see infinitely can see nothing fully; and since each particular part relates to the whole in general, it can know no perfect or true relation of anything in a world that is not perfectly and fully known.

"But if you would willingly explore this thought further and consider how much we ought not only to be satisfied with our view of things but even to admire its clarity, imagine someone entirely a stranger to navigation and ignorant of the nature of the sea or waters. How easily would he see that the whole is one regular structure, with all things depending on one another: the uses of the rooms below, the quarters, and the conveniences for men and supplies? But being ignorant of the intent or design of everything above deck, would he pronounce the masts and rigging to be useless and cumbersome, and for this reason condemn the frame and despise the architect? O my friend! Let us not betray our ignorance in this way, but consider where we are and in what a universe. Think of the many parts of the vast machine into which we have so little insight, and whose ends and uses it is impossible for us to know, when—instead of seeing the highest pennants—we see only some lower deck and are in this dark casing of flesh, confined even to the hold and the lowliest station of the vessel.

Our temperament is the only thing left ungoverned, while it governs everything else.

The beauty of the river, the sea, the heavens, and the heavenly constellations all flow from here as from a source eternal and incorruptible. As beings participate in this, they are fair, flourishing, and happy; as they lose connection to this, they are deformed, perished, and lost.”

When Theocles had finished speaking, he was formally complimented by our two companions. I was going to add something in the same manner, but he immediately stopped me, saying he would be scandalized if, instead of praising him, I did not choose—according to my character—rather to criticize some part or another of his long discourse.

"If it must be so then," I replied, "in the first place, allow me to wonder why, instead of the many arguments commonly brought as proof of a <term>deity</term>, you use only a single one to build upon. But regarding all of this, you are silent."

As for what is said about “A material, unthinking substance being never able to have produced an immaterial, thinking one,” I readily grant it, but only on the condition that this great maxim—of nothing ever being made from nothing—may hold as well on my side as on my adversary’s. And then, I suppose, that as long as the world lasts, he will be at a loss for how to assign a beginning to matter, or how to suggest a possibility of destroying it. The spiritual men may, as long as they please, represent to us in the most eloquent manner, “That matter, considered in a thousand different shapes, joined and separated, varied and modified to eternity, can never, of itself, provide one single thought, nor ever cause or give rise to anything like sense or knowledge.” Their argument holds up against a Democritus, an Epicurus, or any of the ancient or modern <term>atomists</term>. But it will be turned back on them by an inquiring <term>Academist</term>; and when the two substances are fairly set apart and considered separately as different kinds, it will be just as logical and just as good an argument to say the same of the immaterial kind: “Do with it as you please—modify it a thousand ways, purify it, exalt it, refine it, torture it as much as you like, or rack it, as they say, with thinking—you will never be able to produce or force the opposite substance out of it.” The lowly dregs of wretched matter can no more be made out of the simple, pure substance of immaterial thought than the high spirits of thought or reason can be extracted from the gross substance of heavy matter. So let the <term>dogmatists</term> make of this argument what they can.

“But for your part,” I continued, “as you have stated the question, it is not about what was first or foremost, but what is instant and now in being. ‘For if a deity really exists now, and if by any good sign it appears that there is at this present a universal mind, it will easily be granted that there always was one.’ . . . This is your argument. . . . You rely (if I may say so) upon fact, and would prove that things actually are in such a state and condition; if they truly were, there would indeed be”

He presses hard upon our frontier, and one day, likely, shall by a furious invasion recover his lost right, conquer his rebel state, and reunite us to primitive discord and confusion."

This, I said, Theocles! (concluding my discourse) is all I dare offer in opposition to your philosophy. I imagined, indeed, you might have given me more scope; but you have retreated into narrower bounds. So that, to tell you the truth, I look upon your theology to be hardly as fair or open as that of our clergymen in general. They are strict, it is true, regarding names, but allow a greater latitude in things. They can hardly bear a direct attack, a downright questioning of the deity; but in return they always give fair play against Nature, and allow her to be challenged for her failings. She may freely err, and we as freely criticize her. The deity, they think, is not accountable for her.

"Do not let this trouble you," replied *Theocles*, "but feel free to criticize Nature, whatever the consequence may be. It is only my hypothesis that can suffer. I leave them to dispute this ground with you whenever they see fit. As for my own arguments, if they can be considered part of this defense at all, they may be viewed only as distant lines or outer fortifications, which might perhaps be easily won, but without any danger to the main fortress."

"Even though you are willing," I said, "for me to attack Nature formally, I choose to spare her on all other subjects except man. Why is it, I ask you, that in this noblest of creatures—the one most worthy of her care—she should appear so very weak and powerless, while in mere animals and irrational species she acts with so much strength and exerts such hardy vigor? Why is her power exhausted so soon in feeble man, who is found more subject to diseases and lives for fewer years than many of the wild creatures? They roam securely, resistant to all the injuries of the seasons and weather; they need no help from human art but live in carefree ease, exempt from labor and freed from the cumbersome baggage of a needy human life. More capable in infancy, vigorous in old age, with quicker senses and more natural wisdom, they pursue their interests, joys, and recreations. They cheaply obtain both their food and upkeep, clothed and armed by Nature herself, who provides them with both a bed and a home. This is how Nature has provided for the rest of the creatures. Such is their hardiness, robustness, and vigor. Why is it not the same for man? . . ."

What duty or obligation would have ever been thought of? What respect or reverence for parents, magistrates, their country, or their kind? Would not their full and self-sufficient state have more strongly driven them to cast off Nature, and deny the purposes and author of their creation?"

So that either a hundred different states of Nature must be counted, or if only one, it can be only that in which Nature was perfect and her growth complete. Here, where she rested and attained her end, must be her state, or nowhere.

Could she then rest, do you think, in that desolate state before society? Could she maintain and propagate the species, such as it now is, without fellowship or community? Show it to us.

He must have better provisions and choicer food than raw grass; a better bed and covering than the bare earth or open sky. How many other kinds of conveniences does he need? What union and strict society is required between the sexes to preserve and nurse their growing offspring? This kind of society will surely not be denied to man, which is known to be appropriate and natural to every beast of prey. And can we allow this social nature to man and go no further? Is it possible he should pair, and live in love and fellowship with his partner and offspring, and still remain wholly wild and speechless, without those arts of storing, building, and other economy, which are surely as natural to him as to the beaver, or to the ant or bee? Where, therefore, should he break off from this society once it has begun? For it is plain that it began this way, as early as procreation, and grew into a household and economy.

Tombs and churchyards were not such powerful scenes to me as the mountains, the plains, the solemn woods and groves, whose inhabitants I much preferred to hear about than those of the other. And I was more ready to imagine truth in those poetic fictions which Theocles used than in any of his friend’s ghastly stories, so pompously presented in the usual way, with a lofty tone of authority and an air of assuming they were true.

However, I am still charitable enough to think there is more innocent delusion than voluntary trickery in the world, and that those who have most deceived mankind have been fortunate in a certain ability to first deceive themselves; by this, they have a kind of excuse for their consciences, and are all the more successful as they can act their part more naturally and realistically. Nor should it be considered a riddle that men's dreams should sometimes have the good fortune of being taken by them for truth, when we consider that in some cases, something that was never even dreamed of, or related as truth, comes afterward to be believed by someone who has often told it.

So that the greatest impostor in the world, he replied, may at this rate be considered sincere.
