Taking it for granted then, I replied, that simplicity and weakness are more characteristic of the credulous than of the unbelieving, I still do not see how we are not just as liable to suffer by our weakness in this case as in the contrary case through an over-refined wit. For if we cannot command our own belief, how are we secure against those false prophets and their deluding miracles of which we have been given such warning? How are we safe from heresy and false religion? Credulity is that which delivers us up to all impostures of this sort, and which actually at this day holds the Pagan and Mahometan <note>Muslim</note> world in error and blind superstition. Either, therefore, there is no punishment due to wrong belief, because we cannot believe as we wish, or if we can, why should we not promise never to believe incorrectly? Now, in respect to miracles to come, the surest way never to believe incorrectly is never to believe at all. For being satisfied of the truth of our religion by past miracles, so as to need no others to confirm us, the belief in new ones may often do us harm, but can never do us good. Therefore, as the truest mark of a believing Christian is to seek after no future sign or miracle, so the safest position in Christianity is his who can be moved by nothing of this kind, and is thus miracle-proof. This question, upon further debate, happened to divide our two companions. For the elderly gentleman, my opponent, maintained "that the giving up of miracles for the present time would be of great advantage to the atheists." The younger gentleman, his companion, questioned "whether allowing them might not be of just as much advantage to the fanatics <note>enthusiasts</note> and religious dissenters <note>sectaries</note> against the national church; he thought this was the greater of the two dangers, both to religion and the state." He told us quite amusingly what an adventurer he had been in that regard, and how many groups he had joined, involving a type of people who were always on the hot scent of some new marvel or apparition, some sudden revelation or prophecy. This, he thought, was true wandering fanaticism. He had seen enough of this visionary pursuit and would wander no more in dark corners of the world, as he had previously been accustomed, in the ghostly company of spirit-hunters, witch-finders, and those seeking out hellish stories and diabolical events. There was no need, he thought, for such reports from hell to prove the power of heaven and the existence of a God. And now at last he began to see the absurdity of placing such importance on these matters, as if a providence

The heathens, he said, who lacked Scripture, might resort to miracles; and Providence perhaps had allowed them their oracles and wonders as an imperfect kind of revelation. The Jews too, because of their stubborn hearts and even more stubborn understandings, were granted this allowance when they stubbornly asked for signs and wonders. But Christians, for their part, had a far better and truer revelation; they had clearer oracles, a more rational law, and clearer Scripture, which carried its own weight and was, moreover, so well attested as to admit no dispute. And if I were to assign the exact time when miracles probably first ceased, he continued, I would be tempted to imagine it was when Sacred Writ was established and completed.

This is a notion indeed, replied the grave gentleman, and a very dangerous one for that Scripture which you claim is so well attested by itself. The testimony of men long dead, on behalf of miracles past and over, can surely never be of equal force with miracles present; and of these, I maintain, a sufficient number are never lacking in the world to guarantee a divine existence. If there were no miracles nowadays, the world would be inclined to think there never were any. The present must account for the credibility of the past. This is “God witnessing for Himself,” not “men witnessing for God.” For who shall witness for men if, in matters of religion, they have no testimony from heaven on their behalf?

What might make the reports of men credible, said the younger gentleman, is another question. But as for mere miracles, it seems to me that they cannot properly be said “to witness either for God or men.” For who shall witness for the miracles themselves? And even if they are ever so certain, what security do we have that they are not performed by demons? What—

The young gentleman, I saw, was somewhat intimidated by this harsh treatment from his friend, who was still continuing his verbal attack. No then, I said, interposing, it is I who must answer for this young gentleman, whom you label as my disciple. And since his modesty, I see, will not allow him to pursue what he has so handsomely begun, I will attempt it myself, if he will give me leave.

The young gentleman agreed, and I went on explaining his fair intention of establishing, first of all, a rational and just foundation for our faith, so as to defend it from the charge of having no immediate miracles to support it. He would have done this, I said, undoubtedly by showing what good proof we already had for our sacred oracles from the testimony of the dead, whose characters and lives might vouch for them regarding the truth of what they reported to us from God. This, however, was by no means “witnessing for God,” as the zealous gentleman had hastily expressed himself, for this was beyond the reach of either men or miracles. Nor could God witness for himself, or assert his existence to men in any other way, than “by revealing himself to their reason, appealing to their judgment, and submitting his ways to their evaluation and calm deliberation.” The contemplation of the universe, its laws and government, was, I maintained, the only means which could establish a sound belief in a Deity. For what if innumerable miracles from every direction assailed the senses and gave the trembling soul no rest? What if the sky should suddenly open and all kinds of prodigies appear, voices be heard, or signs be read? What would this prove more than “that there were certain powers that could do all this”?

“what powers, whether one or more, whether superior or subordinate, mortal or immortal, wise or foolish, just or unjust, good or bad”; this would still remain a mystery, as would the true intention, the infallibility, or the certainty of whatever those powers asserted. Their word could not be taken in their own case. They might indeed silence men, but not convince them; since “power can never serve as proof of goodness,¹ and goodness is the only pledge of truth.” Trust is created by goodness alone. By goodness, superior powers may win belief. They must allow their works to be examined and their actions criticized; and thus, and only thus, can they be trusted: “When their benevolence is proved by repeated signs, and their character of sincerity and truth established.” Therefore, to the person for whom the laws of this universe and its government appear just and uniform, they speak of the government of one Just One; to him they reveal and bear witness to a God; and by laying the foundation of this first faith in him, they prepare him for a subsequent one.² He can then listen to historical revelation, and is then prepared (and not until then) to receive any message or miraculous notice from above, where he knows beforehand that all is just and true. But no power of miracles, nor any power besides his reason, can make him know or understand this.

But now, I continued, since I have been the defendant for so long, I am resolved to take up offensive weapons and be the aggressor in my turn, provided Theocles is not angry with me for borrowing ground from his hypothesis.

Whatever you borrow from him, replied my antagonist, you are almost certain to spoil; and as it passes through your hands, you had better beware lest you seem to reflect poorly on him rather than on me.

By searching heaven and earth for wonders, and studying how to turn everything into a miracle, you bring confusion to the world. You break its uniformity and destroy that admirable simplicity of order from which the one infinite and perfect principle is known. Perpetual strife, convulsions, violence, breaches of laws, and the variation and unsteadiness of order show either a lack of control or several uncontrolled and unsubordinated powers in Nature. We have before our eyes either the chaos and atoms of the **atheists**, or the magic and demons of the **polytheists**. Yet this tumultuous system of the universe is asserted with the greatest zeal by some who wish to uphold a **Deity**. This is the face of things, and these are the features by which they represent divinity. The eyes of our more inquisitive and candid youth are turned toward this view with care, lest they see anything other than this perplexed and bewildering perspective—as if **atheism** were the most natural conclusion that could be drawn from a regular and orderly state of things! But after all this mangling and disfigurement of Nature, if it happens (as it often does) that the bewildered student, coming to his senses and searching leisurely into Nature's ways, finds more order, uniformity, and constancy in things than he suspected, he is, of course, driven toward **atheism**. This happens merely because of the impressions he received from that absurd system which taught him to seek for a **Deity** in confusion and to discover **Providence** in an irregular, disjointed world.

"And when you," he replied, "with your newly adopted system, have made all things as uniform, plain, regular, and simple as you could wish, I suppose you will send your student to seek for a **Deity** in mechanism—that is to say, in some exquisite system of self-governed matter. For what else do you **naturalists** make of the world than a mere machine?"

"Nothing else," I replied, "if you allow the machine to have a mind. For in this case, it is not a self-governed but a **God-governed machine**."

"And what are the signs," he said, "which should convince—"

The ones we have now, I replied, are sufficient. It could not possibly give stronger signs of life and steady thought. Compare our own machines with this great one, and see whether, by their order, management, and motions, they signify either such a perfect life or such a complete intelligence. The one is regular, steady, and permanent; the others are irregular, variable, and inconstant. In one there are the marks of wisdom and determination; in the other, of whim and conceit. In one, judgment appears; in the other, only fancy. In one, will; in the other, caprice. In one, truth, certainty, and knowledge; in the other, error, folly, and madness. But to be convinced there is something above that thinks and acts, we seem to require the latter of these signs, as if we supposed there could be no thought or intelligence besides what is like our own. We grow sick and weary of the orderly and regular course of things. Cycles, established laws, and revolutions—just and proportional—do not affect us or win our admiration. We must have riddles, miracles, and matters for surprise and horror! Through harmony, order, and concord, we are made atheists; through irregularity and discord, we are convinced of a Deity!

> "The world is mere accident if it proceeds in its normal course, but an effect of wisdom if it runs mad!"

In this way, I took on the role of a sound theist while I endeavored to refute my antagonist and show that his principles favored atheism. The zealous gentleman took great offense, and we continued debating warmly until late at night. But Theocles acted as moderator, and we finally retired to our rest, all calm and friendly. However, I was not a little rejoiced to hear that our companions were to leave early the next morning and leave Theocles alone with me.

## PART III

### SECTION I

**I**t was still deep night (as I imagined) when I woke with the noise of people up in the house. I called to find out what was the matter and was told that Theocles had, a little before, parted with his friends, after which he went out to take his morning walk, but would return, they thought, quite soon: for so he had left word, and that nobody in the meantime should disturb my rest.

This was disturbance enough when I heard it. I immediately got up, and finding it light enough to see the hill, which was a short distance from the house, I soon went there, and at the foot of it overtook Theocles, to whom I complained of his unkindness. For I was certainly not (I told him) so effeminate and weak a friend as to deserve that he should treat me like a woman; nor had I shown such an aversion to his manners or conversation as to be thought more fit for the dull luxury of a soft bed and ease than for business, recreation, or study with an early friend. He had no other way, therefore, of making amends to me than by allowing me from now on to share in his serious thoughts, as he saw I was resolved to be part of his hours and exercises of this kind.

Here he stopped short, and starting as if out of a dream, he said, “Now, Philocles, inform me: how have I appeared to you in my fit? Did it seem a sensible kind of madness, like those transports permitted to our poets? Or was it downright raving?”

For I was beginning to see wonders in that Nature you taught me, and was coming to know the hand of your divine Artificer. But if you stop here, I shall lose the enjoyment of the pleasing vision. And already I begin to find a thousand difficulties in imagining such a universal genius as you describe.”

“Why,” he said, “is there any difficulty in imagining the universe to be one entire thing? From what is visible, can one think of it otherwise than as everything hanging together as a single piece? Grant that; and what follows? Only this: that if it may indeed be said of the world ‘that it is simply one,’ there should be something belonging to it which makes it one.”

“In what way?”

“In no other way than what you may observe in everything. For example, in what we see before us: I know you look upon the trees of this vast forest to be different from one another; and this tall oak, the noblest of the company—just as it is by itself a different thing from all its fellows in the forest, yet with its own wood of numerous spreading branches (which seem like so many different trees), it is still, I suppose, one and the same tree. “At this rate indeed,” I said, “you have found a way to make very adorable places of these forest dwellings. “We wrong them then,” replied Theocles, “to say ‘they belong to these trees,’ and not rather that ‘these trees belong to them.’ But as for their immortality, let them look to that themselves. "What you philosophers are," I replied, "may perhaps be hard to determine; but for the rest of mankind, I can confidently say that few remain themselves for even three and a half years. It is good fortune if a man remains one and the same person for even a day or two. A single year brings more revolutions than can be numbered."

"True," he said; "but though this may happen to a man—and especially to one whose conflicting vices so often put him at odds with himself—yet when he comes to suffer or be punished for those vices, he finds himself, if I am not mistaken, still one and the same person. And you, Philocles, who—though you reject philosophy—are yet such a devoted follower of <term>Pyrrhonism</term>, should you at last feel the power of the Genius I preach and be persuaded to accept the divine hypothesis, admitting a total change in all your principles and opinions through this new way of thinking, you would still be the very same Philocles. You would simply be a better version, in my opinion, than the present one, much as I love and value him. You see, therefore, there is a remarkable singleness in this 'you' and 'me,' in that they should really remain one and the same when not one atom of the body, not one passion, nor one thought remains unchanged. As for that weak attempt to prove this sameness or identity of being through some unchanging matter or particle of matter that is supposed to stay with us when everything else changes, it is all the more foolish because matter itself is not really capable of such..."

But whatever is supposed of uncompounded matter (a thing at best quite difficult to conceive), continued Theocles, yet when it is compounded and put together in a certain number of parts that unite and work together in these bodies of ours and others like them, if it can present us with so many innumerable instances of particular forms which share this simple principle—by which they are really *One*, live, act, and have a nature or genius peculiar to themselves and mindful of their own welfare—how shall we at the same time overlook this in the whole and deny the great and general *One* of the world? How can we be so unnatural as to disown divine Nature, our common parent, and refuse to recognize the universal and sovereign Genius?

Sovereigns, I said, require no notice to be taken of them when they travel *incognito*, nor any homage where they do not appear in due form. We may even have reason to assume they would be displeased with us for being too meddlesome in trying to discover them when they keep themselves either wholly invisible or in very dark disguise. As for the notice we take of these invisible powers in the ordinary practice of our religion, we have our visible sovereigns to answer for us. Our lawful superiors teach us what we are to acknowledge and perform in worship. And we are dutiful in complying with them and following their example. But in a philosophical way, I find no justification for our being such earnest recognizers of a disputed title. However that may be, you must at least allow one to understand the controversy and know the nature of these described powers. May one not inquire, "of what substances are they made? whether material or immaterial?"

"Allow me then, good Philocles," he replied, "the same privilege of skepticism in this respect, since it does not affect the matter before us which way we decide, or whether we reach any decision at all on this point. "Bless me," I said, "Theocles, into what a superstition you are likely to lead me! "I must confess," said I, "that by this reckoning, the presumption is entirely on your side. Yet this is still only a presumption."

"Take a demonstration then," said he, "if you can tolerate me reasoning so abstractly and dryly. The appearances of evil, you say, are not necessarily the evil they represent to us."

"I admit it."

"Therefore, what they represent may possibly be good."

"It may."

"And therefore there may possibly be no real evil in things, but everything may perfectly coincide with one interest—the interest of that universal ONE."

"It may be so."

"Well, then, if it may be so (do not be surprised), 'it follows that it must be so,' because of that great unity and simple self-principle which you have granted exists in the whole. For whatever is possible for the whole, the nature or mind of the whole will put into execution for the good of the whole; and if it is possible to exclude evil, it will exclude it. Therefore, since despite the appearances, it is possible that evil may actually be excluded, you can count on the fact 'that it actually is excluded.' For nothing merely passive can oppose this universally active principle. If anything active opposes it, that would be another principle."

"I allow it."

"It is impossible. For if there were two or more principles in nature, they would either have to agree or not. If they do not agree, everything must be in confusion until one becomes predominant. If they do agree, there must be some natural reason for their agreement; and this natural reason cannot come from chance, but from some particular design, contrivance, or thought, which brings us back again to ONE principle and makes the other two subordinate. And thus, when we have compared each of the three opinions—namely, 'that there is no designing active principle,' 'that there is more than one,' or 'that finally there is but ONE'—we will perceive that the only consistent opinion is the last one. And since one or another of these opinions must necessarily be true, what can we conclude other than that the last one is, and must be so, demonstrably? If it is a demonstration 'that among three opinions,"

infinity of bodies, each belonging (as we may well presume) to systems as complete as our own world, since even the smallest spark of this bright galaxy may rival our own sun, which, shining now in full, gives us new life, exalts our spirits, and makes us feel divinity more present.

“Prodigious orb! Bright source of vital heat, and spring of day! . . . Soft flame, yet how intense, how active! How diffusive, and how vast a substance; yet how collected thus within itself, and in a glowing mass confined to the center of this planetary world! . . . Mighty being! Brightest image and representative of the Almighty! Supreme of the corporeal world! Unperishing in grace, and of undecaying youth! Fair, beautiful, and hardly mortal creature! By what secret ways do you receive the supplies which maintain you still in such unwearied vigor and unexhausted glory; notwithstanding those externally emitted streams and that continual expenditure of vital treasures which enlighten and invigorate the surrounding worlds? . . .

“Around him all the planets, with this our earth, alone or with attendants, continually move, seeking to receive the blessing of his light and lively warmth! Toward him they seem to tend, with a downward descent, as to their center, but fortunately controlled still by another impulse, they keep their heavenly order; and in precise numbers and exactest measure, go their eternal rounds.

But, O you who are the author and modifier of these various motions! O sovereign and sole mover, by whose high art the rolling spheres are governed, and these stupendous bodies of our world hold their unrelenting courses! O wise economist <note>manager or steward of the divine order</note>, and powerful chief, whom all the elements and powers of Nature serve! How have you animated these moving worlds? What spirit or soul have you infused? What bias have you fixed? Or how have you encompassed them in liquid ether, driving them as with the breath of living winds, your active and unwearied ministers in this intricate and mighty work?

> “Yet is this mansion-globe, this vessel for humanity, of a much narrower compass even than its other fellow-wanderers of our system. How narrow then must it appear compared with the vast system of its own sun? And how narrow, or as nothing, in respect to those countless systems of other suns? Yet how immense a body it seems compared with ours of human form, a borrowed remnant of its changing and frequently transformed surface? Though animated with a sublime celestial spirit by which we have relation and tendency to You, our Heavenly Father, center of souls, to whom these spirits of ours by nature tend, as earthly bodies to their proper center. Oh, if only they moved as unerringly and constantly! . . . But You alone settle the disorders of the physical world, and from the restless and clashing elements create that peaceful harmony and conspiring beauty of the always-flourishing creation. Even so can You transform these jarring motions of rational beings, and in due time and manner cause them to find their rest; making them contribute to the good and perfection of the universe, Your all-good and perfect work.”

Here again he stopped, looking at me as if he expected I should speak; when he found plainly that I would not, but continued still in a posture of contemplative thought, he said: Why, Philocles! with an air of wonder; what can this mean, that you should allow me thus to run on without the least interruption? Have you at once given up your skeptical philosophy, to let me roam thus at will through these airy spaces and imaginary regions where my whimsical imagination or simple faith has led me? I would have you consider better, and know, my Philocles, that I had never trusted myself with you in this streak of enthusiasm, had I not relied on you to govern it a little better.

"I find, then," I said (rousing myself from my musing posture), "you expect I should serve you in the same capacity as that musician whom an ancient orator used at his elbow, to strike such moving notes as raised him when he was perceived to sink, and calmed him again when his impetuous spirit was transported in too high a strain.

"You imagine correctly," replied Theocles; "and therefore I am resolved not to go on until you have promised to pull me by the sleeve when I grow extravagant." "So be it," I said; "you have my promise. But what if, instead of rising in my transports, I should grow flat and tiresome? What lyre or instrument would you employ to raise me?"

The danger, I told him, could hardly be supposed to lie on that side. His creative vein was a plentiful one, and his enthusiasm was in no likelihood of failing him. His subject, as well as his rhythm, would support him. And with the advantage of the rural scene around us, his rhythmic prose, I thought, took the place of the best pastoral song. For in the state I was now worked up to, it was as agreeable to me to hear him, in this kind of passion, invoke his stars and elements, as to hear one of those amorous shepherds complaining to his flock and making the woods and rocks resound with the name of the woman he adored. . . . "Begin therefore," I continued, still pressing him, "begin anew, and lead me boldly through your elements. Wherever there is danger, on either side, I promise to give you warning when I perceive it."

"Let us begin, then," he said, "with this, our element of earth, which over there we see cultivated with such care by the early laborers now working in the plain below—"

O Philocles, he said, it is well remembered. I find I was growing too warm; as I might well be, indeed, in this hot element. Indeed, I said, you might well expect the fate of Icarus for your high soaring. But this, indeed, was not what I feared. For you were beyond danger; and, with that devouring element on your side, you had mastered not only the sun itself, but *every* thing that stood in your way. I was afraid it might, in the end, lead to what they tell us of a universal conflagration; in which I did not know how it might go, possibly, with our Genius.

I am glad, Philocles, he said, to find this has become such a concern for you. But you may rest secure here, if the case you meant was that periodical conflagration spoken of by some philosophers. For there the Genius would necessarily be all in all; and in those intervals of creation, when no form or species existed anywhere outside of the divine mind, all then was Deity; all was that One, collected thus within itself, and existing (as they imagined) in a more simple and perfect manner than when multiplied in many ways; and becoming productive, it unfolded itself in the various map of Nature and this fair visible world.

The infection spreads; and nations, now viewing one another as profane, war more fiercely, and in the cause of religion forget their humanity; while savage zeal, with a meek and pious appearance, carries out a dreadful massacre and, for heaven’s sake (a horrid pretense!), makes the earth desolate. . . .

“Here let us leave these monsters (gladly, if we could confine them here!) and, detesting this dire, fertile soil, fly to the vast deserts of these parts. All ghastly and hideous as they appear, they do not lack their own peculiar beauties. This wildness pleases. We seem to live alone with Nature. We view her in her inmost recesses and contemplate her with more delight in these original wilds than in the artificial labyrinths and fake wildernesses of the palace. The objects of this place—the scaly serpents, the savage beasts, and poisonous insects—however terrible or contrary to human nature they may be, are beautiful in themselves and fit to raise our thoughts in admiration of that divine wisdom, which is so far superior to our limited views. Unable to explain the use or service of all things in this universe, we are nonetheless assured of the perfection of all, and of the justice of that <term>economy</term> <note>The "divine economy" or the organized system of the universe.</note> to which all things are subservient. In respect to that system, things seemingly deformed are lovely, disorder becomes regular, corruption becomes wholesome, and poisons (such as those we have seen) prove to be healing and beneficial.

See with what trembling steps poor mankind treads the narrow brink of deep precipices, from which with giddy horror they look down, distrusting even the ground that bears them, while they hear the hollow sound of torrents underneath and see the ruin of the overhanging rock, along with falling trees that hang with their roots upward and seem to draw more ruin after them. Here thoughtless men, seized by the novelty of such objects, become thoughtful and willingly contemplate the incessant changes of this earth’s surface. They see, as if in an instant, the revolutions of past ages, the fleeting forms of things, and the decay even of this our globe, whose youth and first formation they consider, while the apparent destruction and irreparable breaches of the wasted mountain show them the world itself only as a noble ruin and make them think of its approaching end. . . . 

But here, midway up the mountain, a spacious border of thick wood shelters our weary travelers, who have now come among the evergreen and lofty pines, the firs, and noble cedars, whose towering heads seem endless in the sky, while the rest of the trees appear only as shrubs beside them. And here a different horror seizes our sheltered travelers when they see the day diminished by the deep shades of the vast wood, which, closing thick above, spreads darkness and eternal night below. The faint and gloomy light looks as dreadful as the shade itself; and the profound stillness of these places imposes silence upon men, who are struck by the hoarse echoes of every sound within the spacious caverns of the wood. Here space astonishes; silence itself seems pregnant, while an unknown force works on the mind, and uncertain objects move the wakeful senses. Mysterious voices are either heard or imagined, and various forms of deity seem to present themselves and appear more manifest in these sacred woodland scenes—the kind that in ancient times gave rise to temples and favored the religion of the old world. Even we ourselves, who may read of divinity in plain characters from so many bright parts of the earth, choose these instead...

   Here he paused for a while and began to look around, his eyes having previously seemed fixed. He looked more calm, with an open face and relaxed manner, by which—and other signs—I could easily see we had come to the end of our descriptions. Whether I wanted to or not, Theocles was now resolved to leave the subject of the sublime, since the morning was over and the forenoon was by this time well advanced.

### SECTION II

I THINK, he said, Philocles (changing to a familiar voice), we had better leave these lonely places where our imagination has carried us and return to ourselves here again in our more sociable woods and temperate climates. Here, neither extreme heat nor cold annoys us, nor do precipices or waterfalls overwhelm us. Nor do we need to be afraid of our own voices here, while we hear the notes of such a cheerful choir and find the echoes quite pleasant, inviting us to talk.
   I confess, I said, those foreign nymphs (if there were any in those miraculous woods) were beauties far too intimidating to please me. I found our familiar home-nymphs much more to my liking. Yet for all that, I cannot help being disappointed that you stopped just when we had traveled halfway across the world and only needed to include America on our way home. Indeed, as for Europe, I could excuse you for not taking a long tour there, because of the little variety it would offer us. Besides, it would be difficult to view it in any way without constantly encountering the political state of affairs, which would disturb us too much in our philosophical flights. But as for the western region, I cannot imagine why you should neglect such noble subjects as are found there, unless perhaps the gold and silver—to which I see you are such a bitter enemy—frightened you away from a mother-soil so full of it. And as for the others—the dead forms of Nature, the metals and stones, however precious and dazzling—I am resolved to resist their splendor and regard them as lowly things, even in their highest pride, when they pretend to enhance human beauty and are dutifully brought to assist the beautiful.

Do you not see then, replied Theocles, that you have established three degrees or orders of beauty? How so? Why first, the dead forms, as you properly called them, which have a shape and are formed, whether by man or Nature, but have no forming power, no action, or intelligence. Correct. Next, and as the second kind, are the forms which form—that is, those which have intelligence, action, and operation. Correct again. Here, therefore, is double beauty. For here is both the form (the effect of the mind) and the mind itself. The first kind is low and despicable compared to this other, from which the dead form receives its luster and the force of its beauty. For what is a mere body, even a human one, no matter how perfectly fashioned, if inward form is missing and the mind is monstrous or imperfect, as in an idiot or a savage? This too I can understand, I said, but where is the third order?

"Have patience," *he replied*, "and see first whether you have discovered the whole force of this second beauty. How else should you understand the force of love, or have the power of enjoyment? Tell me, I beg you, when you first named these the 'forming forms,' did you think of any other products of theirs besides the inanimate kinds, such as palaces, coins, or bronze and marble statues of men? Or did you think of something closer to life?"

"I could easily have added," *said I*, "that these forms of ours had the power of producing other living forms like themselves. But I thought this power of theirs came from another form above them, and could not properly be called their own power or art if, in reality, there was a superior art—or something like an artist—which guided their hand and used them as tools in this impressive work."

"Well thought," *said he*; "you have avoided a criticism that I hardly imagined you could escape. And here you have unknowingly discovered that third order of beauty, which forms not only what we call mere forms, but even the forms which form. For we ourselves are notable architects of matter and can show lifeless bodies brought into form and fashioned by our own hands; but that which fashions even minds themselves contains within itself all the beauties fashioned by those minds, and is consequently the principle, source, and fountain of all beauty."

"It seems so."

"Therefore, whatever beauty appears in our second order of forms, or whatever is derived or produced from them, all of this exists eminently, principally, and originally in this final order of supreme and sovereign beauty."

"True."

"Thus architecture, music, and everything of human invention resolves itself into this final order."

"Right," *said I*; "and thus all the enthusiasms of other kinds resolve themselves into ours. The fashionable kinds borrow from us and are nothing without us. We undoubtedly have the honor of being the originals."

Unlike other parents, this mind is never spent or exhausted, but gains strength and vigor by producing. So you, my friend, have proved it through many a work, not allowing that fertile part of yourself to remain idle and inactive. From this come those good qualities which, starting from a natural genius, you have raised through proper improvement. And here, as I cannot help but admire that fertile genius and 'parent-beauty,' I am also satisfied that the offspring is, and will always be, beautiful."

I accepted the compliment and told him I wished the case were truly as he imagined, so that I might justly deserve his esteem and love. My study, therefore, should be to grow beautiful in his sense of beauty; and from now on I would do all I could to propagate that lovely race of "mental children," happily born from such a high enjoyment and from a union with what was fairest and best. "But it is you, Theocles," I continued, "who must help my struggling mind and be, as it were, the midwife to these conceptions; which otherwise, I fear, will fail to come to life."

"You do well," he replied, "to give me the midwife’s part only; for the mind, conceiving by itself, can only be assisted in the birth, as you say. Its pregnancy comes from its own nature. Nor could it ever have been thus impregnated by any other mind than that which formed it at the beginning; and which, as we have already proved, is the source of all mental beauty as well as all other kinds."

"Do you maintain then," I said, "that these mental children—the notions and principles of the fair, just, and honest, along with the rest of these ideas—are innate?"

"Anatomists," he said, "tell us that the eggs, which are the principles of the body, are innate, being formed already in the fetus before birth. But when it is—whether before, at, or after the birth, or at what time after—that either these or other principles, organs of sensation, or sensations themselves, are first formed in us, is a matter, undoubtedly, of curious speculation, but of no great importance. The question is whether the principles spoken of are from art or Nature? If they are from Nature purely, the timing does not matter; nor would I argue with you even if you should deny life itself to be innate, imagining it followed rather than preceded the moment of birth. But I am certain of this: that life and the sensations which accompany life, whenever they come, are from pure Nature and nothing else. Therefore, if you dislike the word *innate*, let us change it, if you will, for *instinct*, and call instinct that which Nature teaches, excluding art, culture, or discipline."

"I agree," I said.

"Leaving then," he replied, "those admirable speculations to the <term>virtuosi</term>, the anatomists, and the <term>school divines</term>, we may safely assert, with all their consent, that the various organs, particularly those of generation, are formed by Nature. Do you think there is also an instinct from Nature for the later use of them? Or must learning and experience imprint this use?"

"It is imprinted," I said, "quite enough, in all conscience. The impression or instinct is so strong in this case, that it would be..."

For we can indeed see this much in the preparatory labors and skills of these wild creatures, which demonstrate their anticipating imaginations, pre-conceptions, or pre-sensations, if I may use a word you taught me yesterday.<note>1</note>

"I accept your expression," said Theocles, "and will try to show you that the same pre-conceptions, of a higher degree, exist in humankind."

"Please do so," I said, "I entreat you; for I am so far from finding in myself these pre-conceptions of the fair and beautiful, in your sense, that I think until recently I have hardly known anything like them in Nature."

"How then," he said, "would you have recognized that outward fairness and beauty of humankind if such an object (a beautiful human being) in all its beauty had appeared to you for the first time, while you were alone this morning in these groves? Or do you think, perhaps, you would have been unmoved, and would have found no difference between this form and any other, if you had not first been taught?"

"I hardly have any right," I replied, "to argue for this last opinion after what I have just admitted."

"Well then," he said, "so that I do not seem to take advantage of you, I will set aside the dazzling form that carries such a force of complex beauties, and I am content to consider separately each of those simple beauties which, taken all together, create this wonderful effect. Leaving aside, therefore, the latter three and their dependent charms, let us look at the charm in what is simplest of all: mere shape. Nor do we need to look so high—

Why are the sphere or globe, the cylinder, and the obelisk preferred, and the irregular figures, in comparison to these, rejected and despised?

I am ready, I replied, to admit there is a natural beauty in certain figures,<note>1 Inquiry, book 1, part 2, § 3.</note> which the eye finds as soon as the object is presented to it.

Is there then, he said, a natural beauty of figures? And is there not an equally natural one of actions? No sooner does the eye open upon figures, or the ear to sounds, than immediately the beautiful results, and grace and harmony are known and acknowledged. No sooner are actions viewed, no sooner are the human affections and passions discerned (and most of them are discerned as soon as they are felt), than immediately an inward eye distinguishes and sees the fair and shapely, the amiable and admirable, separate from the deformed, the foul, the odious, or the despicable. How is it possible, therefore, not to admit "that as these distinctions have their foundation in Nature, the discernment itself is natural, and from Nature alone"?

If this were as you represent it, I told him, I thought there could never be any disagreement among men concerning actions and behavior—as to which was base and which worthy; which handsome and which deformed. But now we find perpetual variance among mankind, whose differences are chiefly founded on this disagreement in opinion: "One person affirming, the other denying, that this or that was fitting or decent."

Even by this, then, he replied, it appears there is fitness and decency in actions; since the fit and decent are always presupposed in this controversy. And while men are at odds about the specific subjects, the thing itself is universally agreed upon. For there is no more agreement in judgments about other forms of beauty.

It is debated "which is the finest building, the loveliest shape or face"; but without debate it is allowed "there is a beauty of each kind." No one sets out to teach this, nor is it learned by anyone, but it is confessed by all. Everyone acknowledges the standard, rule, and measure; but in applying it to things, disorder arises, ignorance prevails, and self-interest and passion breed disturbance. Nor can it happen otherwise in the affairs of life, as long as that which interests and engages men as *good* is thought to be different from that which they admire and praise as *honest* [virtuous]. But with us, Philocles, it is better settled, since for our parts we have already decreed "that beauty and good are always the same."

"I remember," I said, "what you forced me to acknowledge more than once before. And now, good Theocles, now that I have become such a willing disciple, I think I do not need so much to be convinced as to be confirmed and strengthened. And I hope this last work may prove to be your easiest task."

"Not unless you help in it yourself," replied Theocles, "for this is necessary as well as appropriate. It would indeed have been shameful for you to have yielded without putting up a good resistance. To help oneself be convinced is to forestall reason and invite error and delusion. But upon fair conviction, to give our heart up to the side of evidence and reinforce that impression—this is to help reason heartily. And in this way, we may be said honestly to persuade ourselves. Show me, then, how I may best persuade myself."

there is no such thing as real value or worth; nothing in itself estimable or lovely, hateful or shameful. Everything is opinion. It is opinion which makes beauty and unmakes it. The graceful or ungraceful in things, propriety and its opposite, the lovely and unlovely, vice, virtue, honor, and shame—all of this is founded in opinion alone. Opinion is the law and the standard. What shall we say to such a person? How can we show him his absurdity and excess? Will he stop any sooner? Or shall we ask what shame exists for someone who acknowledges nothing as shameful? Yet he mocks and cries, "Ridiculous!" By what right? By what title? For this is how I would defend myself if I were *Philocles*: "Am I ridiculous? In what way? What is ridiculous? Everything? Or nothing?" Ridiculous indeed! But then there is something that is ridiculous; and the notion, it seems, is correct—that there is "something shameful and ridiculous in things."

How then shall we apply this notion? For if it is wrongly applied, it cannot help but be ridiculous itself. Or will the person who cries "shame" refuse to acknowledge any shame in himself in turn? Does he not blush or seem embarrassed on any occasion? If he does, the case is very different from that of mere grief or fear. The unease he feels comes from a sense of what is shameful and hateful in itself, not from what is hurtful or dangerous in its consequences. For the greatest danger in the world can never produce shame; nor can the opinion of the whole world force us to feel it if our own opinion does not agree. We may be afraid of appearing rude and may therefore fake modesty. But we can never truly blush for anything except what we think is truly shameful, and what we would still blush for even if our interests were perfectly secure and we were beyond the reach of any inconvenience that could result from the thing we were ashamed of.

<summary>Theocles argues against the idea that morality and beauty are merely subjective opinions, using the involuntary reaction of shame as evidence that humans recognize an inherent standard of what is shameful regardless of external consequences.</summary>

"Thus," he continued, "I should be able to defend myself in advance. By looking closely into men’s lives and what influences them on all occasions, I would have enough evidence to say to myself: 'Whoever chooses to be my opponent in this opinion, I will find that in some way or another he is already convinced of the very thing he seeks to talk me out of.' Does he feel gratitude or resentment, pride or shame? Whichever way it is, he acknowledges a sense of what is just and unjust, and what is worthy and base. If he is grateful or expects gratitude, I ask, 'Why? And on what basis?' If he is angry, or if he indulges in revenge, I ask, 'How? And in what case? Revenged for what? For a stone or a madman?' Who is so insane? 'But for what? For a random injury? An accident occurring without thought or intention?' Who is so unjust? Therefore, there is justice and injustice; and related to them is a natural presumption or intuition on which resentment or anger is based. For what else would make even the most wicked of men often prefer the pursuit of their revenge over all other interests—even over life itself—except for a sense of wrong natural to all men, and a desire to pursue that wrong at any cost? They do not do this for their own sake, since they sacrifice their very existence for it, but out of hatred for the perceived wrong and from a certain love of justice. In this example, even in unjust men, justice is shown to be more important than life itself.

In the same way, regarding pride, I ask: 'Why proud? Why conceited? And of what? Does anyone who feels pride think poorly or indifferently of himself?' No; but honorably. And how can this be if there is no real honor or dignity presupposed? For self-valuation implies self-worth; and in a person conscious of real worth, there is either no pride at all, or a pride that is just and noble. In the same manner, self-contempt implies a personal baseness or defectiveness; it may be either a proper modesty or an unwarranted humility. But this much is certain: whoever is proud must be proud of something. And we know that men of thorough pride will be proud even in the lowliest circumstances, and

"If animals, therefore," he said, "are incapable of knowing and enjoying beauty because they are animals and possess only physical sense (the animalistic part) for their share, it follows 'that neither can man, by the same sense or animalistic part, conceive of or enjoy beauty; but all the beauty and good he enjoys is in a nobler way, and by the help of what is noblest: his mind and reason.' Here lies his dignity and highest interest; here is his capacity for goodness and happiness. His ability or incompetence, his power of enjoyment or his impotence, is founded in this alone. As the mind is sound, fair, noble, and worthy, so too are its subjects, acts, and employments. For just as the chaotic mind, captive to the senses, can never compete or contend for beauty with the virtuous mind cultivated by reason, neither can the objects which allure the former compare with those which attract and charm the latter. And when each gratifies itself in the enjoyment and possession of its object, how much more clearly beautiful are the acts which join the latter pair, and provide a soul the enjoyment of what is noble and good? This at least, Philocles, you will surely allow: that when you place a joy anywhere other than in the mind, the enjoyment itself will not be a beautiful subject, nor of any graceful or pleasant appearance. But when you consider how friendship is enjoyed—as well as honor, gratitude, candor, kindness, and all internal beauty; how all the social pleasures, society itself, and everything which constitutes the worth and happiness of mankind are enjoyed—you will surely recognize beauty in the act here. You will think it worthy to be viewed and reviewed often by the joyful mind, which is happily conscious of its own noble part and of its own advancement and growth in beauty."

"Thus, Philocles," he continued, after a short pause, "thus have I presumed to treat of beauty before so great a judge and such a skillful admirer as yourself. For, taking my start from Nature’s beauty, which transported me, I gladly ventured further in the pursuit and have accompanied you in search of beauty as it relates to us and constitutes our highest good in its sincere and natural enjoyment. And if we have not spent our hours idly, nor wandered in vain through these deserted regions, it should appear from our rigorous search that there is nothing as divine as beauty. Since beauty belongs not to the body, nor has any principle or existence except in mind and reason, it is discovered and acquired only by this more divine part when it inspects itself—the only object worthy of itself. For whatever is void of mind is emptiness and darkness to the mind’s eye. This eye languishes and grows dim whenever it is detained by foreign subjects, but thrives and attains its natural vigor when employed in the contemplation of what is like itself. It is in this way that the improving mind, briefly surveying other objects and passing over bodies and common forms (where only a shadow of beauty rests), ambitiously presses onward to its source and views the original of form and order in that which is intelligent.

And thus, O Philocles, we may improve and become artists of this kind, learning 'to know ourselves, and what that is which, by improving, we may be sure to advance our worth and real self-interest.' For this knowledge is not acquired by the contemplation of bodies or outward forms, the viewing of pageantry, or the study of estates and honors. Nor is he to be esteemed as a self-improving artist who makes a fortune out of these; but he (and he alone) is the wise and capable man who, with little regard for these things, applies himself to cultivate another soil and builds with a material different from stone or marble. Having more correct models in his eye, he becomes in truth the architect of his own life and fortune by laying within himself the lasting and sure foundations of order, peace, and concord. . . . But now it is time to think of returning home. The morning is far spent. Come!"

Tell the truth now, Theocles: can anything be more odd or dissonant from the common voice of the world than what we have determined in this matter?”

“Whom shall we follow, then?” he replied. “Whose judgment or opinion shall we take concerning what is good and what is its opposite? If all or any part of mankind were consistent with themselves and could agree on this, I would be content to leave philosophy and follow them. If it is otherwise, why should we not adhere to what we have chosen? . . . Let us, then, consider how this matter stands from another perspective.”

All tell me different things. “Since, therefore, riches are not good in themselves (as most of you declare), and since there is no agreement among you on how they become good, why may I not hold the opinion that they are neither good in themselves nor directly any cause or means of good?”

If there are those who completely despise fame, and if among those who desire it, he who wants it for one reason despises it for another, or he who seeks it from some people despises it from others, why may I not say "that I do not know how any fame can be called a good thing"?

If among those who desire pleasure, those who admire one kind are superior to another kind, why may I not say "that I do not know which of these pleasures, or how pleasure itself, can be called good"?

If among those who desire life ever so earnestly, the life that is desirable and lovely to one is despicable and vile to another, why may I not say "that I do not know how life itself can be thought of as a good thing in itself"?

To tell you the truth, I said, I was considering what would become of me if, after all, I should become a philosopher because of you. The change, truly, would be somewhat extraordinary, replied *Theocles*. But do not be concerned. The danger is not so great. Experience shows us every day that just because people talk or write about philosophy, they are not at all closer to being philosophers.

But, I said, the very name is a kind of reproach. The word "idiot" formerly stood as the opposite to "philosopher," but nowadays it more commonly means nothing other than the philosopher himself.

Yet, in effect, he replied, what else do we all do in general than philosophize? If philosophy is, as we understand it, the study of happiness, must not everyone, in some manner or another, either skillfully or unskillfully philosophize? Is not every deliberation concerning our main interest, every correction of our taste, every choice and preference in life to be reckoned as this kind of study? For "if happiness is not allowed to come from the self and from within, then it is either from outward things alone, or from the self..."

Therefore, "if happiness comes partly from the self and partly from outward things, then each must be considered, and a certain value set on concerns of an inward kind, which depend on the self alone." If so, and if I consider "how and in what ways these are to be preferred; when and on what occasion they are appropriate or inappropriate; when they should properly take place and when they should yield," what is this, after all, but to philosophize?

Yet even this is still enough to put one out of the ordinary way of thinking, and give one an unfortunate distaste for business and the world. Right! For this also is to be considered and well weighed. And therefore, this is still philosophy: "to inquire where and in what respect one may be the greatest loser; which are the greatest gains and the most profitable exchanges," since everything in this world goes by exchange.

Nothing is gained for nothing. Favor requires courtship; influence is gained by solicitation; honors are acquired with risk; riches with hardship; learning and accomplishments by study and application. Security, rest, and leisure are to be had at other prices. They may be thought, perhaps, to come easily. For "what hardship is there? Where is the harm? It is only to reduce one's fame and fortune. It is only to waive the point of honor and share somewhat less of one's influence." If this is easy, all is well. Some patience, you see, is necessary in this case. Privacy must be endured, and even obscurity and contempt. Such are the conditions. And thus, everything has its price. Power and promotions are to be had at one rate, pleasures at another, and liberty and honesty at another. A good mind must be paid for just like other things.

But we had better beware lest, perhaps, we pay too dearly for it. Let us be assured we have a good bargain. Come on then. . . . Let us calculate. . . . "What is a mind worth? What..."

Is it likely to decide just as well when unexercised as when thoroughly exercised or ever so expert? Consider, please, in mathematics whose is the better reason of the two, and fitter to be relied on? The practitioner’s, or his who is unpracticed? Whose is better in the way of war, of policy, or civil affairs? Whose in trade, law, or physic <note>medicine</note>? And in morality and life, I still ask, whose? Might he not, perhaps, be considered the best judge of living who studies life and endeavors to shape it by some rule? Or is he indeed to be esteemed most knowledgeable in the matter who examines it only slightly, and who accidentally and unknowingly philosophizes?

"Thus, Philocles," he said, concluding his discourse, "thus is philosophy established. For every one, of necessity, must reason concerning his own happiness—'what his good is and what his harm is.' The question is only, 'who reasons best?' For even he who rejects this reasoning or deliberating part does it from a certain reason, and from a persuasion 'that this is best.'"

By this time we found ourselves having arrived home without noticing. Our philosophy ended, and we returned to the common affairs of life.

# MISCELLANY I

## CHAPTER I

->Of the nature, rise, and establishment of Miscellanies—The subject of these which follow—Intention of the writer.<-

Peace be with the soul of that charitable and courteous author who, for the common benefit of his fellow authors, introduced the ingenious method of miscellaneous writing! It must be acknowledged that since this happy method was established, the harvest of wit has been more plentiful, and the laborers more numerous than before. It is well known to the skilled practitioners in the art of writing "that as easy as it is to conceive wit, it is the hardest thing imaginable to be delivered of it under certain conditions." Nothing could be more severe or rigid than the conditions formerly prescribed to writers, when criticism held sway, and regularity and order were thought essential in a treatise. The notion of a genuine work—a legitimate and proper piece—has certainly caused great timidity and hesitation among the adventurers in wit; and the imposition of such strict laws and rules of composition has weighed heavily on the free spirits and bold geniuses of mankind. It was a yoke, it seems, which our forefathers bore, but which we, for our part, have generously thrown off. In effect, the hateful distinctions of bastardy and legitimacy being at last removed, the natural and lawful offspring of the brain comes with

<keywords>miscellaneous writing, wit, literary criticism, composition rules, creative freedom, authorship, literary history</keywords>

This "miscellaneous manner of writing," it must be admitted, has successfully achieved this. It has made almost every soil productive. It has revealed those various seeds of wit which lay suppressed in many a heart, and has raised countless fanciful ideas and curious fancies which the natural roughness and harshness of their native soil would have held back, or at least would not have permitted to rise above the ground. From every field, from every hedge or hillock, we now gather fruits as delicious and flowers as fragrant as we did of old from the richest and best-cultivated gardens. Wretched were those ancient planters who, not understanding how to adapt themselves to the crude taste of unrefined mankind, made it such a difficult task to serve the world with intellectual entertainments and provide the feasts of literature and science.

There was certainly a time when the name of "author" stood for something significant in the world. To succeed well in such a labor as writing a treatise or a poem was taken as a sure sign of understanding and good sense. The task was difficult, but, it seems, it was honorable. How the situation came to be so reversed over time is hard to say. The early authors, perhaps being few in number and highly respected for their art, fell under the weight of envy. Being aware of their misfortune in this respect, and being motivated, as is probable, by the example of some popular genius, they abandoned their regular schemes and precise forms of craftsmanship in favor of those wits who could not possibly be accepted as authors under such difficult conditions. It was necessary, it seems, that the foundation of wit should be expanded. It was advisable that more hands should be brought into the work, and nothing could better serve this popular purpose than the method of the miscellany or common essay, in which the most confused mind, if filled with a little creativity and provided with common-

<meta>This page continues the critique of "miscellaneous writing," comparing the transition from structured, original literary works to modern "patchwork" writing to the shift in textile manufacturing from harmonious patterns to flashy, disorganized scraps.</meta>

To better explain how this revolution in letters has been brought about, it might not be improper if we were to compare our writing artists to manufacturers of fabric or silk. Among them, it is considered a primary skill to design a pattern or plan of workmanship in which the various colors are agreeably arranged, with such proportionate adjustment of the various figures and designs as may, on the whole, create a kind of harmony for the eye. According to this method, each piece must actually be an original. For to copy what has come before can be of no use. The fraud would easily be noticed. On the other hand, to work originally, and in a sense create anew each time, must be a matter of great weight, suited only to the strength and capacity of none but the finest workmen.

Therefore, a method has been invented to confuse this simplicity and consistency of design; patchwork is substituted. Scraps and shreds of learning, with various fragments and points of wit, are drawn together and stitched in any fanciful form. If they happen to shine and spread a kind of lively glare, the miscellany is approved and the complex form and texture of the work is admired. The eye, which before was won by regularity and had remained true to measure and strict proportion, is by this means pleasantly drawn aside to commit a kind of excess and amuse itself with gaudy colors and distorted shapes of things. Meanwhile, custom has not only tolerated this lack of restraint but rendered it even commendable, and brought it into the highest reputation. The wild and whimsical, under the name of the odd and pretty, take the place of the graceful and the beautiful. Accuracy and precision of thought are set aside as being too restrictive and having too painful an appearance to be endured in the agreeable and easier social exchange of gallantry and modern wit.

For whatever is capricious and odd is sure to create a diversion for those who look no further. And where there is nothing resembling nature, there is no room for the troublesome work of thought or contemplation. It is the perfection of certain grotesque painters to stay as far from nature as possible. To find a likeness in their works is to find the greatest fault imaginable. A natural connection is a flaw. Coherence, design, and meaning are against their purpose and destroy the very spirit and genius of their craftsmanship.

I remember formerly, when I was a spectator in the French theatre, I found it the custom at the end of every grave and solemn tragedy to introduce a comic farce or miscellany which they called the *little piece*. We have indeed a method still more extraordinary upon our own stage, for we think it agreeable and right to mix the little piece or farce with the main plot or story throughout every act. This perhaps may be chosen instead, because our tragedy is so much deeper and bloodier than that of the French, and therefore needs more immediate refreshment from the elegant style of drollery and burlesque wit. This wit, being thus closely interwoven with its opposite, creates that most accomplished kind of theatrical miscellany called by our poets a *tragi-comedy*.

I could go further perhaps, and demonstrate from the writings of many of our serious clergymen, the speeches of our senators, and other principal models of our national learning, "that the miscellaneous manner is at present in the highest esteem." According to this method, while I serve as critic or interpreter to this new writer, I may the better correct his sluggishness <note>"flegm" or phlegm: a lack of energy, dullness, or cool temperament.</note> and give him more of the fashionable air and manner of the world, especially in what relates to the subject and manner of his two last pieces, which are contained in his second volume. Nor should the title of a miscellaneous writer be denied me on the account that I have based my miscellanies upon a certain set of treatises already published. Grounds and foundations are of no importance in a kind of work which, according to modern standards, has properly neither top nor bottom, beginning nor end. Besides that, I shall in no way confine myself to the precise contents of these treatises, but, like my fellow miscellaneous writers, shall take the opportunity to vary often from my proposed subject and make what deviations or excursions I shall think fit as I proceed in my random essays.

## CHAPTER II

->Of controversial writings: answers, replies—Polemic divinity, or the<-
->writing Church militant—Philosophers, and the bear-garden—Authors<-
->paired and matched—The matchmakers—Football—A dialogue<-
->between our author and his bookseller.<-

Among the many improvements daily made in the art of writing, there is none perhaps which can be said to have attained a greater height than that of controversy, or the method of answer and refutation. It is true indeed that in ancient times the intellects of men were for the most part occupied with other employment.

<page-num>161</page-num>
<sig>M</sig>

<summary>The author justifies his use of the "miscellaneous" style as a way to make his more formal previous works accessible to modern readers who prefer variety and distraction. He also introduces a discussion on the modern heights of controversial and polemic writing.</summary>

--- Page 174 ---
<meta>This page continues the author's exploration of "miscellaneous writing," contrasting the past state of intellectual debate with the modern preference for controversy and "frays" between authors.</meta>

<header>SHAFTESBURY'S CHARACTERISTICS</header>

If authors wrote poorly they were despised; if they wrote well, they were supported by one party or another. For there would necessarily be parties and sects of every kind in learning and philosophy. Everyone sided with whomever they liked, and having the liberty of hearing each side speak for itself, they stood in no need of explicit warnings against supposed sophistry or dangerous reasoning. Specific answers to single treatises were thought to be of little use. And it was not considered a compliment to a reader to help them so carefully in judging every piece that was published. Whatever sects existed in those days, the passion for party causes did not run so high as to give the reader a taste of those personal insults which might pass in a debate between different partisans.

This was how matters stood in the past, when the method of writing controversy had not yet been turned into an art, nor had the feuds of competing authors become the chief amusement of the learned world. But we currently have such a high appetite for this kind of thing that the writings of the learned are never truly flavorful <note>"gustful": full of flavor or relish.</note> until they have reached what we may properly enough call their due ripeness and have started a fight. Once the answer and reply are established, our curiosity is piqued; we begin then, for the first time, to sharpen our attention and listen closely.

For example, let a zealous theologian and passionate champion of our faith, when inclined to appear in print, choose some formidable mystery of religion previously opposed by some damnable <term>heresiarch</term> <note>A leader of a heretical sect.</note>. Having vehemently refuted him, he turns toward the orthodox opinion and supports the true belief with the highest eloquence and deepest erudition; despite this, he shall perhaps remain in deep obscurity, to the great distress of his bookseller and the regret of all who hold a just respect for Church history and the ancient purity of the Christian faith. He can never rise again. Do you really think so? Or if he should, it would be a pleasure to see how you would handle him.”

These are the triumphs. This is what sharpens the appetite; this gives the author his edge and excites the reader’s attention, when the trumpets are thus sounded to the crowd, and a kind of amphitheatrical entertainment is exhibited to the multitude by these gladiatorial writers.

The author of the preceding treatises, being by profession a precise observer of the ridiculous side of things, must in all probability have formed some such views as those which hindered him from engaging in the way of controversy. For when, by accident, the first of these treatises ¹ (a private letter, and in the writer’s estimation little worthy of the public’s notice) came to be read abroad in copies, and afterwards in print, the sharpest answers which came out against it could not, it seems, move our author to form any reply. It must be admitted that when a writer of any kind is so significant as to deserve the labor and efforts of some shrewd minds to refute him in public, he may, in his capacity as an author, be justly congratulated on that occasion. It is necessarily assumed that he must have written with some kind of ability or wit. But if his original work is in truth no better than ordinary, his responder’s task must certainly be very trivial. He must be very poorly occupied who would take it upon himself to answer nonsense formally, ridicule what is already a joke in itself, and force the world to read a second book for the sake of the irrelevancies of the first.

Taking it, however, for granted “that a poor treatise may be the foundation of a significant answer,” a reply must still certainly be ridiculous whichever way we look at it. For either the author, in his original work, has been truly refuted or not. If refuted, why does he defend himself? If not refuted, why trouble himself? What does the public have to do with his private quarrels or his adversary’s impertinence? Or supposing the world, out of curiosity, may delight to see a pedant exposed by a man of better wit, and a controversy thus unequally carried on between two such opposite parties, how long is this diversion likely to last? And what will become of these polemic writings a few years from now? What has already become of those mighty controversies with which some of the most eminent authors amused the world within the memory of the youngest scholar? It will surely be admitted by those who have learned to judge elegance and wit merely through modern languages that we could have little appreciation for the best letters of a Balzac or Voiture if we were completely ignorant of the characters of the prominent people to whom those letters were actually written. Let the best of Tully’s<note>Marcus Tullius Cicero</note> Epistles be read with such a narrow view as this, and they will certainly prove very dull. If a real Brutus or a real Atticus is not assumed, there will be no real Cicero. The elegant writer will disappear, as will the immense labor and art with which this eloquent Roman wrote those letters to his illustrious friends. There was no kind of composition in which this great author took more pride or pleasure than in this, where he endeavored to shed the demeanor of the philosopher and orator, while in effect he employed both his rhetoric and philosophy with the greatest power. Those who can read an epistle or satire of Horace with something more than a mere academic appreciation will understand that the concealment of order and method in this manner of writing constitutes the chief beauty of the work. Even the satirical or miscellaneous style of the refined ancients required as much organization as the most formal works. But the skill lay in removing every such sign or appearance, giving an improvised air to what was written, and allowing the effect of art to be felt without revealing the artifice. It is a different case indeed when the title of "Epistle" is improperly given to works that were never written for any purpose other than to be made public, or to serve as exercises or examples of the author's wit. Such were the countless Greek and Latin Epistles written by the ancient sophists, grammarians, or rhetoricians. and noble things, both relevant and tangential, accidentally as words led him (for he plays with words perpetually), with infinite wit, but with little or no coherence, without a shape or body to his work, and without a real beginning,¹ a middle, or an end. Of a hundred and twenty-four Epistles, you may, if you please, make five hundred or just ten. You may divide a long one, for instance, into five or six. You may attach a short one to another, and that to another, and so on. The unity of the writing will remain the same; the life and spirit will be just as well preserved. It is not only whole letters or pages that you may change and manage in this way at your pleasure; almost every period, almost every sentence, is independent and may be taken apart, transposed, postponed, moved forward, or set in any new order as you fancy.

This is the style of writing so much admired and imitated in our age that we scarcely have the idea of any other model. Indeed, we know little of the difference between one model or character of writing and another. Everything follows the same tune and beats exactly one and the same rhythm. One would think nothing could be more tedious than this uniform pace. I am persuaded that the common amble or "Canterbury" pace is no more tiresome to a good rider than this see-sawing of essay writers is to a capable reader. The proper composer of a legitimate piece is like a skilled traveler who precisely measures his journey and considers—

There is a great difference between a courtier who takes a interest in philosophy and a philosopher who takes an interest in a court. Now, Seneca was born a courtier, being the son of a court rhetorician; he was raised in the same manner and taken into favor for his wit and genius—his admired style and eloquence—rather than for his learning in the books of philosophy and the ancients. For his learning, indeed, was not very profound. In short, he was a man of wonderful wit and fluency of thought and language, an able minister, and an honest courtier. And what has been passed down to his prejudice was written by the common enemy of all the free and generous Romans: that imitative, shallow historian and court flatterer, Dion Cassius. He lived in a debased era when barbarism (as can be easily seen in his own work) was advancing quickly, and the very traces and features of virtue, science, and knowledge were fading out of the world.

# SHAFTESBURY'S CHARACTERISTICS

his ground, plans his stages and intervals of rest and focus until the very end of his undertaking, so that he successfully arrives where he first intended when he set out. He does not immediately use the spur or start at full speed, but walks his horse leisurely out of his stable, settles himself in his stirrups, and, when a fair road and good season allow, moves perhaps to a steady trot, then into a gallop, and after a while slows down. As a hill, meadow, or shady lane appears, he adjusts his pace accordingly, taking care of his horse; and he is sure not to bring him gasping and overheated into the final inn. 

But the "post-way" style has become highly fashionable with modern authors. The very same pace starts you off and brings you home. Nothing delays or interrupts. Hill or valley, rough or smooth, thick or thin; there is no difference, no variation. When an author sits down to write, he thinks he has no other business than to be witty and take care that his sentences are well-structured or, as they commonly say, run smoothly. In this manner, he expects to earn a reputation for being brilliant. When he has written as many pages as he likes, or as his flight of fancy permitted, he then perhaps considers what name he had best give to his new work; whether he should call it a letter, an essay, a miscellany, or something else. The bookseller perhaps is the one to determine this at last, when everything besides the preface, the dedication, and the title page is finished.

# MISCELLANY II

## CHAPTER I

->Review of enthusiasm—its defense and praise—its use in business as well as pleasure—its operation through fear and love—modifications of enthusiasm: magnanimity, heroic virtue, honor, public zeal, religion, superstition, persecution, martyrdom—the energy of ecstatic devotion in the female sex—an account of ancient priesthood—religious war—reference to a succeeding chapter.<-

Whether there is, in fact, any real enchantment, any influence of the stars, or any power of demons or external natures over our own minds, is considered questionable by many. Some assert the negative and attempt to explain appearances of this kind through the natural operation of our passions and the common course of outward things. For my own part, I cannot help but perceive at this moment a kind of enchantment or magic in what we call enthusiasm; since I find that, having touched lightly on this subject, I cannot so easily part with it as I please.

After making some brief reflections on our author’s letter,<note>Namely, the *Letter Concerning Enthusiasm*, mentioned above.</note> I thought I might have sufficiently fulfilled my duty on this topic, until passing to his next treatise, I found myself even further engaged. I perceived clearly that I had as yet hardly entered into our author’s spirit, or felt anything of that passion which, as he informs us, is so easily communicated and naturally engaging.
