I have indeed heard that the very reading of treatises and accounts of melancholy is prone to generate that passion in the over-diligent and attentive reader. And this, perhaps, may be the reason why our author himself (as he seems to suggest toward the conclusion of his first letter) did not really care to grapple closely with his subject or give us a precise definition of enthusiasm all at once. This, however, we may, along with our author, venture to infer from the coldest of all studies—even from criticism itself (which we have been discussing lately)—“that there is a power in numbers, harmony, proportion, and beauty of every kind, which naturally captivates the heart and raises the imagination to a belief or conception of something majestic and divine.”

Whatever this subject may be in itself, we cannot help being transported by the thought of it. It inspires us with something more than ordinary and raises us above ourselves. Without this imagination or conception, the world would be but a dull circumstance and life a sorry pastime. We could scarcely be said to live. The animal functions might be carried on in their course, but nothing further would be sought for or regarded. The gallant sentiments, the elegant fancies, the *belles passions* which all have this beauty in view, would be set aside and would likely leave us no other employment than satisfying our coarsest appetites at the cheapest rate to attain a state of lazy indolence and inactivity.

Slender would be the enjoyments of the lover, the ambitious man, the warrior, or the *virtuoso* (as our author has elsewhere<note>*Moralists*, part iii. § 2.</note>

<summary>The author argues that enthusiasm and a sense of beauty are essential to human life, as without them, existence would be reduced to mere animal function and the pursuit of basic appetites. He suggests that harmony and proportion naturally elevate the human mind toward the divine.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on enthusiasm, asserting that it is a natural passion and that even virtue and honesty are forms of "noble enthusiasm" directed toward moral beauty and order.</meta>

<header>SHAFTESBURY'S CHARACTERISTICS</header>

This is what our author proposes when, on behalf of enthusiasm, he quotes its formal enemies and shows that they are as capable of it as its greatest confessors and supporters. He is so far from degrading enthusiasm or disclaiming it in himself that he looks on this passion, considered simply, as the most natural, and its object as the most just in the world. Even virtue itself he takes to be nothing other than a noble enthusiasm, justly directed and regulated by that high standard which he supposes exists in the nature of things.

He seems to assert <note>1</note> “that there are certain <term>moral species</term> or appearances so striking and of such force over our natures, that when they present themselves they bear down all contrary opinion or notion, all opposite passion, sensation, or mere bodily affection.” Of this kind, he considers virtue itself to be the chief, since of all views or contemplations this, in his account, is the most naturally and strongly affecting. The exalted part of love is only borrowed from this source. That of pure friendship is its immediate self. He who yields his life as a sacrifice to his prince or country; the lover who performs as much for his beloved; the heroic, the amorous, and the religious martyrs, who draw their views—whether visionary or real—from this pattern and exemplar of divinity; all these, according to our author’s sentiment, are alike motivated by this passion, and prove themselves in effect to be so many different enthusiasts.

Nor is thorough honesty, in his hypothesis, anything other than zeal or passion moving strongly upon the species or view of the decorum and sublime of actions. Others may pursue <note>2</note> different

It is indeed peculiar to the nature of that cool philosophy described above,<sup>2</sup> that as it denies the order or harmony of things in general, so by a logical consequence and truth of reasoning, it rejects the habit of admiring or being charmed by whatever is called beautiful in particular. According to the regimen prescribed by this philosophy, it must be acknowledged that the evils of love, ambition, vanity, and luxury—along with other disturbances derived from flowery, high, and elegant ideas of things—must in appearance be on their way to being radically cured.

It should not be thought surprising that religion itself should, in the account of these philosophers, be considered among those vices and disturbances which it concerns us to root out in this manner. If the idea of majesty and beauty in other inferior subjects is in reality distracting, it must especially be so in that principal subject which is the basis and foundation of this notion. Now, if the subject itself does not exist in nature, neither the idea nor the passion grounded on it can be properly considered natural; thus, all admiration ceases, and enthusiasm is at an end. But if such a passion exists naturally, it is evident that religion itself is of that kind and must therefore be natural to man.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of enthusiasm, moving from its status as a natural passion to its potential for corruption and its relationship with superstition.</meta>

<header>MISCELLANEOUS REFLECTIONS</header>

Enthusiasm is in itself a very natural, honest passion, and properly has nothing as its object but what is good and honest. <note>The beautiful and the good.</note> It is indeed apt, he confesses, to go astray. And by modern examples we know, perhaps even better than by any ancient ones, that in religion the enthusiasm which works through love is subject to many strange irregularities, and that which works through fear to many monstrous and horrible superstitions. Mystics and fanatics are known to abound as much in our reformed churches as in the Roman Catholic churches. The alleged floods of grace poured into the bosoms of the Quietists, Pietists, and those who favor the ecstatic way of devotion, raise such transports that their own followers confess they have something strangely agreeable, and in common with what ordinary lovers are accustomed to feeling. And it has been remarked by many that the female saints have been the greatest developers of this soft part of religion. What truth there may be in the reported operations of this alleged grace and amorous zeal, or in the accounts of what has usually passed between the saints of each sex in these devout ecstasies, I shall leave the reader to examine, assuming he will find enough credible accounts to convince him of the dangerous progress of enthusiasm in this amorous lineage.

There are many branches, indeed, that are more common, such as fear, melancholy, consternation, suspicion, and despair. And when the passion turns more toward the astonishing and frightening side than toward the amiable and delightful side, it creates what we call superstition rather than enthusiasm. I must confess, moreover, that what we commonly call zeal in matters of religion is seldom without a mixture of both these extravagances. The ecstatic motions of love and admiration are seldom unaccompanied by the horrors and consternations of a lower sort of devotion. These paroxysms of zeal are in reality like the hot and cold fits of a fever, and depend on the different and occasional views or aspects of the divinity, according to whether the worshiper is guided from without or affected from within by his particular constitution. <note>See below, *Miscellaneous Reflections* ii. ch. iii., end.</note>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of enthusiasm and religious zeal, moving from the internal experience of the "soft" part of religion to the volatile and often contradictory passions found in zealots.</meta>

These aspects are seldom so definite and fixed as to constantly inspire the exact same spirit of devotion. Therefore, in religions that emphasize love, there is generally room left for terrors of the deepest kind. Nor is there any religion so diabolical that, in its portrayal of divinity, it leaves no room for admiration and esteem. Whatever divine figure or specter is worshipped, a certain esteem and love is generally claimed by its worshippers. Or if, in the devotion paid to it, there is in truth no real or absolute esteem, there is nonetheless a certain astonishing delight or rapture excited.

This passion is experienced in common by every worshipper of the zealot type. The impulse, when unguided and left entirely to itself, is in its nature turbulent and provocative. It disturbs the natural order and relaxes the ordinary tone or mood of the mind. In this state, the reins are loosened for every passion that arises; and the mind, as far as it is able to act or think in such a state, approves the chaos and justifies the wild effects by the supposed sacredness of the cause. Every dream and frenzy is turned into inspiration; every feeling into zeal. And in this persuasion, the zealots—no longer self-governed but set adrift on the wide sea of passion—can, within the same spirit of devotion, express the opposite passions of love and hatred. They can unite affectionately and abhor furiously; curse, bless, sing, mourn, exult, tremble, caress, assassinate, inflict and suffer martyrdom,¹ with a thousand other intense efforts of shifting and contradictory emotions.

<meta>This page continues the analysis of the Egyptian priesthood's growth, attributing it to both legal privileges and the unique natural environment of Egypt.</meta>

Now if, besides the method of propagation by descent, other methods of increase were allowed in this order of men—if volunteers were also admitted at will, without any restriction or limitation to a specific number—it is not difficult to imagine how enormous the growth would be of such a science or profession. This profession, being thus recognized by the magistrate, thus invested with lands and power, and thus entitled to whatever extent of riches or possessions could be acquired through practice and influence over the superstitious part of mankind, would expand immensely.

There were, besides, in Egypt some natural causes of superstition beyond those which were common to other regions. This nation might well abound in prodigies, when even their country and soil itself was a kind of prodigy in nature. Their solitary, idle life while shut up in their houses by the regular inundations of the Nile; the unwholesome vapors arising from the new mud and slimy remains of their river exposed to the hot sun; their various meteors and phenomena, along with the long periods of leisure they had to observe and comment on them; the necessity, moreover, which—on account of their navigation and the measurement of their yearly flooded lands—compelled them to promote the studies of astronomy and other sciences, from which their priesthood could gain significant advantages; all these may perhaps be considered as additional causes for the immense growth of superstition and the enormous increase of the priesthood in this fertile land.

It will, however, as I conceive, be found unquestionably true, according to political arithmetic in every nation whatsoever, “that the quantity of superstition (if I may so speak) will in proportion nearly correspond to the number of priests, diviners, soothsayers, prophets, or those who gain their livelihood or receive advantages by officiating in religious affairs.” For if these dealers are numerous, they will force a trade. <meta>This page continues the argument that civil support and natural conditions allow professional orders, particularly the priesthood, to grow to an unsustainable size, eventually making them difficult for the civil authority to reform.</meta>

the generous hand of the magistrate can easily raise swarms of this kind where they are already present in only a moderate proportion; so where, through any other cause, their number—steadily increasing by degrees—is allowed to grow beyond a certain measure, they will soon create such a ferment in men’s minds that it will at least compel the magistrate, however aware of the grievance, to be cautious in proceeding with a reform.

We may observe in other necessary professions built upon the infirmities and defects of mankind (as, for instance, in law and medicine), “that with the slightest help from the generosity or kindness of the magistrate, the number of the practitioners and the scope of the profession is found to increase excessively.” New difficulties are raised, new subjects of contention; legal deeds and instruments grow more numerous and wordy; hypotheses, methods, and regimens become more various; and the *materia medica* becomes more extensive and abundant. Therefore, what must naturally have happened over time in the case of religion among the Egyptians can easily be inferred.

Nor is it strange that we should find that the property<sup>1</sup> and power of the Egyptian priesthood in ancient times reached such a height as to essentially swallow up the state and the monarchy. A worse accident befell the Persian crown: the hierarchy, having gained absolute possession of it, once had a fair chance for a universal empire. Superstition will never be lacking among the ignorant and common people as long as the capable and cunning have the power to acquire inheritances and possessions by exploiting this human weakness.

Moreover, we find that in the early days of this ancient priestly nation of whom we have been speaking, it was also thought useful, for the sake of increasing devotion, to enlarge their system of deities. Whether by mystical genealogy, consecration, or canonization, they multiplied their revealed objects of worship and raised new divine personages in their religion. They proceeded, it seems, in the course of time, to increase the number of their Gods,¹ so much so that at last they became in a sense countless. What odd shapes, species, and forms of deity were exhibited in later times is well known. Scarcely an animal or plant existed that was not adopted into some share of divinity.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of how religious institutions in ancient Egypt expanded their influence, shifting from the internal growth of deities and orders to the external expansion of their rituals and doctrines through colonization and cultural prestige.</meta>

<header>SHAFTESBURY'S CHARACTERISTICS</header>
<page-num>188</page-num>

It is no wonder that a nation so abundant in religious orders sought spiritual conquests in foreign countries, established colonies abroad,¹ and dispatched missionaries on expeditions in this thriving service. It was in this way that a fanatical people—influenced from ancient times by their very region and climate, and who over a long period of time, under a unique policy, had been raised by both art and nature to an immense growth in religious science and mystery—gradually came to spread their variety of rites and ceremonies. They spread their distinguishing marks of separate worship and secret communities throughout the distant world, but especially through their neighboring and dependent countries.

We learn from history that even when the Egyptian state was at its weakest in military power, it was still respected for its religion and mysteries. It drew strangers from all parts to witness its wonders. And the fertility of its soil forced the neighboring people, and wandering nations who lived dispersed in single tribes, to visit them, seek their alliance, and ask for trade and commerce with them on whatever terms. These strangers, no doubt, might easily accept religious rites and doctrines from those to whom they owed their survival and daily bread.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the Egyptian priesthood and how their professional and economic interests influenced the development of religious structures and social dynamics.</meta>

<header>SHAFTESBURY’S CHARACTERISTICS</header>
<page-num>194</page-num>

It appears also, from these considerations, how prone the religious profession was to spread itself widely in this region of the world, and what efforts would naturally be made by the more needy of these unlimited practitioners toward a fortune or maintenance for themselves and their successors.

Simple arithmetic will, in this case, demonstrate to us “that as the proportion of so many laymen to each priest grew every day less and less, so the wants and necessities of each priest must grow more and more.” The magistrate too, who, according to this Egyptian regulation, had resigned his title or share of right in sacred things, could no longer govern as he pleased in these affairs, or check the growing number of these practitioners. The spiritual generations were left to prey on others, and (like predatory fish) even on themselves, when destitute of other prey and confined within too narrow limits. What method, therefore, was there left to increase the zeal of worshippers and augment their liberality, but “to encourage their competition, prefer worship to worship, faith to faith, and turn the spirit of <term>enthusiasm</term> toward sacred horror, religious hatred, and mutual discord between worshippers”?

Thus provinces and nations were divided by the most contrary rites and customs which could be devised in order to create the strongest repulsion possible between creatures of a like species. For when all other hostilities are allayed, and anger of the fiercest kind appeased, religious hatred, we find, continues still, as it began, without provocation or voluntary offense. The presumed unbeliever and blasphemer, as one rejected and abhorred by God, is, through a pious imitation, abhorred by the opposing worshipper whose enmity must naturally increase as his religious zeal increases.

From this the opposition rose of temple against temple, convert against convert. The most zealous worship of one God was best expressed (as they conceived) by the open defiance of another. Surnames and titles of divinity passed as watch-

This resulted in deep-seated religious animosity between nations, where piety is expressed through the abhorrence of those with different beliefs.</summary>

Nor did philosophy,<note>2 *Below, Miscellaneous ii. ch. ii.*</note> when introduced into religion, extinguish this zeal; rather, it inflamed it, as we may perhaps show more particularly in our following chapter, if we return to this subject again, as is likely. For we perceive this is the kind of subject that is prone to expand in our hands. Therefore, we shall observe here only what is obvious to every student of sacred antiquities: that from the contentious learning and sophistry of the ancient schools (at a time when true science, philosophy, and the arts were already deep in their decline<note>3 Treatise iii. part ii. § 1; and part iii. § 3 in the notes. *Below, Miscellaneous ii. ch. ii.*</note>), religious problems of a similarly contentious form sprang up. Certain doctrinal tests were framed by which religious parties were engaged and enlisted against one another with more animosity than had ever been known in any other cause or quarrel. Thus religious massacres began and were carried out; temples were demolished, holy utensils destroyed, and sacred ceremonies trodden underfoot and insulted; and the insulters, in their turn, were exposed to the same treatment in their persons as well as in their worship. Thus madness and confusion were brought upon the world, like that chaos which the poet wonderfully describes in the speech of his mad hero, when even in celestial places disorder and blindness reigned; “No dawn of light”—

## CHAPTER II

->Judgment of divines and grave authors concerning enthusiasm—Reflections upon skepticism—A skeptic Christian—Judgment of the inspired concerning their own inspirations—Knowledge and belief—History of religion resumed—Zeal offensive and defensive—A Church in danger—Persecution—Policy of the Church of Rome.<-

What I had to remark of my own concerning enthusiasm I have thus dispatched; what others have remarked on the same subject I may, as an apologist for another author, be allowed to cite, especially if I take notice only of what has been mentioned very naturally by some of our most approved authors and ablest divines.

It has been thought an odd kind of boldness in our author to assert<note>1 Namely, in his *Letter concerning Enthusiasm*.</note> “that even atheism itself was not wholly exempt from enthusiasm, that there have been in reality enthusiastical atheists, and that even the spirit of martyrdom could, upon occasion, exert itself as well in this cause as in any other.” Now, besides what has been suggested in the preceding chapter, and what in fact may be demonstrated from the examples of Vaninus and other martyrs of a similar principle, we may hear an excellent and learned divine<note>2 Dr. Cudworth’s *Intellectual System*, p. 134.</note> of highest authority at home and fame abroad, who, after having described an enthusiastical atheist and one atheistically inspired, says of this very sort of men “that they are fanatics too, however that word seems to have a more peculiar respect to something of a deity; all atheists being that blind Goddess Nature’s fanatics.”

And again, “All atheists,” he says, “are possessed with a certain kind of madness that may be called *pneumatophobia*<note>3 The good doctor makes use here of a stroke of mockery against the overly-frightened anti-superstitious gentlemen, with whom our author reasons</note>

at length in his second Treatise (part ii. § 1). It is indeed the nature of fear, as with all other passions when excessive, to defeat its own purpose and prevent us from achieving what we naturally intend for our own benefit. Superstition itself is merely a certain kind of fear which, by overwhelming us with the perceived wrath or displeasure of divine powers, prevents us from judging what those powers truly are in themselves, or what conduct of ours might most reasonably be considered suitable to such highly rational and superior natures. Now, if the direction of this fear begins to change after experiencing many gross delusions of a superstitious kind, it is natural for it to run with equal violence in the opposite direction. The extreme passion for religious objects turns into an aversion. And a certain horror and dread of being deceived causes as much disturbance as the deception itself had caused previously. In such a situation, the mind may easily be blinded in either respect. It is plain that both these disorders carry something with them that reveals us to be, in some way, deprived of our reason and unable to properly use our judgment and understanding. For how can we be said to trust or use our reason if, in any case, we fear being convinced? How are we masters of ourselves when we have acquired the habit of bringing horror, aversion, favor, fondness, or any mood other than that of mere indifference and impartiality into the judgment of opinions and the search for truth?

with full confidence and trust in the opinions<note>1. *Advice to an Author*, toward the end; *Miscellaneous Reflections* ii. 3; v. 1, 3.</note> established by law. And if this is not sufficient to free him from the reproach of skepticism, he must, for all I can see, be content to endure it.

To tell the truth, I have often wondered to find such an outcry raised over the simple name of skeptic.<note>2. *The Moralists*, part i. § 2; *Miscellaneous Reflections* v. 3.</note> It is certain that, in its original and plain meaning, the word signifies no more than simply "that state or frame of mind in which everyone remains regarding every subject of which he is not certain." He who is certain, or presumes to say he knows in that particular instance—whether he is mistaken or in the right—is a *dogmatist*. Between these two states or mental situations, there can be no middle ground. For he who says "that he believes for certain, or is assured of what he believes," either speaks ridiculously or says in effect, "that he believes strongly, but is not sure." So that whoever is not personally aware of revelation, nor has certain knowledge of any miracle or sign, can be nothing more than a skeptic in that case; and the best Christian in the world, who, being destitute of the means of certainty, depends only on history and tradition for his belief in these particulars, is at best but a *skeptic Christian*. He has no more than a carefully critical<note>3. *Wit and Humour*, part iv. § 3; *Miscellaneous Reflections* v. 3.</note> historical faith, subject to various speculations and a thousand different criticisms of languages and literature.

He will naturally find this to be the case if he attempts to research the original sources in order to be his own judge and proceed on the foundation of his own discernment and understanding. If, on the other hand, he is not a critic, nor sufficiently learned in these original sources, it is plain he can have no original judgment of his own, but must still rely on the opinion of those who have the opportunity to examine such matters, and whom he takes to be the unbiased and disinterested judges of these religious narratives. His faith is not in ancient facts or people, nor in

No matter how positive or dogmatic a person may seem regarding these high points of learning, he is still in reality no dogmatist, nor can he in any way free himself from a certain kind of skepticism. He must know that he is still capable of doubting; or if, out of fear of doubt, he strives to banish every opposing thought and resolves not even to deliberate on the case, this still will not clear him. We are so far from being able to be sure whenever we choose to be; indeed, we can never be thoroughly sure except when we cannot help it, and find by necessity that we must be so, whether we wish to be or not. Even the highest implicit faith is in reality nothing more than a kind of passive skepticism: “*a resolution to examine, remember, consider, or hear as little as possible that might damage that belief which, having once embraced it, we are ever afterward afraid to lose.*”

The holy founders and inspired authors of our religion did not require, it seems, such a strict assent or such implicit faith on behalf of their original writings and revelations as later uninspired doctors—without the help of divine testimony or any miracle on their side—have required on behalf of their own comments and interpretations. It is said that the earliest and worst of heretics were those called Gnostics, who took their name from an audacious pretense to certain knowledge and comprehension of the greatest mysteries of faith. If the most dangerous state of opinion was this dogmatic and presumptuous sort, the safest, in all likelihood, must be the skeptical and modest.

Nothing is more evident than that our holy religion, in its original constitution, was set so far apart from all philosophy or refined speculation that it seemed, in a manner, diametrically opposed to it. A man might have been not only a skeptic in all the controversial points of the academies or schools of learning, but even a perfect stranger to everything of this kind, and yet be complete in his religion, faith, and worship.

The different provinces of religion and philosophy were upheld, as we know, without interfering with each other in the least. If in some primitive nations the philosopher and priest were joined as one, it is observable that the mysteries, whatever they were, which sprang from this extraordinary union were kept secret and undisclosed. It was satisfaction enough for the priest-philosopher if the initiated person preserved his respect and veneration for the tradition and worship of the temple by complying in every respect with the required performances and rites of worship. No account was afterwards taken of the philosophical faith of the convert or worshiper. His opinions were left to himself, and he might philosophize according to whatever foreign school or sect he fancied. Even among the Jews themselves, the Sadducee (a materialist and denier of the soul's immortality) was as well accepted as the Pharisee—who, from the schools of Pythagoras, Plato, or other later philosophers of Greece, had learned to reason about immaterial substances and the natural immortality of souls.

It is no astonishing reflection to observe how fast the world declined in wit and sense <note>*Advice*, part ii. § 1, and in the preceding chapter, at the end.</note>, in manhood, reason, science, and in every art once the Roman Empire had prevailed and spread a universal tyranny and oppression over mankind. Even the Romans themselves, after the early pleasures of one peaceful and long reign, began to groan under that yoke of which they had been the imposers. How much more must other nations and mighty cities at a far distance have abhorred this tyranny and recognized their common servitude under a people who were themselves no better than mere slaves?

It may be looked upon, no doubt, as providential that at this time, and in these circumstances of the world, there should arise such a high expectation of a divine deliverer; and that from the eastern parts and borders of Judea, the opinion should spread of such a deliverer to come, with strength from heaven sufficient to break that Empire, which no earthly

When, along with this, the schools of the ancient philosophers,¹ which had been in decline for a long time, were finally dissolved, and their sophistical teachers became ecclesiastical instructors, the unnatural union of religion and philosophy was completed. The monstrous product of this match soon appeared in the world. The odd external shapes of deities, temples, and holy utensils, which had formerly been set in battle against each other by the Egyptian sects,² were now transformed into philosophical forms and phantoms. Like flags and banners, these were displayed in a hostile manner and carried offensively by one party against another. In former times, those aforementioned barbarous nations were the only warriors in these religious causes; but now the entire world became engaged when other banners were erected instead of storks and crocodiles. Now, sophistical fantasies, obscure notions, bombastic phrases, grammatical blunders, absurdities, and a thousand monsters of a scholastic breed were unleashed and made the subject of popular animosity and dispute.

Here first began that spirit of bigotry which broke out in a more raging manner than had ever been known before, and was less capable of restraint or moderation than any species, form, or mixture of religion in the ancient world. Mysteries which were previously treated with profound respect, and remained hidden from common eyes, became public and corrupted. They were enforced with terrors and urged with compulsion and violence upon the inadequate capacities and understandings of mankind. Even the Jewish traditions and cabalistic learning underwent this fate. That which was naturally the subject of profound speculation and inquiry was made the required subject of a strict and absolute agreement. The allegorical, mythological account of sacred

Thus a sort of philosophical enthusiasm spread across the world. And **bigotry**<note>2. Let anyone who carefully considers the meaning and force of the word "bigotry" try to translate it into either of the ancient languages, and he will find what a unique passion it implies, and how different it is from the mere feeling of enthusiasm or superstition.</note> (a species of superstition hardly known before) took hold of men’s affections and armed them with a new jealousy against each other. Barbarous terms and idioms were introduced every day, monstrous definitions were invented and imposed, new schemes of faith were erected from time to time, and the fiercest imaginable hostilities were exercised on these occasions. So the enthusiasm or zeal, which was usually shown by mankind on behalf of their particular forms of worship, and which for the most part had previously been defensive only, now became universally offensive.

It may be expected of me, perhaps, that having moved from remote antiquity to later periods, I should speak on this occasion with more than ordinary exactness and regularity. It may be argued against me that I talk here at random and without evidence, neglecting to produce my authorities or continue my quotations according to the professional style and manner in which I began this present chapter. But as there are many greater privileges—by way of variation, interruption, and digression—allowed to us writers of **Miscellany**, and especially to those who are commentators upon other authors, I shall be content to remain mysterious in this respect and explain myself no further than by a well-known story, which seems to suit our author’s purpose and the present argument.

It is observable from Holy Scripture that the ancient Ephesian

Nothing could be more moderate and wise, nothing more agreeable to that magisterial science or policy which our author recommends,^1 than the behavior of the town clerk or recorder of the city, as he is represented on this occasion in Holy Scripture. I must confess indeed, he went quite far in the use of this moderating art. He ventured to assure the people “that everyone agreed in their ancient worship of the great Goddess, and in their tradition of the image which fell down from Jupiter; that these were undeniable facts, and that the new sect neither intended the pulling down of their church, nor even offered to blaspheme or speak poorly of their Goddess.”

This, no doubt, was stretching the point enough, as may be understood by the events that followed later. One might, perhaps, have suspected this recorder of being a dissenter himself, or at least an <term>occasional conformist</term>, who could answer so confidently for the new sect and guarantee that the church was secure from damage and out of all danger for the future. Meanwhile, the riot was calmed; no harm befell the temple at that time. The new sect accepted what had been spoken on their behalf. They allowed the apology of the recorder. Accordingly, the zeal of the heathen church, which was only defensive, gave way, and the new religionists were prosecuted no further.

Hitherto, it seems, the face of persecution had not openly shown itself in the wide world. It was sufficient security for every man that he caused no disturbance to what was publicly established. ### JULIAN TO THE BOSTRENIANS

> "I should have thought, indeed, that the Galilæan leaders would have felt themselves more indebted to me than to him who preceded me in the administration of the Empire. For in his time, many of them suffered exile, persecution, and imprisonment. Multitudes of those whom they call heretics in their religion were put to the sword; so much so that in Samosata, Cyzicus, Paphlagonia, Bithynia, Galatia, and many other countries, entire towns were leveled with the earth. The exact opposite has been observed in my time. The exiles have been recalled, and the outlawed restored to the lawful possession of their estates. But these people have arrived at such a height of fury and madness that, because they are no longer allowed the privilege to tyrannize over one another, or to persecute either their own dissenters or the followers of the lawful church, they swell with rage. They leave no stone unturned and miss no opportunity to raise turmoil and rebellion; they have so little regard for true piety and so little obedience to our laws and constitutions, however humane and tolerant they may be. For we are still determined and steadily resolved never to allow one of them to be drawn involuntarily to our altars. . . . As for the common people, indeed, they appear driven to these riots and rebellions by those among them whom they call clerics, who are now enraged to find themselves restrained in the use of their former power and unrestrained rule. . . . They can no longer act as the magistrate or civil judge, nor assume authority to draft people’s wills, push aside relatives, seize other men’s inheritances, and, by deceptive pretenses, transfer everything into their own possession. . . . Nevertheless, they may assemble in their congregations as they please and crowd around their leaders, performing worship, receiving doctrine, and praying, according as they

In this extreme situation, it might perhaps have been considered the best wish for mankind that one of these conflicting parties of incompatible religious groups should eventually triumph over the others, so that, through universal and absolute power, they could define orthodoxy,¹ and make that opinion effectively universal (catholic) which, in their specific judgment, had the best right to that name. I will conclude by observing how skillfully the Roman-Christian and once-universal (catholic) church, with the help of their converted emperors,² proceeded in establishing their growing hierarchy. > are taught and guided by them; but if there is any tendency toward rebellion, let them be careful how they listen or agree, and remember that it is at their own risk if they are secretly stirred up to mutiny and insurrection. . . . Therefore, I repeatedly command and charge the zealous followers of the true religion in no way to injure, harass, or insult the Galilean people." Thus spoke the generous and mild Emperor, whom we may indeed call a heathen, but not so accurately an apostate; since, having been transferred to different schools or universities at various times during his youth and raised under tutors of each religion (both heathen and Christian), he happened, upon reaching adulthood, to make his choice (though very unfortunately) in the former and adhered to the ancient religion of his country and ancestors. They are indeed so far from being suspicious of mere enthusiasm or the ecstatic manner of devotion that they allow their mystics to write and preach in the most rapturous and seraphic styles. They allow them, in a sense, to bypass all external worship and triumph over outward forms, until these refined religious thinkers go so far as to—either explicitly or apparently—discourage the practice of the common and established ceremonial duties. And then, indeed,<note>Witness the case of Molinos, and of the pious, worthy, and ingenious Abbé Fénelon, now Archbishop of Cambray.</note> they restrain the supposedly excessive enthusiasm, which would prove dangerous to their hierarchical state.

If modern visions, prophecies, and dreams, charms, miracles, exorcisms, and the rest of this kind are included in what we call fanaticism or superstition, they allow this spirit full reign; meanwhile, on the other hand, they grant candid writers the liberty to politely question these spiritual feats performed in monasteries, or here and there by their mendicant or traveling priests and spiritual missionaries.

This is that ancient hierarchy which, regarding its original foundation, its policy, and the consistency of its entire structure and constitution, cannot help but appear in some respect grand and venerable, even to those whom we do not usually consider to have weak judgment. These are the spiritual conquerors who, like the first Caesars, established the foundations of an almost universal monarchy from small beginnings. It is no wonder if, today, a direct view of this hierarchical residence—the city and court of Rome—is found to have an extraordinary effect on foreigners from other, more recent churches. It is no wonder if the amazed observers are hereafter so inclined either to feel the most intense aversion to all priestly government or, on the contrary, to admire it so much that they even wish for a merger or reunion with this ancient mother church.

## CHAPTER III

->On the power of humor in religion—Support of our author’s argument in his essay on the freedom of wit and raillery—Zeal discussed. Spiritual surgeons, executioners, and carvers—The origin of human sacrifice—The exhilaration of religion—Various aspects arising from outward causes.<-

THE celebrated wits of the <term>miscellanarian</term> race—the essay writers, casual conversationalists, coiners of reflections, founders of meditations, and other irregular kinds of writers—may plead as their peculiar advantage “that they follow the variety of Nature.” And in a climate such as ours, their plea is no doubt very just. We islanders, famous for other forms of changeability, are particularly noted for the variableness and inconstancy of our weather. And if our taste in literature is found to correspond to this temperature of our climate, it is certain that a writer must, in our estimation, be considered more valuable in his field the more he can agreeably surprise

Were it not for the known prevalence of this taste, and the apparent deference paid to those geniuses who are said to elevate and surprise, the author of these Miscellanies might, in all probability, be afraid to entertain his reader with this varied, complex, and rambling kind of reading. It is certain that if we consider the beginning and progress of our present work, we shall find sufficient variation in it. From a declared levity, we have slid into a kind of seriousness unsuitable to our manner of starting out. We have steered an adventurous course and seem newly come out of a stormy and rough sea. It is time indeed that we should enjoy a calm; and instead of expanding our sails before the swelling gusts, it is right for us to shelter near the shore and ply our oars in smooth water.

It is the philosopher, the orator, or the poet whom we may compare to some first-rate vessel which launches out into the wide sea and, with a proud motion, defies the oncoming waves. We essay-writers are of the small craft or galley kind. We move chiefly by starts and bounds, according to how our motion is renewed at frequent intervals. We have no great adventure in view, nor can we tell certainly where we are headed. We undertake no mighty voyage by the help of stars or compass, but row from creek to creek, keep up a coastal trade, and are fitted only for fair weather and the summer season.

Therefore, it is happy for us in particular that, having finished our course on Enthusiasm and followed our author into his second treatise,<note>Namely, *An Essay on the Freedom of Wit and Humour*.</note> we are now at last obliged to turn toward more pleasant reflections and have such subjects in view as must naturally lead us to a more familiar style. Wit and humor (the declared subject of the treatise now before us) will hardly bear to be examined in ponderous sentences and balanced discourse. We might now perhaps do best to lay aside the seriousness of strict argument and resume the way of casual conversation, which, through an aversion—

And an abundance of forced instruction and solemn advice may have made men just as averse to anything delivered with an air of high wisdom and science—especially if it is presented as being so high that it is set above all human art of reasoning, and even above reason itself, according to its sublime dispensers.

However, since certain formalists of this sort may object to us that "we can prove nothing properly without proving it in a formal way," we may for once give in to their demand, state our case formally, and divide our subject into parts, according to precise rules and methods.

Our purpose, therefore, being to defend an author who has been accused of being too presumptuous for introducing the use of wit and humor into religious investigations, we shall endeavor to show:

1st. That wit and humor support religion and promote true faith.

2nd. That they are used as appropriate tools of this kind by the holy founders of religion.

3rd. That despite the gloomy disposition and sour temperament of some religious teachers, it may be rightly said that we have, overall, a witty and good-humored religion.

Among the acquaintances of my early youth, I remember specifically a club of three or four merry gentlemen who had long kept company with one another and were seldom apart during any social gathering or diversion. They happened once to be on a traveling adventure and arrived in a country where they were told for certain that they would find the worst hospitality, as well as the worst roads imaginable. One of the gentlemen, who seemed the least concerned about this disaster, said casually and without any apparent ulterior motive, "that the best solution for them in this emergency would be to keep themselves in high spirits and try to praise everything..."

...which the place afforded." The other gentlemen immediately took the hint, but, as it happened, kept silent, moved past the subject, and took no further notice of what had been proposed.

Having entered the dismal country, through which they proceeded without the least complaint, it was remarkable that if by any great chance they came to any tolerable bit of road or any ordinary view, they did not fail to say something or other in its praise. They would often come upon such pleasant fancies and descriptions that the objects actually became agreeable.

When most of the day had been spent in this way, and our gentlemen arrived where they intended to stay for the night, the first of them who sampled the food, or tasted either a drink or a dish, recommended it with such an air of confidence and such lively expressions of approval that the others immediately adopted his opinion. They confirmed his enjoyment with many additional praises of their own.

Many clever reasons were given for the various odd tastes and appearances of the things presented to them at the table. "Some meats were healthy, others had a strong flavor, others were prepared according to the customs of this or that foreign country." Every dish had the flavor of some famous recipe; and the wine and other liquors, in their turn, had the benefit of being discussed in the same refined manner. In short, our gentlemen ate and drank heartily and accepted their mediocre fare so well that it was apparent they had convinced themselves they were reasonably well served.

Their servants, meanwhile, having made no such plan for themselves, kept their wits about them and insisted "that their masters had certainly lost theirs. For how else could they eat so contentedly and accept everything set before them as good?"

If I were dealing with a malicious reader, he might perhaps try to infer from this story of my traveling friends that I

But it can surely never be thought that people of true judgment and understanding would set about such a task as perverting their own judgment and giving a wrong bias to their reason. They must easily foresee that an attempt of this kind, if it had even the slightest success, would prove to have far worse consequences for them than any perversion of their taste, appetite, or ordinary senses.

I must admit, however, that in my view, when the right circumstances align and many tempting opportunities arise from self-interest, temperament, or passion, it is no extraordinary case to see people enter into such a plot as this against their own understandings. They endeavor by all possible means to persuade both themselves and others of what they think convenient and useful to believe.

If in many particular cases, where favoritism and affection prevail, we find it so easy to deceive ourselves, it surely cannot be very hard to do so where we assume our highest interest is concerned. Now, it is certainly no small interest or concern for people to believe what is established by authority, since in the case of disbelief, there can be no choice left but either to live as a hypocrite or be considered profane. Even where people are left to themselves and allowed the freedom of choice, they are still eager enough to believe, and can dutifully endeavor to persuade themselves of the truth of any flattering deception.

Nor is it unusual to find people successful in this endeavor; as, among other instances, may appear by the many religious faiths or opinions, however preposterous or contradictory, which we know have been raised, age after age, on the foundation of miracles and pretended commissions from heaven. These have been as generally embraced and passionately cherished as the greatest truths and most certain revelations. It is hardly to be supposed that such combinations should be formed, and

It is certain that in a country where faith has for a long time been inherited, and opinions are fixed by law, there is little room left for the common people to change their persuasion or deliberate on the choice of their religious belief. Whenever a government thinks fit to concern itself with men’s opinions and, by its absolute authority, imposes any particular belief, there is perhaps none so ridiculous or monstrous that the government needs to doubt its success. We may see this thoroughly accomplished in certain countries by a steady policy and consistent application of punishment and reward, assisted by particular courts established for this purpose, unique methods of justice, specific magistrates and officers, proper investigations, and certain “wholesome severities”—not lightly administered or trifled with (as some foolish people suggest), but duly and properly enforced, as is absolutely necessary to achieve strict conformity and unity in one and the same profession and manner of worship.

But should it happen to be the truth itself which was effectively spread by the means we have described, the very nature of such means can, however, allow little honor to the spreaders and little merit to the disciples and believers. It is certain that Islam, Paganism, Judaism, or any other belief may stand just as well as the truest faith upon this foundation. He who is now an orthodox Christian would, by virtue of such discipline, have been just as surely a true Muslim or as wandering a heretic, had he been born in another place.

# MISCELLANEOUS REFLECTIONS

magistrate, it will have a sufficient advantage, without any help from force or threats on one hand, or extraordinary favor and partial treatment on the other. If the belief is in any measure consistent with truth and reason, it will find as much favor in the eyes of mankind as truth and reason could desire. Whatever difficulties there may be in any particular speculations or mysteries belonging to it, the better sort of men will endeavor to pass them over. They will believe (as our author <gloss>1</gloss> says) to the full extent of their reason, and spur on their faith, in order to be more sociable and conform better to what their interest, in conjunction with their good humor, inclines them to accept as credible and observe as their religious duty and devotional task.

This is where good humor will naturally take over, and the hospitable disposition of our traveling friends mentioned above will easily transfer itself into religion, and operate in the same manner with respect to the established faith (however miraculous or incomprehensible) under a tolerant, mild, and gentle government.

Everyone knows, indeed, that by heresy is understood a stubbornness of the will, not merely a defect in the understanding. On this account, it is impossible that an honest and good-humored man should be a schismatic or heretic, or choose to separate from his national worship for slight reasons or without severe provocation.

To be pursued by petty inquisitors; to be threatened with punishment or penal laws; to be singled out as dangerous and suspicious; to be ranted against in high places with all the studied wit and art of slander, are indeed sufficient provocations to ill humor, and may force people to divide who at first never had any such intention. But the virtue of good humor in religion is such that it can even reconcile people to a belief in which they were never raised, or toward which they had previously held a prejudice.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on religious tolerance, moving from the benefits of "good humor" and social conformity to the failures and psychological impact of religious persecution.</meta>

From these considerations, we must naturally conclude, “That there is nothing so ridiculous regarding policy, or so wrong and hateful regarding common humanity, as a moderate and halfway persecution.” It only irritates the wound; it stirs up the bad temper of mankind; excites those with sharper spirits; causes outrage in observers; and sows the very seeds of division in men’s hearts. A determined and blatant persecution leaves no time or opportunity for these developing ailments or gathering resentments. It does the work all at once, through extermination, banishment, or massacre; and, like a bold stroke in surgery, completes with one quick amputation what a clumsy hand would only make worse and worse, to the endless suffering and misery of the patient.

If there is any way on earth to make the most sacred truth seem suspicious, it is by supporting it with threats and pretending to terrify people into believing it. This is a way of challenging humanity in a cause where they know they are superior and out of reach. The weakest person finds within himself that although he may be outsmarted and deceived, he can never be forced regarding his opinion or agreement. And there are few men so ignorant of human nature, and of what they share in common with their kind, that they do not understand “that when someone expresses great intensity regarding something that concerns only someone else, it is rarely without some private interest of his own.”

In ordinary arguments, the angry debater makes even the best cause look like the worst. A countryman once took a fancy to hear the Latin debates of scholars at a university. He was asked what pleasure he could find in watching such combatants, when he could not even know which of the parties was winning. “As for that,” replied the countryman, “I am not such a fool either; I can see who is the first to make the other lose his temper.” Nature itself taught this lesson to the countryman: that the person with the better argument would be relaxed and good-tempered, but the one unable to support his cause with reason would naturally lose his temper and become violent.

If two travelers agreed to tell their story separately in public, one being a man of sincerity but firm and dogmatic, and the other less sincere but easygoing and good-humored; even if the accounts of the latter gentleman were of a more miraculous sort, they would still gain belief sooner and be more favorably received by mankind than the strongly asserted reports and vehement narratives of the other fierce defender of the truth.

That good humor is a primary cause of compliance or agreement in matters of faith can be proved from the very spirit of those we commonly call critics. It is a known prejudice against gentlemen of this character "that they are generally ill-humored and irritable." The world insists that their bad temper disturbs them. And I must confess I think the world in general is right in this notion: that although perhaps not all critics are necessarily irritable, all irritable people (whether naturally so or made so by ill-treatment) have a necessary inclination toward criticism and satire. When men are at ease with themselves, they let others remain so, and can readily go along with what seems plausible and is thought to contribute to the peace or good relations of mankind. They strive to raise no difficulties or doubts. And in religious affairs, it is rare for them to be eager to entertain bad thoughts or suspicions as long as they are unmolested. But if they are disturbed by groundless accusations and suspicions, by unnecessary insults and bitter speeches, and by a contentious, quarrelsome version of religion, they naturally become critics and begin to question everything. The spirit of satire rises with a bad mood; and the primary passion of men who are thus afflicted and driven out of good humor is to find fault, censure, unravel, confuse, and leave nothing without exception or controversy.

These are the skeptics or scrupulists, against whom such an outcry is raised. Meanwhile, it is evident that the outcry itself, joined with the usual threats and display

Should anyone who happens to read these lines perceive in himself a rising animosity against the author for asserting thus zealously the notion of a religious liberty and mutual toleration, it is my wish that he would maturely deliberate on the cause of his disturbance and ill-humor. If he would deign to look closely into himself, he would undoubtedly find that it is not zeal for religion or the truth which moves him on this occasion. For had he happened to be in a nation where he was not a conformist, nor had any hope or expectation of obtaining the priority for his own manner of worship, he would have found nothing preposterous in this our doctrine of indulgence. It is an indisputable fact that whatever sect or religion is the underdog—though it may have persecuted at any time before—as soon as it begins to suffer persecution in its turn, it returns instantly to the principles of moderation and maintains this our plea for civility, sociability, and good humor in religion. We come now (as traditional rhetoricians express themselves) to our second main topic, which we should again subdivide into first and second points, except that this manner of dividing a subject has recently become quite unfashionable.

It was the custom of our ancestors, perhaps as far back as the days of our hospitable King Arthur, to have nothing served at the table but what was whole and substantial. It was a whole boar or a solid ox that made the feast. The figure of the animal was preserved entire, and the carving was performed formally by the appointed carver—a man of strength as well as profound skill and notable dexterity. He was seen standing tall, with a handsome appearance and movement, displaying the heads and limbs, dividing them according to his art, and distributing his subject matter into proper portions, suitable to the appetites of those he served. In more recent days, it has become the fashion to eat with less ceremony and method. Everyone chooses to carve for himself. The learned manner of carving is no longer in demand; instead, a certain method of cookery has been introduced by which the anatomical science of the table is entirely set aside. Ragouts and fricassees are the reigning dishes, in which everything is so dismembered and thrown out of all order and form that no part of the mass can properly be divided or distinguished from another.

In this respect, religion—according to the common practice in many sects—may be compared to the type of courtship about which women are known often to complain. In the beginning of a romance, when these innocent charmers are first approached, they hear of nothing but tender vows, submission, service, and love. But soon afterward, when won by this appearance of gentleness and humility, they have surrendered themselves and are no longer their own, they hear a different note and are taught to understand "submission" and "service" in a sense they little expected. Charity and brotherly love are very appealing sounds; but who would imagine that out of abundant charity and brotherly love should come steel, fire, gallows, rods, and such a vigorous and thorough application of these remedies? These are used to simultaneously advance the worldly greatness of religious leaders and the specific interests of private souls, for whom they are so charitably concerned.

When the affairs of the Jewish nation grew desperate, and everything seemed to be tending toward a total conquest and captivity, the style of their holy writers and prophets might well differ from those of earlier days during the rise and vigor of their commonwealth, or during the first splendor of their monarchy, when the princes themselves prophesied and powerful kings were among the number of the sacred writers. Witness the case of the prophet Jonah, whose character is so naturally described in Holy Scripture.

Irritable as this prophet was—unmanly, and resembling some stubborn, boyish pupil instead—it may be said that God, like a kind tutor, was pleased to humor him, bear with his anger, and in a playful manner expose his childish stubbornness and show him his true self.

But the next morning a worm came, and an east wind; the arbor was withered, the sun shone intensely, and the prophet’s head was heated as before. Soon the bad mood returns, and the prophet is back to his old state. “Better to die than live at this rate. Death—death alone can satisfy me. Let me hear no longer of living. No! It is useless to talk of it.”<note>Ibid. 7-8.</note>

Again God reasons with him; but he is cut short and answered rudely by the irritable prophet. “He is angry, he ought to be angry, and he will be angry until his death.”<note>Ibid. 9.</note> But the Almighty, with the greatest pity toward him in this gloomy and stubborn mood, reveals the folly of it. He encourages him toward mildness and good humor in the most tender manner and through the most familiar and pleasant imagery; while He shows significantly more regard and tenderness toward the very cattle and brute animals than the prophet shows toward his own human kind, and even toward those very disciples whom he had converted by his preaching.<note>See the last verse of this prophet [Jonah 4:11].</note>

As for our Savior’s style, it is no more vehement and majestic in his gravest criticisms or declamatory speeches than it is sharp, humorous, and witty in his repartees, reflections, fictional narrations or parables, similes, comparisons, and other methods of milder censure and reproof; his exhortations to his disciples, his particular description of their manners, the pleasant images under which he often hides his morals and practical rules; even his miracles themselves (especially the first he ever performed<note>John 2:11.</note>) carry with them a certain festivity, cheerfulness, and good humor so remarkable that I would consider it impossible not to be moved in a pleasant way by their recital.

Now, if what I have asserted here in favor of pleasantry and humor is found to be just and true regarding the Jewish and Christian religions, I do not doubt it will be granted to me, regarding the ancient heathen institutions, that the highest care was taken by their original founders and subsequent reformers to make religion cheerful, and to correct that melancholy and gloominess to which it is subject, according to those different forms of enthusiasm specified above.<note>Above, chapters 1, 2.</note>

and gravity. I have very solemnly pleaded for cheerfulness and good humor; I have spoken out against pedantry in scholarly language and opposed excessive formality; I now find myself somewhat impatient to get free from the constraint of method. I claim the right to exercise the privilege I have asserted of rambling from subject to subject, from style to style, in my miscellaneous manner, according to my current profession and character.

I may, in the meantime, probably be criticized for skipping over my third point. But the methodical reader, if he is scrupulous about it, may content himself with looking back; if he can possibly pick it out of my second point, he will forgive this anticipation in a writing that is governed less by form than by humor. I had indeed decided to make a large collection of passages from our most eminent and learned theologians in order to set forth this latter section of my chapter, and by better authority than my own to have demonstrated “that we had, in the main, a good-humored religion.” But after considering a little while, I came to this brief conclusion: “that it was better not to cite at all than to cite partially.” Now, if I cited fairly what was said on both the gloomy and the cheerful sides of our religion, I found the matter would be quite doubtfully balanced. The result in the end would be this: “that, generally speaking, whenever a theologian was in a good mood, we would find religion to be the sweetest and most good-humored thing in nature; but at other times (and quite often), we would find a very different state of affairs.”

Thus, we are alternately exalted and humbled, cheered and dejected, depending on how our spiritual<gloss>1</gloss> director is himself influenced. This is done, perhaps, for our edification and advantage, “so that by these contradictions and changes we may be made more flexible and compliant.” If we are very low and down, we are lifted up; if we are up and high, we are brought down. This is discipline; this is authority and command. Did

Because of this, we might perhaps become more resistant toward its spiritual teachers, and be less inclined to submit ourselves to those who, by appointment and authority, represent it to us in whatever lights they deem most appropriate and convenient.

I shall therefore conclude not only abruptly but even skeptically on this, my final point, referring my reader to what has already been said in my preceding sections for the mere probability "that we have, overall, a witty and good-humored religion."

This, however, I may venture to claim: that there are undoubtedly some countenances or aspects of our religion which are humorous and pleasant in themselves, and that the more mournful representations of it are often so excessively sad and gloomy that they are likely to provoke a passion quite opposite to what is intended by those who represent it.

Having already asserted my privilege as a miscellaneous or essay writer of the modern establishment to write on every subject and in every method as I fancy, to use order or lay it aside as I think fit, and to treat of order and method in other works, though free perhaps and unconfined as to my own; I shall presume, in this place, to consider the present method and order of my author’s treatises as they are arranged in this joint edition.

Notwithstanding the high airs of skepticism which our author assumes in his first piece, I cannot, after all, but imagine that even there he proves himself at the bottom a real dogmatist, and shows plainly that he has his private opinion, belief, or faith, as strong as any devotee or religionist of them all. Though he affects perhaps to strike at other hypotheses and schemes, he has something of his own still in reserve, and holds a certain plan or system peculiar to himself, or at least such a one in which he has at present but few companions or followers.

Even in this, his third piece, he maintains the same skeptical manner; and what he offers as a project or hypothesis is very faint, hardly spoken aloud, but muttered to himself in a kind of doubtful whisper or feigned soliloquy. What may be justly argued in his defense when we join him to investigate such solemn and profound subjects seems very doubtful. Meanwhile, as his affairs stand so far in this, his treatise of advice, I shall be content to join him and proceed in my miscellaneous style, to give my advice also to notable men, whether they are authors or politicians, <term>virtuosi</term> or fine gentlemen; including him, the said author, as one of those being advised, and myself too (if the occasion arises) following his own example of self-warning and private address.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the history of arts and sciences, specifically focusing on how philosophy followed other arts and reached its height in Greece.</meta>

other arts had been raised and advanced in a certain proportion before it. And as this was of the greatest dignity and weight, it was the last to take form. It spent a long time clearing itself of the affected style of sophists or the enthusiastic air of poets, and appeared late in its genuine, simple, and true beauty.

The reader may perhaps rightly excuse our author for having so overloaded his margins in this section with those weighty authorities and ancient citations <note>¹ *Advice to an Author*, part ii. § 2.</note>, once the reader realizes that there are many serious professors of the humanities and literature among the moderns who are puzzled by this investigation, and who write in opposition both to one another and to the plain and natural evidence of the case. The real lineage and succession of wit is indeed plainly founded in Nature, as our author has endeavored to demonstrate through both history and fact. Just as the Greek nation is original to us regarding these polite arts and sciences, it was also, in reality, original to itself. For whether the Egyptians, Phoenicians, Thracians, or barbarians of any kind might have fortunately stumbled upon this or that particular invention—whether in agriculture, building, navigation, or letters—or whichever group might have introduced this religious rite, this title of a deity, this or that musical instrument, or this or that festival, game, or dance (for there are intense debates among the learned on this matter), it is evident beyond a doubt that the arts and sciences were formed in Greece itself. It was there that music, poetry, and the rest began to take shape and be distinguished into their various orders and degrees. Whatever flourished or was raised to any degree of correctness or real perfection of its kind was due to Greece alone, and achieved by that uniquely polite, most civilized, and accomplished nation.

Nor can this seem strange when we consider the fortunate constitution of that people. For though they were composed of different tribes, distinct in their laws and governments, divided by seas and continents, and dispersed across distant islands, they were nonetheless originally of the same descent, united by a single language, and animated

--- Page 254 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion on how the arts and sciences were uniquely formed and refined within the free and social environment of ancient Greece, having achieved internal development before being exported.</meta>

<page-num>242</page-num>
<header>SHAFTESBURY’S CHARACTERISTICS</header>

Through that social, public, and free spirit which—despite the animosity of their various warring states—led them to establish such heroic assemblies and powers as those which constituted the Amphictyonian councils, the Olympic, Isthmian, and other games, they could not help but naturally polish and refine each other. It was in this way that they brought their beautiful and comprehensive language to a proper standard, leaving only such variety in the dialects as made their poetry, in particular, all the more pleasant. This standard was similarly applied to other arts; the necessary distinctions were made; the various categories were identified and set apart; the performers and masters of every kind were honored and admired; and, finally, even critics themselves were acknowledged and accepted as masters over all the rest. From music, poetry, and rhetoric, down to the simple prose of history, and through all the <term>plastic arts</term> of sculpture, statuary, painting, architecture, and the rest; everything inspired by the muses, graceful, and exquisite was rewarded with the highest honors and pursued with the utmost passion and competition. Thus Greece, though she exported arts to other nations, essentially had no imports of that kind for herself. The most that could be mentioned would amount to no more than raw materials in a crude and primitive form. Therefore, the nation was clearly original in art; and among them every noble study and science was (as the great master <note>Aristotle</note>, so often cited by our author, says of certain kinds of poetry) self-formed,¹ crafted out of Nature, and drawn from the necessary operation and course of things, developing, as it were, of their own accord and natural tendency.

---

¹ αὐτοσχεδιαστική <note>improvisational</note>. Treatise iii. part ii. § 2. It is in this sense of the natural production and self-formation of the arts, in this free state of ancient Greece, that the same great master uses this word a little earlier, in the same chapter of his *Poetics* (the 4th), speaking in general of the poets: κατὰ μικρὸν προάγοντες, ἐγέννησαν τὴν ποίησιν, ἐκ τῶν αὐτοσχεδιασμάτων. <note>“Advancing step by step they produced poetry out of their improvisations.”—Aristotle, *Poetics* iv. 6.</note> And shortly after, λέξεως δὲ γενομένης, αὐτὴ ἡ φύσις τὸ οἰκεῖον μέτρον εὗρε. <note>“When dialogue was introduced, Nature herself found out the appropriate meter.”—Ibid. iv. 14.</note>

He notes that this process established standards for language, poetry, and all the fine arts, eventually giving rise to the authority of critics.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the development of the arts in ancient Greece, moving from the initial stages of artistic expression to the refinement of taste and simplicity, and begins a comparison with the history of English public discourse.</meta>

<page-num>243</page-num>
<header>MISCELLANEOUS REFLECTIONS</header>

Now, according to this natural growth of arts peculiar to Greece, it would necessarily happen that at the beginning, when the force of language came to be first proved, when the admiring world made its first judgment and tried its taste in elegancies of this sort, the lofty, the sublime, the astonishing, and the amazing would be the most in fashion and preferred. Metaphorical speech, a multiplicity of figures, and high-sounding words would naturally prevail. Although in the commonwealth itself and in the affairs of government men were originally used to plain and direct speech, yet when speaking became an art and was taught by sophists and other pretended masters, the high poetic and figurative way began to prevail even at the Bar and in the public assemblies; so much so that the grand-master <note>Aristotle</note>, in the above-cited part of his *Rhetorics*, where he extols the tragic poet Euripides, rebukes the rhetoricians of his own age who retained that very bombastic style which even poets—and those of the tragic kind—had already discarded, or at least considerably softened. But the taste of Greece was now being refined. A better judgment was soon formed once a Demosthenes was heard and had found success. The people themselves (as our author has shown) now came to reform their comedy and familiar manner, after tragedy and the higher style had been brought to its perfection by the final hand of an Euripides. And now in all the principal works of ingenuity and art, simplicity and Nature began chiefly to be sought; and this was the taste which lasted through so many ages, until the ruin of all things under a universal monarch.

If the reader should perhaps be led by his curiosity to seek some kind of comparison between this ancient growth of taste and that which we have experienced in modern days and within our own nation, he may look back to the speeches of our ancestors in Parliament. He will find them, generally speaking, to have been very short and plain, but coarse and what we properly call home-spun, until learning came into fashion and science was known among us. If the senators became scholars, they spoke scholastically. And the pedantic style was prevalent from the first dawn of literature, around the time of the Reformation, until long afterward. Witness the best-written discourses, the admired speeches, orations, or sermons through several reigns, down to these recent ones which we count within the present age. It will undoubtedly be found that until very recently, the fashion of speaking and the style of wit followed a figurative and florid manner. Nothing was as acceptable as the high-sounding phrase, the far-fetched comparison, the clever point, and play on words; and nothing was as despicable as that which was merely plain or natural. So it must either be confessed that, compared to the preceding age, we have fallen very low in taste, or that, if we are in reality improved, the natural and simple manner which conceals and hides art is the most truly artful, and of the most refined, truest, and best-studied taste, as has been discussed more extensively above.¹

Now, therefore, regarding our author's philosophy itself—as it lies concealed in this treatise,² but is more openly professed and formal in his next³—we shall proceed gradually according to his own method, since it is not fitting for one who has undertaken the role of his lighthearted assistant and humorous commentator to enter suddenly, without good preparation, into his dry reasonings and moral researches regarding the social passions and natural affections, of which he is such a meticulous examiner.

# MISCELLANEOUS REFLECTIONS

...enjoying the happiness of a real constitution and <term>polity</term> by which they are free and independent. There are few such citizens or free men so corrupt as to directly discourage or condemn this passion of love for their community and national brotherhood. The indirect way of opposing this principle is the most common. We often hear the complaint, "That there is little of this love existing in the world." From this, it is hastily concluded, "That there is little or nothing of friendly or social affection inherent in our nature or belonging to our species." It is, however, apparent that there is hardly a human being who does not possess at least some lower degree or humbler kind of this natural affection for a country.

->By some unknown sweetness, our native soil draws<-
->those captured by it.<sup>1</sup><-

It is a wretched view of humanity that we imagine for ourselves when we try to reduce the very essence and foundation of this noble passion to a relationship with mere clay and dust, excluding anything sentient, intelligent, or moral. I must admit that all natural affection depends in some measure on certain<sup>2</sup> relations or relative proportions. And in this view, I confess it cannot be denied that each of us has a certain relation to the mere earth itself—the very soil or surface of that planet on which, along with other animals of various kinds, we (poor reptiles!) were also bred and nourished. But if it had happened that one of us British men had been born at sea, could we not therefore properly be called British men? Would we be considered citizens of no kind, having no distinct relation to any particular soil or region; no original neighborhood except with the aquatic inhabitants and sea monsters? Surely, if people are one. Absolute power annuls the public. And where there is no public or constitution, there is in reality no mother country or nation. See *Treatise iii. part iii. § 1*.
