<meta>This page continues Shaftesbury's argument that the love of one's country is not merely a physical attachment to soil, but a social and moral bond rooted in law and human connection.</meta>

<header>SHAFTESBURY'S CHARACTERISTICS</header>
<page-num>246</page-num>

...we were born of lawful parents, lawfully employed, and under the protection of law, wherever they might be then detained, to whatever colonies sent, or wherever driven by any accident, or in expeditions or adventures in the public service or that of mankind, we should still find we had a home and country ready to claim us. We would still be obligated to consider ourselves as fellow citizens, and might be allowed to love our country or nation as honestly and heartily as the most inland inhabitant or native of the soil. Our political and social capacity would undoubtedly come into view, and be acknowledged as fully as natural and essential in our species as the parental and filial kind, which gives rise to what we specifically call <term>natural affection</term>. Or, supposing that both our birth and parents had been unknown, and that in this respect we were in a sense younger brothers in society to the rest of mankind, yet from our nurture and education we would surely support some country or another, and joyfully embracing the protection of a <term>magistracy</term>, should of necessity and by the force of nature join ourselves to the general society of mankind—especially those with whom we had entered into a closer sharing of benefits and a deeper sympathy of affections. It may therefore be considered nothing better than a petty excuse of narrow minds to assign this natural passion for society and a country to a relationship like that of a mere fungus or common growth to its parent mold or nursing dunghill.

<margin>1 Treatise ii. part iii. § 1; Treatise v. part ii. § 4.</margin>
The relationship of being a fellow countryman, if it is granted any value at all, must imply something moral and social. The notion itself presupposes a naturally civil and political state of mankind, and refers to that particular part of society to which we owe our chief advantages as men and rational creatures, such as are <sup>1</sup> naturally and necessarily united for each other’s happiness and support, and for the highest of all joys and enjoyments: “the intercourse of minds, the free use of our reason, and the exercise of mutual love and friendship.”

<summary>Shaftesbury argues that citizenship and patriotism are natural moral and social obligations that exist regardless of one's physical birthplace. He asserts that the bond between countrymen is based on shared reason, law, and mutual support rather than mere geography.</summary>

--- Page 259 ---
<meta>This page continues Shaftesbury's exploration of the concept of "country," moving from a social and legal definition toward a critique of defining it purely by physical birth or the "soil" itself.</meta>

<header>MISCELLANEOUS REFLECTIONS</header>
<page-num>247</page-num>

An ingenious modern physician, considering the natural dependence of the vegetable and animal kinds on their common mother earth, and observing that both the one and the other draw their continuous sustenance from her (some rooted and fixed down to their first abodes, others unconfined and wandering from place to place to seek their nourishment), consequently, as I recall, styles this latter animal race her emancipated sons, *filios terrae emancipatos*. Now, if this is our only way of accounting for mankind, we may indeed call ourselves sons of the earth at large, but not of any particular soil or district. The division of climates and regions is fantastic and artificial; even more so are the limits of particular countries, cities, or provinces. Our *natale solum*, or mother earth, must by this account be the actual globe itself which carries us, and in respect of which we must allow the common animals, and even the plants of all degrees, to claim an equal brotherhood with us under this common parent.

According to this calculation, we must of necessity extend our relationship as far as the whole material world or universe, where alone it can prove complete. But for the particular district or tract of earth which in a common sense we call our country, however bounded or geographically divided, we can never, at this rate, establish any logical relationship to it, nor consequently assign any natural or proper affection toward it.

If, unfortunately, a man had been born either at an inn or in some dirty village, he would hardly, I think, limit himself so narrowly as to accept a title or character from those nearest surroundings or local circumstances of his birth. One should be so far from making the hamlet or parish the defining characteristic in such a case, that even the shire or county itself, however rich or flourishing, would hardly be included in the honorary term or name of one’s country.

Southern Jersey and Guernsey? What about the Plantations <note>the colonies</note> and poor Ireland?" Behold, here, is a very questionable boundary!

But what, after all, if there is a conquest or captivity involved? A migration? A national secession, or the abandonment of our native lands for some other soil or climate? We know this has happened to our ancestors. And as great and powerful a people as we have been recently—and have always shown ourselves to be under the influence of free councils and a reasonable government—should we relapse again into slavish principles, or be governed for long by such leaders who, having no thought of liberty for themselves, can have even less for Europe or their neighbors, we may at last experience a war at home, become the site of it, and in the end, be conquered. We might then gladly embrace the hard conditions of our predecessors and exchange our beloved native soil for that of some remote and uninhabited part of the world. Now, if this should possibly be our fate—if some significant colony or group were formed afterward from our remains, or met, as if by miracle, in some distant climate—would there be no Englishman remaining in the future? Would there be no common bond of alliance and friendship by which we could still call ourselves countrymen, as before? How, I ask, did we get our ancient name of Englishmen? Did it not travel with us over land and sea? Did we not indeed bring it with us previously from as far as the remote parts of Germany to this island?

I must confess, I have sometimes been inclined to be very angry with our language for denying us the use of the word *Patria*, and offering us no other name to express our native community than that of "country," which already carried two different meanings separate from humanity or society.¹ Dominant words are often powerful enough to influence us considerably in our understanding of things. Whether it is from such a cause as this, I do not know; but it is certain that in the idea of a civil state or nation, we Englishmen are inclined to include something more than usually crude and material. ...who owed so much to a constitution, and so little to a soil or climate, were ever known to be so unconcerned toward the one, and so passionately fond of the other. One would imagine from the common discourse of our countrymen that the finest lands near the Euphrates, the Babylonian or Persian paradises, the rich plains of Egypt, the Grecian Tempe, the Roman Campania, Lombardy, Provence, the Spanish Andalusia, or the most delicious tracts in the East or West Indies were contemptible countries compared to Old England.

Now, with the kind permission of these worthy patriots of the soil, I must take the liberty to say that I think Old England was in every respect a very mediocre country, and that "Late England," of a century or two ago—even since Queen Bess’s <note>Queen Elizabeth I</note> days—is indeed very much improved for the better. In the beginning of her grandfather’s <note>Henry VII</note> reign, we were under a sort of Polish nobility <note>A reference to a system of weak central monarchy and powerful, fractious aristocrats</note>, and had no other liberties than what were common to us along with the then-fashionable monarchies and Gothic lordships of Europe. In terms of religion, indeed, we were highly famous above all nations for being the most subject to our clergy at home and the most loyal tributaries and servants to the Holy See abroad.

I must go further still, and admit that I think "Late England," since the Revolution <note>The Glorious Revolution of 1688</note>, is better still than Old England by many degrees, and that on the whole we make a somewhat better figure in Europe than we did a few reigns ago. But however our people may have flourished lately, or our reputation and credit have risen, or our trade and navigation, our manufactures, or our agriculture have been improved, it is certain that our region, climate, and soil are in their own nature still one and the same. And whatever refinement we may suppose ourselves to have already reached, we must confess that we are the most recently barbarous, the last civilized or polished people of Europe. We must allow that our first conquest by the Romans brought us out of a state hardly equal to the Indian tribes, and that our last conquest by the Normans brought us only into the capacity of receiving arts...

and civil accomplishments from abroad. They came to us by degrees from remote distances, at second or third hand; from other courts, states, academies, and foreign nurseries of wit and manners.

Despite this, we have as arrogant an opinion of ourselves as if we had a claim to be original and native to the soil. As often as we have changed masters and mixed races with our various successive conquerors, we still pretend to be as legitimate and genuine possessors of our soil as the ancient Athenians considered themselves to have been of theirs. It is remarkable, however, that in those truly ancient, wise, and witty people—as fine as the territories and noble countries they possessed were, and as indisputable masters and superiors as they were in all science, wit, politeness, and manners—they were yet so far from a conceited, selfish, and ridiculous contempt of others that they were even, in a contrary extreme, "admirers of whatever was in the least degree ingenious or curious in foreign nations." Their great men were constant travelers. Their legislators and philosophers made their voyages into Egypt, passed into Chaldea and Persia, and did not fail to visit most of the scattered Greek governments and colonies throughout the islands of the Aegean, in Italy, and on the coasts of Asia and Africa. It was mentioned as a wonder, in the case of a great philosopher <note>Socrates</note>, though known to have been always poor, "that he should never have traveled, nor had ever gone out of Athens for his improvement." What a modest reflection for those who were themselves Athenians!

For our part, we neither care for foreigners to travel to us <note>An ill sign of our being thoroughly civilized, since in the judgment of the polite and wise this inhospitable disposition was always considered among the principal marks of barbarism. It seems that our best strategy and manners are "to look abroad as little as possible, to limit our views to the narrowest scope, and to despise all knowledge, learning, or manners that are not home-grown." <meta>This page continues the discussion on English insularity, transitioning into Shaftesbury’s project of cultivating "good taste" through both internal reflection and broad engagement with the world.</meta>

<page-num>252</page-num>
<header>SHAFTESBURY'S CHARACTERISTICS</header>

...current in philosophy and morals. To support this design of his, he seems intent chiefly on this single point: "to discover how we may to the best advantage form within ourselves what in the polite world is called a relish or good taste."

He begins, it is true, as near home as possible, and sends us to the narrowest of all conversations: that of soliloquy or self-discourse. But this correspondence, according to his calculation, is wholly impracticable without a previous interaction with the world; and the more extensive this interaction is, the more practicable and improving the other, he thinks, is likely to prove. The sources of this improving art of self-correspondence he derives from the highest politeness and elegance of ancient dialogue and debate in matters of wit, knowledge, and <term>ingenuity</term>. And nothing, according to our author, can so well revive this self-corresponding practice as the same search and study of the highest politeness in modern conversation. For this, we must necessarily take the trouble of going further abroad than the province we call home. And by this account it appears that our author has little hope of being either appreciated or understood by any of his countrymen other than those who delight in the open and free interaction with the world, and are rejoiced to gather views and receive light from every quarter in order to judge best what is perfect, and according to a just standard and true taste in every kind.

It may be proper for us to remark, in favor of our author, that the sort of ridicule or mockery which is apt to fall upon philosophers is of the same kind that commonly falls on the <term>virtuosi</term> or refined wits of the age. In this latter general category we include the real fine gentlemen, the lovers of art and <term>ingenuity</term>, such as have seen the world and informed themselves of the manners and customs of the various nations of Europe; searched into their antiquities and records; considered their <term>police</term> <note>civil administration and internal regulation</note>, laws, and constitutions; observed the situation, strength, and ornaments of their cities, their principal arts, studies, and amusements; their architecture, sculpture, paint—

Until now, there can be no ridicule, nor the least scope for satiric wit or raillery. But when we push this <term>virtuoso</term> character a little further and lead our polished gentleman into more refined researches; when, from the view of mankind and their affairs, our speculative genius and minute examiner of Nature's works proceeds with equal or perhaps superior zeal in the contemplation of insect life—the conveniences, habitations, and economy of a race of shellfish; when he has set up a cabinet in due form and made it the real pattern of his mind, filled with the same trash and trumpery of corresponding empty notions and fanciful conceits—he then indeed becomes the subject of sufficient raillery and is made the jest of common conversations.

A worse thing than this commonly happens to these inferior <term>virtuosi</term>. In seeking so earnestly for rarities, they fall in love with rarity for its own sake. Now the greatest rarities in the world are monsters. So that the study and taste of these gentlemen, thus diligently employed, becomes at last in reality monstrous; and their whole delight is found to consist in selecting and contemplating whatever is most monstrous, discordant, out of the way, and to the least purpose of anything in Nature.

In philosophy, matters correspond exactly to this <term>virtuoso</term> scheme. Let us suppose a man who, having this resolution merely—how to employ his understanding to the best purpose—considers "who or what he is; where he arose or had his being; to what end he was designed; and to what course of action he is by his natural frame and constitution destined." Should he descend on this account into himself and examine his inward powers and faculties, or should he ascend beyond his own immediate species, city, or community, to discover and recognize his higher <term>polity</term> or community (that common and universal one of which he is born a member), nothing surely of this kind could reasonably draw upon him the least contempt or mockery. On the contrary, the finest gentleman must after all be considered

“Where are we? Under what roof? Or on board what vessel? Where are we bound? On what business? Under whose pilotage, government, or protection?” These are questions which every sensible man would naturally ask if he were suddenly transported into a new scene of life. It is remarkable, indeed, to consider that a man could have been in the world for a long time, carrying his reason and sense about with him, and yet have never seriously asked himself this single question: “Where am I? Or what am I?” But, on the contrary, he should proceed regularly to every other study and inquiry, postponing this alone as the least significant, or leaving the examination of it to others who are commissioned—as he supposes—to understand and think for him on this subject. To be tricked, or deceived by any false advice in this affair, is, it seems, of no consequence. We take care to examine accurately, by our own judgment, the affairs of other people and the concerns of the world which least belong to us. But what relates more immediately to ourselves, and is our chief self-interest, we charitably leave to others to examine for us, and readily accept the first people we encounter, on whose honesty and good faith it is presumed we may safely rely.

Here, I think, the ridicule turns more against the philosophy-haters than the <term>virtuosi</term> or philosophers. While philosophy is understood (as it ought to be in its primary sense) as mastery over life and manners, it is likely to maintain a good reputation in the world, regardless of whatever impertinences may prevail or however extravagant the times may prove. Many things external to and outside of ourselves, having no relation to our real interests or to those of society and mankind, are diligently investigated; Nature’s most distant operations, deepest mysteries, and most difficult phenomena are discussed and whimsically explained; hypotheses and fanciful systems are built, a universe dissected, and—by some notable scheme <note>Shaftesbury, *The Moralists*, part 1, section 1.</note>—so solved and reduced as to appear like an easy trick or secret to those who have the key. Creation itself can, on occasion, be displayed; transmutations, projections, and other philosophical <term>arcana</term>, such as in the physical world can accomplish all things; while in the intellectual world, a fixed framework of <term>metaphysical phrases</term> and distinctions can serve to solve whatever difficulties may be proposed either in logic, ethics, or any true science of whatever kind.

It appears from this that the defects of <term>philosophy</term> and those of <term>virtuosoship</term> are of the same nature. Nothing can be more dangerous than a wrong choice or misapplication in these affairs. But as ridiculous as these studies are rendered by their senseless managers, it appears, however, that each of them is, in its nature, essential to the character of a fine gentleman and a man of sense.

To philosophize, in a proper sense, is only to carry <term>good breeding</term> a step higher. For the perfection of breeding is to learn whatever is decent in company or beautiful in arts; and the essence of <term>philosophy</term> is to learn what is just in society and beautiful in <term>Nature</term> and the order of the world.

It is not mere wit, but a disposition which must form the well-bred man. In the same manner, it is not a head merely, but a heart and resolution which must complete the real philosopher. Both characters aim at what is excellent, aspire to a correct taste, and keep in view the model of what is beautiful and becoming. Accordingly, the respective conduct and distinct manners of each party are regulated; the one according to the most perfect ease and pleasant engagement of company, the other according

Whether each of these duties or social roles is in itself as suitable as it is appropriate is the great question which must somehow be decided. The well-bred man has already decided this for himself and declared in favor of what is honorable; for whatever he practices in this regard,<note>1. *Wit and Humor*, part 4, § 1.</note> he considers no more than what he owes purely to himself, without regard to any further advantage. The pretender to philosophy—who either does not know how to determine this matter, or if he has determined it, does not know how to pursue his point with constancy and firmness—remains, in respect to philosophy, what a boor or a fool is in respect to breeding and behavior. Thus, according to our author, a taste for beauty and an appreciation for what is decent, just, and amiable perfect the character of the gentleman and the philosopher. And the study of such a taste or appreciation will, as we suppose, always be the great employment and concern of him who desires to be as wise and good as he is agreeable and polite.

And it is in this method and management that, as his interpreter or paraphraser, I have proposed to imitate and accompany him, as far as my miscellaneous character will permit.

Our joint endeavor, therefore, must appear to be this: to show “that nothing which is found charming or delightful in the refined world, nothing which is adopted as pleasure or entertainment of whatever kind, can in any way be accounted for, supported, or established without the prior establishment or assumption of a certain taste.” Now, it is supposed that a taste or judgment can hardly come into the world with us already fully formed. Whatever principles or materials of this kind we may possibly bring with us—whatever good faculties, senses, or anticipating sensations and imaginations may be of Nature’s growth and arise properly of themselves, without our art, promotion, or assistance—the general idea which is formed of all this management and the clear notion we attain of what is preferable and most important in all these subjects of choice and estimation will not, I imagine, be taken by anyone for innate. Use, practice, and culture must precede an understanding and intelligence of such an advanced size and growth as this. A legitimate and just taste can neither be begotten, made, conceived, nor produced without the preceding labor and pains of criticism.

For this reason, we presume not only to defend the cause of critics, but to declare open war against those indolent, passive authors, performers, readers, listeners, actors, or spectators who, making their whim alone the rule of what is beautiful and agreeable, and having no explanation to give for such a whim or odd fancy, reject the criticizing or examining art, by which alone they are able to discover the true beauty and worth of every object.

According to the artificial ridicule that these dull remarks try to cast on fair critics, the enjoyment of all real arts or natural beauty would be entirely lost; at this rate, we would in time become as barbaric in our behavior and manners as we are in our pleasures and diversions. I would assume, however, regarding these critic-haters, that they are not yet so uncivilized or lacking in all social sense as to maintain "that the most barbaric life or brutish pleasure is as desirable as the most polished or refined."

For my own part, when I have sometimes heard men of recognized ability join in with that weak, complaining tone of invective against critics, I have really thought they intended to hold back the developing geniuses of the youth—their rivals—by turning them away from that examination and investigation on which all good performance as well as good judgment depend. I have many times seen a well-bred man, who himself had a truly good taste, give way with a malicious politeness to the mood of a group where—mainly to please the ladies—this soft, faint contempt for critics and their work has been the topic of conversation. "Wretched creatures! (says one) these critics, as you call them, are such annoying things! As if one could not know what was agreeable or pretty without their help. It is fine, indeed, that one should not be allowed to choose for oneself. Now, even if a thousand critics told me that Mr. A——'s new play was not the wittiest in the world, I would not listen to them one bit."

This true man of wit listens patiently and perhaps adds his own comment, "that he thinks it is truly somewhat hard, regarding people's diversion and entertainment, that they should be forced to choose what pleased others and not themselves." Soon after this, he goes to the play himself and finds one of his weak companions praising or admiring it at the wrong moment. He turns to the person sitting next to him and asks privately, "What do you think of his companion’s taste?"

Such is the malice of the world! They who by effort and

At an auction of books or pictures, you shall hear these gentlemen persuading every one “to bid for what he fancies.” But at the same time they would be soundly mortified themselves if, by such as they esteemed good judges, they should be found to have purchased by a wrong fancy or ill taste. The same gentleman who commends his neighbor for ordering his garden or apartment as his mood leads him, takes care his own should be so ordered as the best judgments would advise. Being once a judge himself, or but tolerably knowing in these affairs, his aim is not “to change the being of things, and bring truth and Nature to his mood; but, leaving Nature and truth just as he found them, to accommodate his mood and fancy to their standard.” Would he do this in a yet higher case, he might in reality become as wise and great a man as he is already a refined and polished gentleman. By one of these tastes he understands how to lay out his garden, model his house, fancy his equipage, appoint his table; by the other he learns of what value these amusements are in life, and of what importance to a man’s freedom, happiness, and self-enjoyment. For if he would try effectually to acquire the real science or taste of life, he would certainly discover “that a right mind and generous affection had more beauty and charm than all other symmetries in the world besides.” And “that a grain of honesty and native worth was of more value than all the adventitious ornaments, estates, or preferments; for the sake of which some of the better sort so oft turn knaves, forsaking their principles and quitting their honor and freedom for a mean, timorous, shifting state of gaudy servitude.”

A little better taste (were it a very little) in the affair of life itself would, if I mistake not, mend the manners and secure the happiness of some of our noble countrymen, who come with high advantage and a worthy character into the public. They may perhaps consider this a shrewd bargain. But very unfortunate drawbacks will be found in it when the situation is actually experienced. They may truly be descended from the most glorious ancestors, patriots, and those who suffered for their nation's liberty and welfare; they may have entered the world upon this foundation of anticipated fame and honor; they may have been promoted because of this to positions of dignity which they were thought to have deserved. But when they are persuaded to change their honest ways and sacrifice their cause and friends for an imaginary private interest, they will soon find through experience that they have lost their relish and taste for life; and for the sake of dull, wretched, and deceitful honors, they have unhappily exchanged a lovely and sweet honor that had a sincere and lasting appeal and good flavor. After this, they may play-act as they see fit and hear qualities and virtues attributed to them under titles such as "graces," "excellencies," "honors," and the rest of this fake praise and imitative titles. They may even be told with serious expressions about their honor and worth, their principles, and their country; but they know better in their own hearts, and they have reason to find that, in the end, the world also knows better—and that their few friends and admirers possess either a very shallow intelligence or a very deep hypocrisy.

It is not in one party alone that these purchases and sales of honor are carried on. I can imagine a well-known patriot and reputed pillar of the religious side of our constitution, who—having gained a reputation for thorough zeal within his own party and for sincerity and honor even among his enemies through many years of service and steady conduct—suddenly (the time having come when the full measure of his reward was offered to him) complacently submits to the proposed bargain and sells himself for what he is worth, in a vile, detestable old

Meanwhile the year runs on, but the year’s income does not match its expenses. For “which of these articles can be reduced? In what way can he pull back, after having started out like this?” A princely whim has created all this, and a princely slavery and dependence on the court must maintain it.

The young gentleman is now led into a chase in which he will have a meager catch, though toil enough. He is himself caught. Nor will he so easily get out of that labyrinth to which he chose to commit his steps, rather than the more direct and plainer paths in which he walked before. “Farewell to that generous, proud spirit, which used to speak only what it approved, commend only whom it thought worthy, and act only what it thought right! There is another sort of suitor to power, and traffickers of inner worth and liberty for outward gain, whom one would naturally be drawn to pity. They are themselves of a humane, compassionate, and friendly nature, well-wishers to their country and mankind. They could, perhaps, even embrace poverty contentedly rather than submit to anything that would diminish either their inner freedom or national liberty. But what they can endure for themselves, they cannot bring themselves to endure for those who are to come after them. Here the best and noblest of affections are overcome by the excess of the next best: those of tenderness for relatives and close friends.

Such captives as these would, however, disdain to devote themselves to any prince or ministry whose goals were wholly tyrannical and irreconcilable with the true interest of their nation. In other cases of less degeneracy, they may perhaps bow down in the temple of Rimmon <note>A biblical reference to 2 Kings 5:18, meaning to reluctantly conform to a corrupt system or false worship for the sake of one's position</note>, supporting the weight of their lazy lords, and propping up the steps and failing reputation of their corrupt patrons.

This is drudgery enough for such honest natures, who only by hard fate could have been made dishonest. But as for pride or insolence on account of their outward advancement and apparent elevation, they are so far from anything resembling it that one may often observe the exact opposite in these better types of men. For though they were perhaps known to be somewhat rigid and severe before, you see them now grown submissive and obliging in reality. ...an entertaining subject of conversation, rather than focusing on the public interest or their own personal advancement.

Nothing is so close to virtue as this behavior; and nothing is so far from it—nothing is so certain a sign of the most corrupt manners—as the opposite. In a free government, it is so much in the interest of everyone in office, who profits from the public, to conduct himself with modesty and submission, that to appear immediately more insolent and haughty upon such a promotion is the mark only of a contemptible mind, and of a lack of true understanding, even in the narrow sense of self-interest and private gain.

Thus we see, after all, that it is not merely what we call principle, but a *taste* which governs men. They may think for certain, "this is right, or that is wrong"; they may believe "this is a crime, or that is a sin; this is punishable by man, or that by God"; yet if the taste for things runs contrary to honesty; if the imagination is extravagant and the appetite strong toward the lesser beauties and lower order of worldly symmetries and proportions, their conduct will inevitably turn toward the latter.

Even conscience, I fear—the kind that is due to religious discipline—will play only a minor role where this taste is misaligned. Among the common people, perhaps, it may work wonders. A devil and a hell may prevail where a jail and gallows are thought insufficient. But such is the nature of the liberal, polished, and refined part of mankind. They are so far from the simple innocence of infants that, instead of applying the notion of a future reward or punishment to their immediate behavior in society, they are much more likely, through the whole course of their lives, to show clearly that they look upon pious stories as indeed no better than children's tales or the amusement of the common people:—

I think, therefore, that something more should be considered on behalf of our noble youth regarding the correction of their *taste* or inclination in the affairs of life. For this, ultimately, is what will influence them. And in this respect, the youth alone should be considered. Some hope may still be found for them. The rest are set and hardened in their ways. A middle-aged rogue (no matter how devout or orthodox) is only a common curiosity; an old one is no surprise at all; but a young one is still (thank heaven!) somewhat extraordinary. And I can never sufficiently admire what was once said by a worthy man upon the first appearance of one of these capable young prostitutes, "that he even trembled at the sight to find nature capable of being corrupted so soon; and that he predicted greater calamity for his country from this single example of youthful villainy than from the practices and arts of all the old rogues in existence."

Let us therefore proceed with this view, addressing ourselves to the young adults of our polite world. Let the appeal be to those whose inclination is salvageable, and whose taste may yet be shaped in morals, just as it already seems to be in outward manners and behavior.

That there is truly a standard of this latter kind will be immediately acknowledged at first glance. The only dispute is, "which is right; which is the natural carriage and proper demeanor; and which is the affected and false." There is hardly anyone who does not claim to know and judge what is well-bred and handsome. There are few so deliberately crude as to absolutely disown **good breeding**, and renounce the notion of a beauty in outward manners and conduct. As for people like that, wherever they may be found, I must confess I could hardly be tempted to spend the least effort or labor in convincing them of a beauty in inward sentiments and principles.

Whoever has any sense of what we call gentility or politeness is already so familiar with the decorum and grace of things that he will readily admit a pleasure and enjoyment in the very observation and contemplation of this kind. Now, if in the pursuit of polite pleasure the study and love of beauty are essential, the study and love of symmetry and order, on which beauty depends, must also be essential in the same respect.

It is impossible for us to advance even slightly in any relish or taste for outward symmetry and order without acknowledging that the proportionate and regular state is the truly prosperous and natural one in every subject. The same features which cause deformity create inconvenience and disease. And the same shapes and proportions which create beauty provide an advantage by adapting to activity and use. Even in the imitative or designing arts (to which our author so often refers), the truth or beauty of every figure or statue is measured by the perfection of Nature in her correct adaptation of every limb and proportion to the activity, strength, dexterity, life, and vigor of the particular species or animal intended.

Thus, beauty and truth are plainly joined with the notion of utility and convenience,<sup>1</sup> even in the understanding of every clever artist, the architect,<sup>2</sup> the sculptor, or the painter.

And so, in his characteristic style of soliloquy or internal dialogue, we may imagine him continuing, perhaps beginning with some particular scheme or imagined scale of beauty. According to his philosophy, he strives to establish this scale by distinguishing, sorting, and dividing things into the inanimate, the animate, and the mixed, as follows:

In the inanimate: beginning with those regular shapes and symmetries that delight children, and proceeding gradually to the proportions of architecture and the other arts. The same applies to sounds and music. From beautiful stones, rocks, and minerals, to plants, forests, the collective parts of the world, seas, rivers, mountains, and valleys. The globe. Celestial bodies and their order. The higher architecture of Nature. Nature herself, considered as inanimate and passive.

In the animate: from animals and their various kinds, temperaments, and intelligence, to humans. And from individual people—their private characters, intellects, geniuses, dispositions, and manners—to public societies, communities, or commonwealths. From flocks, herds, and other natural gatherings or groups of living creatures, to human intelligence and social relationships, or whatever is higher in that category. The correspondence, union, and harmony of Nature herself, considered as animate and intelligent.

In the mixed: as in a single person (composed of a body and a mind), the union and harmony of this kind, which constitutes the real person; and the friendship, love, or whatever other affection is formed toward such an object. A household, a city, or a nation, with specific lands, buildings, and other additions or local ornaments which together form that pleasant idea of home, family, and country.

“And what of this?” says a frivolous young man, no friend to meditation or deep thought. “What is the meaning of this catalog or scale, as you are pleased...”

> "It is we ourselves who create and form our taste. If we resolve to have it correct, it is in our power. Thus our monologist, or self-discoursing author, speaks in his usual style when incited to the search for Beauty and the <term>Decorum</term> by common admiration and the universal acknowledgment of the species in outward things, and in the lesser and subordinate subjects. By this inferior species, it seems, our strict inspector disdains to be lured; and refusing to be captivated by anything less than the superior, original, and genuine kind, he walks at leisure, without emotion, in deep philosophical reserve, through all these pompous scenes. He passes unconcernedly by those court pageants, the illustrious and much-envied rulers of the place; he overlooks the rich, the great, and even the beautiful, feeling no other astonishment than what is accidentally raised in him by the view of these deceptions and of this attractive snare. For here he observes those gentlemen to be chiefly caught and fastest held who are the greatest ridiculers of reflections such as his own, and who, in the very height of this ridicule, prove themselves the powerless despisers of a species of beauty which, whether they want to or not, they ardently pursue—some in a face and certain regular lines or features, others in a palace and its apartments, others in a carriage and dress.
> "O effeminacy, effeminacy! Who would imagine this could be the vice of those who appear to be significant men? But one’s person is a subject of flattery that reaches beyond the bloom of youth. In our days, the experienced senator and aged general can manage with a dressing table and arrange his outward form into a very extraordinary adjustment and regulation. All embellishments are sought after, except the true ones. And thus, led by example, while we run in search of elegance and neatness, pursuing beauty and adding, as we imagine, more luster and value to <insert>[</insert>our own persons, we grow, in our real character and true self, deformed and monstrous, servile and abject, stooping to the lowest levels of flattery, and sacrificing all internal proportion, all intrinsic and real beauty and worth for the sake of things which carry scarcely a shadow of that quality."

as we would wish. For who would not rejoice to be always consistent and in harmony with himself, and to constantly have that opinion of things which is natural and proportionate? Thus I have endeavored to follow in my author’s footsteps, and prepare the reader for the serious and straightforward philosophy which, even in this <note>¹ Treatise III (*Advice to an Author*).</note> last commented treatise, our author still keeps as a mystery and does not dare to formally profess. His pretense has been to advise authors and polish styles, but his aim has been to correct manners and regulate lives. He has affected the use of soliloquy, pretending only to criticize himself, but he has taken the opportunity to bring others into his company and deal boldly with personages and characters of no inferior rank. He has given enough room for mockery and humor, and has encroached very largely on the territory of us miscellaneous writers. But the reader is <note>² Treatise IV (*The Inquiry*).</note> now about to see him in a new light: “a formal and professed philosopher, a writer of systems, a dogmatist and an interpreter.” *Habes confitentem reum*.

So I commit him to his philosophy. Though, as my current talent and disposition permit, I still intend to accompany him at a distance, keep him in sight, and escort him as best I can through the dangerous seas he is about to cross.

WE have already, in the beginning of our preceding Miscellany, noted our author’s plan and the connection and dependency of his combined tracts,<note>¹ See above, p. 239; and again below, *Misc.* v. 2.</note> included in two preceding volumes. We have now, in our capacity as commentators, finally arrived at his second volume, for which the three pieces of his first appear to be preparatory. That they were indeed designed this way, the advertisement to the first edition of his *Soliloquy* is sufficient proof. He took the opportunity there, in a line or two under the name of his printer—or, as he otherwise calls him, his <term>amanuensis</term>—to prepare us for a more elaborate and methodical work that was to follow. We have this system before us now. Nor should we wonder, such as it is, that it came into the world with such difficulty, and that our author has produced it with so much effort and after such a long time. It seems his <term>amanuensis</term> and he were not previously on such good terms. It will appear, therefore, in this joint edition of our author’s *Five Treatises* that the first three are preparatory to the fourth, which we are now beginning, and the fifth (with which he concludes) is a kind of apology for this revived Treatise concerning virtue and religion.

As for his Apology, particularly regarding revealed religion and the world to come, I refer the reader to the debating theologians and gentlemen whom our author has introduced in that concluding piece of dialogue writing or rhapsodic philosophy. Meanwhile, we have no other choice but to enter into the author's dry philosophy and rigid style, without any excursions into diverse literature, without help from the comic or tragic muse, or from the flourishes of poetry or rhetoric.

Such is our current model and strict moral task, which our more lighthearted reader, knowing this in advance, may immediately skip over if he pleases—skipping (as is common in many serious works) a chapter or two as he proceeds. To make amends, we shall afterward endeavor, in our following *Miscellany*, to entertain him again with more cheerful fare, and provide him with a dessert to satisfy his palate and leave him with a pleasant final impression.

To the patient and serious reader, therefore, who for the sake of moral reflection can afford to retire into his study, as if for some religious or devout exercise, we presume to offer a few reflections in support of our author’s profound inquiry. That there is undoubtedly something which thinks, our very doubt itself and scrupulous thought demonstrate. But in what subject that thought resides, and how that subject remains one and the same so as to correspond constantly to the supposed train of thoughts or reflections which seem to run so harmoniously through a long course of life, maintaining the same relation still to one single and self-same person—this is not a matter so easily or hastily decided by those who are meticulous self-examiners or searchers after truth and certainty.

<margin>¹ *Monsieur Descartes.*</margin>
"It will not, in this respect, be sufficient for us to use the apparent logic of a famous modern philosopher,¹ and say, 'We think, therefore we are.' This is a notably devised saying, modeled after that similar philosophical proposition, 'What is, is.' Miraculously argued! 'If I am, I am.' Nothing is more certain! For the *Ego* or *I* being established in the first part of the proposition, the *ergo*, no doubt, must hold it good in the latter. But the question is, 'What constitutes the We or I?' and 'whether the I of this instant is the same as that of any instant preceding or to come?' For we have nothing but memory to warrant us, and memory may be false. We may believe we have thought and reflected in such a way; but we may be mistaken. We may be conscious of something as truth which perhaps was no more than a dream, and we may be conscious of something as a past dream which perhaps was never before so much as dreamed of."

This is what metaphysicians mean when they say "that identity can be proved only by consciousness, but that consciousness, moreover, may be just as false as real regarding what is past." So that the same successional We or I must still remain, on this account, undecided.

To the force of this reasoning I confess I must so far submit

Meanwhile, there is no impediment, hindrance, or suspension of action on account of these wonderfully refined speculations. Argument and debate still go on. Conduct is settled. Rules and measures are given out and received. Nor do we hesitate to act as resolutely upon the mere supposition that we exist, as if we had effectively proved it a thousand times to the full satisfaction of our metaphysical or Pyrrhonean antagonist.

This appears to me sufficient ground for a moralist. Nor do I ask for more when I undertake to prove the reality of virtue and morals.

If it is certain that I exist, it is certain and demonstrable who and what I ought to be, even on my own account, and for the sake of my own private happiness and success. For I take the liberty to proceed in this way.

The affections of which I am conscious are either grief or joy, desire or aversion. For whatever mere sensation I may experience, if it amounts to neither of these, it is indifferent and in no way affects me.

That which causes joy and satisfaction when present causes grief and disturbance when absent; and that which causes grief and disturbance when present does, when absent, by the same necessity, occasion joy and satisfaction.

Thus love (which implies desire, with hope of good) must provide the occasion for grief and disturbance when it does not acquire what it earnestly seeks. And hatred (which implies aversion and fear of evil) must, in the same manner, cause grief and calamity when that which it earnestly shunned, or would have escaped, remains present or is altogether unavoidable.

That which, being present, can never leave the mind at rest, but must of necessity cause aversion, is its evil. But that which can be sustained without any necessary abhorrence or aversion

<summary>The author argues that despite metaphysical doubts about the self, practical life and moral philosophy must proceed on the assumption of existence. He begins to derive a moral system from the fundamental human experiences of joy, grief, desire, and aversion.</summary>

In the same way, that which—when absent—can never leave the mind at rest, or without disturbance and regret, is necessarily its good. But that which can be absent without any present or future disturbance to the mind is not its good, but remains indifferent in its own nature. From this, it must follow that the emotion toward it, as a supposed good, is a bad emotion, and creates only disturbance and disease. So, because the emotions of love and hatred, liking and dislike—on which a person’s happiness or prosperity so much depends—are influenced and governed by opinion, the highest good or happiness must depend on right opinion, and the greatest misery must be derived from wrong opinion.

To explain this, I consider, for example, the mental image or imagination I have of death, as I find this subject naturally passing through my mind. To this mental image, perhaps, I find joined an opinion or fear of evil and calamity. Now, the more my fear of this evil increases, the greater I find my disturbance becomes—not only at the approach of the supposed evil, but at the very distant thought of it. Besides that, the thought itself will necessarily occur much more often as the aversion or fear becomes violent and intense.

I must, however, flee from this supposed evil with all the more earnestness as my opinion of the evil increases. Now, if the increase of aversion cannot cause the decrease or reduction of the evil itself, but rather the opposite, then the increase of aversion must necessarily result in the increase of disappointment and disturbance. And so, on the other hand, the reduction or decrease of aversion (if this can be achieved in any way) must necessarily result in the reduction of inward disturbance and the better establishment of inward peace and satisfaction.

For if our loves, desires, hatreds, and aversions are left to themselves, we are necessarily exposed to endless vexation and calamity; but if these are found to be capable of improvement, or in any measure flexible or changeable by opinion, I think we ought at least to try how far we might acquire happiness and contentment by this means.

Accordingly, if we find it evident on one hand that by indulging any wrong appetite (such as debauchery, malice, or revenge), the opinion of the false good increases, and the appetite—which is a real evil—grows that much stronger; we may be just as fully assured, on the other hand, that by restraining this emotion and nourishing an opposing kind in opposition to it, we cannot fail to diminish what is evil and increase what is properly our happiness and good.

On this account, a man may reasonably conclude "that it is appropriate for him, by working upon his own mind, to withdraw the imagination or opinion of good or evil from that to which it is not justly or necessarily joined, and to apply it with the strongest resolution to that with which it naturally agrees." For if the imagination or opinion of good is joined to what is not durable, nor in my power either to acquire or to keep, the more such an opinion prevails, the more I must be subject to disappointment and distress. But if there is that to which, whenever I apply the opinion or imagination of good, I find the imagination more consistent and the good more durable, solid, and within my power and command, then the more such an opinion prevails in me, the more satisfaction and happiness I must experience.

Now, if I join the opinion of good to the possessions of the

mind, if it is in the affections themselves that I place my highest joy, and in those objects, whatever they are, of inward worth and beauty (such as honesty, faith, integrity, friendship, and honor), it is evident I can never possibly, in this respect, rejoice wrongly or indulge myself too far in the enjoyment. This, I know, is very different in another regimen of life. The education of fancy <note>Shaftesbury uses "fancy" here in the sense of the Greek *phantasia*, meaning the internal images, judgments, or "imaginations" we form about things.</note> and pleasure, and the easy philosophy of taking whatever pleases me as good, or which I merely fancy to be so, will in time give me sufficient uneasiness. And since it is fancy merely which gives the force of "good," or the power of passing as such, to things of chance and outward dependency, it is evident that the more I take away from fancy in this respect, the more I confer upon myself. As I am less led or betrayed by fancy into valuing what depends on others, I am the more fixed in valuing what depends on myself alone. And if I have once gained the taste of liberty, <note>Treatise v. part iii. § 3; and below, *Misc.* v. 3.</note> I shall easily understand the force of this reasoning and know both my true self and my true interest.

The method, therefore, required in this, my inward economy, is to make those fancies themselves the objects of my aversion which justly deserve it, by being the cause of a wrong estimation and measure of good and ill, and consequently the cause of my unhappiness and disturbance.

Accordingly (as the learned masters in this science advise), we are to begin with the averse disposition rather than with the prone and forward one. <note>“Give up, then, your aversion to all things which are not within our power, and transfer it to those things contrary to nature which are within our power.” —Epictetus, *Enchiridion*, ch. 2.</note> We are to work rather by the weaning—

Thus at last a mind, by knowing itself and its own proper powers and virtues, becomes free and independent. It sees its hindrances and obstructions, and finds they are wholly from itself, and from wrongly conceived opinions. The more it conquers in this respect (even in the smallest detail) the more it is its own master, feels its own natural liberty, and congratulates itself on its own advancement and prosperity.

For although these first lines (as many other of Horace’s on the subject of philosophy) have the air of the Epicurean discipline and Lucretian style; yet, when the whole is taken together, it appears evidently on what system of ancient philosophy this epistle was formed. Nor was this prohibition of the wondering or admiring habit in early students unique to only one kind of philosophy. It was common to many, however much the reason and explanation of it might differ from one sect to another. The Pythagoreans sufficiently checked their beginners by silencing them for so long during their first courtship of philosophy. And although admiration, in the Peripatetic sense, as mentioned above, may be justly called the inclining principle or first motive to philosophy, yet this mistress, when once espoused, teaches us to admire in a different manner than we did before. However, as serious as morality is presumed to be in its own nature, I consider it an essential matter in its delivery to occasionally adopt a natural air of pleasantry. The first moral lessons ever delivered to the world were in parables, tales, or fables. And the later and most accomplished distributors of morality, in the most refined times, were great storytellers and followers of honest Aesop.

After all the formal demonstrations and deductions of our serious author, I dare say it would be a great relief and satisfaction to his reader to hear an apologue or fable well told, and with such humor that it needs no preachy moral at the end to explain its application.

Our serious inquirer takes pains to show us, at full length, the unnatural and unhappy excursions, wanderings, or expeditions of our ungoverned fancies and opinions over a world of riches, honors, and other ebbing and flowing goods. And I would guarantee success should a merrier moralist of the Aesopian school present himself, and, hearing of this chase described by our philosopher, ask leave to represent it realistically through a common dog or two of his master's ordinary breed.

“Two of this race,” he would tell us, “having been daintily bred and having high thoughts of what they called pleasure and good living, once traveled in search of game and rarities, until they came by accident to the seaside. There, at a distance from the shore, they saw some floating pieces of a wreck, which they took a whim to believe was some wonderfully rich delicacy, richer than ambergris or the finest product of the ocean. They could prove by their appetite and longing that it was nothing less than the quintessence of the sea, an ambrosial substance—the meal of marine deities surpassing everything the earth afforded. . . . By these rhetorical arguments, after long reasoning with one another in this flowery style, they proceeded from one extravagance of imagination to another, until they finally reached this conclusion. Being unaccustomed to swimming, they would not, it seems, out of caution, venture as far out of their depth as was necessary to reach their imagined prize; but being heavy drinkers, they thought to themselves that they might manage to drink everything that lay in their way, even the sea itself, and that by this method they might soon bring their goods safely to dry land. To work, therefore, they went, and drank until they both burst.”

# CHAPTER II

->Passage from *terra incognita* to the visible world — Mistress-ship of Nature — Animal confederacy, degrees, subordination — Master animal man — Privilege of his birth — Serious countenance of the author.<-

As difficult as it was for us in the deep philosophical part of our preceding chapter, and as necessarily committed as we still are to pursuing the same serious inquiry and searching into those dark sources, it is hoped that our remaining philosophy may flow in a more easy vein, and the second running be found somewhat clearer than the first. However it may be, we may at least congratulate ourselves for having thus briefly passed over that metaphysical part to which we have paid sufficient respect. Nor shall we hesitate to declare our opinion "that it is in a way necessary for anyone who wishes to philosophize usefully to have a knowledge in this part of philosophy sufficient to satisfy him that there is no knowledge or wisdom to be learned from it." For nothing besides experience and study will be able to fully convince him of this truth.

When we are even past these empty regions and shadows of philosophy, it will still perhaps appear to be an uncomfortable kind of travel through those other invisible ideal worlds, such as we see the study of morals requires us to visit. Men must acquire a very peculiar and strong habit of turning their eye inward in order to explore the interior regions and recesses of the mind, the hollow caverns of deep thought, the private seats of imagination, and the wastes and wildernesses, as well as the more fruitful and cultivated tracts of that obscure climate.

But what can one do? The fashionable gentlemen, who have never thought to study Nature in their own species, but being captivated by other interests, have applied their talents and genius to the same study in a horse, a dog, a gamecock, a hawk, or any other animal ² of that rank, know very well that to each species belongs a distinct humor, temper, and inward disposition, as real and unique as the figure and outward shape which is observed and admired with such curiosity. If there is anything even the slightest bit amiss or wrong in the inward frame—the humor or temper of the creature—it is readily called vicious; and when it is more than usually wrong, it is called unnatural. The humors of the creatures, for the sake of their correction, are attentively observed: sometimes indulged and flattered, and at other times controlled and checked with proper severity. In short, their affections, passions, appetites, and dislikes are as duly regarded as those in humankind under the strictest discipline of education. Such is the sense of inward proportion and regularity of affections, even among our noble youths themselves, who in this respect are often known to be expert and capable masters of education, although they are not as susceptible to discipline and culture in their own case, after those early indulgences to which their high status has entitled them.

However little favor these sporting gentlemen are presumed to show toward the care or culture of their own species, and however remote their contemplations are thought to be from Nature and philosophy, they plainly confirm and establish our philosophical foundation of the natural ranks, orders, and the interior and exterior proportions of the various distinct species and forms of animal beings. Ask one of these gentlemen, unexpectedly, while he is anxiously careful and busy in the great

This is the main problem which our author demonstrates in more philosophical terms in this treatise,<note>Namely, the *Inquiry concerning Virtue*.</note> “that for a creature whose natural purpose is society, to act as Nature has appointed him towards the good of such a society, or the whole, is in reality to pursue his own natural and proper good. And to act otherwise, or by such feelings as separate him from that common good or public interest, is in reality to work towards his own natural and proper harm.” Now if man, as has been proved, is justly ranked among those creatures whose constitution is based on a collective and public welfare; if it is understood, moreover, that the only state of his feelings which properly corresponds to this public welfare is the regular, orderly, or virtuous state; it necessarily follows “that virtue is his natural good, and vice is his misery and harm.”

As for that further consideration, “whether Nature has orderly and justly distributed the various structures or parts, and whether the defects, failures, or calamities of particular systems are to the advantage of all in general, and contribute to the perfection of the one common and universal system”; we must refer to our author’s deeper speculation in this, his *Inquiry*, and in his following philosophical dialogue. These are our author’s formal and serious sentiments; if they were not truly his and sincerely embraced by him as the actual result of his best judgment and understanding, he would be guilty of a more than common degree of deception. For, according to his own rule,² an affected gravity and feigned seriousness carried on through any subject in such a way as to leave no insight into the fiction or intended mockery is, in truth, no mockery or wit at all. It is instead a coarse, immoral, and narrow-minded way of abuse, foreign to the character of a good writer, a gentleman, or a man of worth.

But since we have thus finished with that serious part, of which our reader was already well-informed, let him now expect us again in our original miscellaneous style and capacity. It is here, as has been explained to him, that mockery and humor are permitted, and flights of fancy, outbursts, and digressions of every kind are found agreeable and necessary. Without this, there might be less safety found, perhaps, in thinking. Every light reflection might lead us into the dangerous state of deep meditation. And in reality, profound thinking is often the cause of shallow thoughts. To prevent this contemplative habit and character, from which we see so little good effect in the world, we have reason perhaps to be fond of an entertaining style in writing and conversation, especially if the subject is of a solemn kind. There is more need, in this case, to interrupt the long-spun thread of reasoning and bring into the mind, through many different glances and fragmented views, what cannot so easily be introduced by one steady focus or continuous stretch of sight.

<header>CHAPTER I</header>

->*The protocol established between author and reader — The author's affectation of precedence — Various claims to inspiration — Bards, prophets, Sibylline Scripture — Written oracles in verse and prose — The common interest of ancient literature and Christianity — The state of wit, elegance, and correctness — Poetic truth — Preparation for a critique of our author in his concluding treatise.*<-

<margin>1 Namely, Treatise III.</margin>
Of all the artificial relationships formed among mankind, the most unpredictable and variable is that of author and reader. Our author, for his part, has stated his opinion on this where he offers his advice to modern authors.<margin>1</margin> And although he assumes that every formal author is, regarding the specific subject he explains, superior in understanding to his reader, he does not allow any author to take the upper hand or pretend to exempt himself from that necessary subjection to external judgment and criticism, which must determine the place of honor on the reader’s side.

It is evident that an author’s art and labor are for his reader’s sake alone. It is to his reader that he makes his appeal—if not openly and explicitly, then at least with implicit courtship. Poets indeed, and especially those of a modern kind, have a peculiar way of handling this matter with a high hand. They pretend to place themselves above mankind. “Their pens are sacred; their style and expression are divine.” They often write as

But here, inferior mortals often presume to intercept their flight and remind them of their fallible and human part. Had those first poets who began this pretense of inspiration been taught a way of communicating their rapturous thoughts and high ideas by some medium other than style and language, the case might have been different. But because the inspiring divinity or muse, in explaining herself, has submitted her wit and sense to the mechanical rules of arbitrary human composition, she must, as a consequence and by necessity, submit herself to human arbitration and the judgment of the literate world. And thus the reader is still superior and keeps the upper hand.

> It is indeed no small absurdity to assert that a work or treatise, written in human language, is above human criticism or censure. For if the art of writing comes from the grammatical rules of human invention and determination; if even these rules are formed on common practice and various uses, there can be no scripture that must not of necessity be subject to the reader’s narrow scrutiny and strict judgment, unless a language and grammar different from any of human structure were delivered down from heaven and miraculously accommodated to human service and capacity.

<meta>This page continues the argument that works written in human language must be subject to human criticism, even if they claim divine origin. <header>SHAFTESBURY’S CHARACTERISTICS</header>

I beg pardon of tradition and assert confidently, “that if the pencil had been heaven-guided it could never have been so lame in its performance.” It is a mere contradiction to all divine and moral truth that a celestial hand, submitting itself to the rudiments of a human art, should sin against the art itself, and express falsehood and error instead of correctness and proportion.

It may be alleged, perhaps, “that there are, however, certain authors in the world who, though of themselves they neither boldly claim the privilege of divine inspiration nor carry indeed the slightest resemblance of perfection in their style or composition, yet they subdue the reader, gain the ascendancy over his thought and judgment, and force from him a certain implicit veneration and esteem.” To this I can only answer, “that if there is neither spell nor enchantment in the case, this can plainly be no other than mere enthusiasm”; except, perhaps, where the supreme powers have given their sanction to any religious record or pious writing. And in this case, indeed, it becomes immoral and profane for anyone to absolutely deny or dispute the sacred authority of the least line or syllable contained in it. But should the record, instead of being single, short, and uniform, appear to be multifarious, voluminous, and of the most difficult interpretation, it would be somewhat difficult, if not wholly impracticable, for the magistrate to allow this record to be universally current and at the same time prevent its being variously understood and commented upon by the several differing temperaments and contrary judgments of mankind.

It is remarkable that in the most refined of all nations, the writings looked upon as most sacred were those of their great poets, whose works indeed were truly divine in respect to art and the perfection of their structure and composition. But there was even more divinity¹ ascribed to them than what is understood in this latter sense. The notions of popular religion were built on their miraculous narrations. The wiser and better sort themselves paid a regard to them in this respect, though they

What those volumes ^1 might have been which the disdainful Sibyl or prophetess committed to the flames, or what the remainder was which the Roman prince received and consecrated, I will not pretend to judge; though it has been accepted as truth by the early Christian fathers that these writings were so far sacred and divine as to have prophesied the birth of our religious founder, and bore testimony to that Holy Writ which has preserved his memory and is justly held in the highest degree of sanctity among Christians.

The policy, however, of ancient Rome was such as to not rest the authority of their religion absolutely on any literary composition. The Sibylline volumes were kept safely locked and were inspected only by those who were ordained or appointed for that purpose. And in this policy, the "new Rome" <note>This refers to the Roman Catholic Church.</note> has followed their example by hesitating to assign the supreme authority and sacred character of infallibility to Scripture itself, and by refusing to submit that Scripture to public judgment, or to any eye or ear except those they qualify for the inspection of such sacred mysteries.

# MISCELLANEOUS REFLECTIONS

The Mahometan clergy seem to have a different policy. They boldly rest the foundation of their religion on a book: one that (according to their claim) is not only perfect, but inimitable. If a real man of letters and a fair critic were permitted to examine this scripture by the known rules of art, he would perhaps soon refute this claim. But so barbarous is the accompanying policy and temperament of these Eastern religionists that they discourage and in effect extinguish all true learning, science, and the more refined arts, along with the ancient authors and languages, which they set aside; and by this infallible method, they leave their Holy Writ as the sole standard of literary work. For by being compared to nothing but itself, or to something of an inferior kind, it must undoubtedly be considered incomparable.

It will be granted, surely, to the honor of the Christian world, that their faith (especially that of the Protestant churches) stands on a more generous foundation. They not only allow a comparison of authors, but are content to derive their proofs of the validity of their sacred record and revelation even from those authors called profane; as they are well aware (according to the maxim of our Divine Master <sup>1</sup>) "that when we bear witness only to ourselves, our witness cannot be established as a truth." Thus, since there is at present no direct testimony of miracles or signs in support of Holy Writ, and since there is nothing miraculous or self-evidently convincing in its own particular composition or style; if the corroborating testimony of other ancient records, historians, and foreign authors were destroyed or completely lost, there would be less of an argument or defense remaining against the natural suspicion of those who are called skeptical: "that the holy records themselves were nothing other than the pure invention or artificial compilation of a self-interested party on behalf of the wealthiest corporation and most profitable monopoly that could be established in the world."

It belongs only to simple <term>enthusiasts</term> and <term>fanatics</term> to plead the sufficiency of a repeatedly translated text, passed down to them through so many channels and subjected to so many variations, of which they are completely ignorant. The result, therefore, of this long deduction is, in the first place, with due compliments in my capacity as an author—and in the name of all modest craftsmen willingly joining me in this representation—to congratulate our English reader on the establishment of what is so advantageous to himself. And in this respect, it is to be hoped he will long enjoy his just superiority and privilege over his humble servants who compose and labor for his sake. The relationship, in all likelihood, must continue and be improved. Our common religion and Christianity, founded on literature and Scripture, promises as much. In verse 4, the word "certainty," *asphaleian*, is interpreted as *akribeian*: validity, soundness, or a good foundation, based on the sense of the preceding verse. Thus, those who were taught were called 'catechumens,' and those who taught were called 'catechists.'"

<meta>This page continues the argument that while great men of action are often too occupied with public affairs to write, many of history's greatest authors were driven to literature only after being forced out of public life by misfortune or exile.</meta>

business, could not, it seems, be easily removed from it to attend to the slender and minute affairs of literature and scholastic science.

It is true, indeed, that without a capacity for action and a knowledge of the world and mankind, there can be no author naturally qualified to write with dignity, or execute any noble or great design. But there are many who, despite having the highest capacity for business, are denied the privilege of that higher sphere by their fortune. Just as there are others who, having once moved in it, have been afterwards necessitated by many impediments and obstructions to retire and exert their genius in this lower degree.

It is to some catastrophe of this kind that we owe the noblest historians (even the two princes and fathers of history<note>Herodotus and Thucydides.</note>) as well as the greatest philosophical writers, the founder of the Academy<note>Plato.</note> and others, who were also noble by birth and suited for the highest positions in public life, but were discouraged from engaging in it because of misfortunes experienced either by themselves or their close friends.

It is to the early banishment and long retirement of a heroic youth from his native country that we owe an original system of works—the most polite, wise, useful, and (to those who can understand the divinity of a just simplicity) the most amiable, and even the most elevating and exalting, of all uninspired and merely human authors.<note>The most sweet and graceful Xenophon, as Athenaeus calls him, xi. <meta>This page continues the analysis of Horace's social standing and his transition from a military officer under Brutus to a private friend of Maecenas and Augustus, emphasizing how he defended his reputation by citing his distinguished background and past services.</meta>

Let authors, therefore, know themselves; and though they are conscious of worth, virtue, and a genius that may justly place them—

> ["Envy will confess against her will that I have always lived with the great."—Horace, *Satires II. i. 76, 77.*]

Where the *vixisse* (having lived) shows plainly whom he principally meant by his *magni* (great ones): his early patrons and great men in the State. His apology and defense here—as well as in the fourth and sixth satires of his first book, and the second epistle of his second book and elsewhere—is still supported by the open and bold assertion of his good education (equal to the highest senators and under the best masters), his employments at home and abroad, and his early interaction and familiarity with former great men, before these new friendships and this later court acquaintance, which his adversaries now envied.

->*Nunc quia sim tibi, Maecenas, convictor : at olim*<-
->*Quod mihi pareret legio Romana tribuno.*<-

> ["Now they envy me because I live familiarly with you, Maecenas, but formerly because a Roman legion obeyed me as its officer." —Horace, *Satires I. vi. 47, 48.*]

The reproach now concerned a Maecenas or an Augustus. It was the same formerly with respect to a Brutus and those who were then the principal and leading men. The complaint or murmur against him for being an upstart or favorite under a Maecenas and Augustus could not be answered by a *vixisse* relating to the same persons, any more than his *placuisse* (having pleased) joined with his *belli domique* (in war and at home) could relate to those under whom he never went to war nor would ever consent to hold any honors. For so he himself distinguishes (*Satires vi. to Maecenas*)—

->*Quia non, ut forsit honorem*<-
->*Jure mihi invideat quivis, ita te quoque amicum.*<-

> ["The two reasons are different because, though perhaps a man might fairly grudge me my commission, yet he cannot fairly grudge me your friendship too."—*Satires I. vi. 49, 50.*]

He was formerly an active participant and involved in the administration of affairs; now he is only a friend to a minister, remaining a private and retired man. It is well known that he refused Augustus's offer of the secretaryship. But in these circumstances, the politeness as well as the artifice of Horace is admirable in making future generations or posterity the speaking party in both those places where he suggests his intimacy and favor with the great. He did this so that there might, in some measure, be room left (though strictly speaking there was hardly any) for an Octavius and a Maecenas to be included. See Treatise III. part ii. § 3, in the notes.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the relationship between authors and their audience, transitioning from Horace’s defense of his social standing to a broader philosophical point about intellectual independence and the responsibility of the reader.</meta>
