<header>SHAFTESBURY’S CHARACTERISTICS</header>

above flattery or mean courtship toward their reader, yet let them reflect that, as authors merely, they are but of the second rank of men. And let the reader also consider "that when he unworthily resigns the place of honor, and surrenders his taste or judgment to an author—no matter how great their name or venerable their antiquity—and not to reason and truth, at whatever risk, he not only betrays himself but also the common cause of author and reader, the interest of letters and knowledge, and the chief liberty, privilege, and prerogative of the rational part of mankind."

It is related in the history of the Cappadocians that when they were offered their liberty by the Romans and permitted to govern themselves by their own laws and constitutions, they were much terrified by the proposal. As if some severe harm had been intended for them, they humbly requested "that they might be governed by arbitrary power, and that an absolute governor might be appointed over them without delay at the discretion of the Romans." For such was their disposition toward mere slavery and subjection that they dared not even pretend to choose their own master. They thought slavery so essential, and the right of mastership so divine a thing, that they dared not be free enough even to presume to give themselves that blessing, which they chose instead to leave to Providence, fortune, or a conqueror to bestow upon them. They dared not make a king, but would rather take one from their powerful neighbors. Had they been forced to hold an election, the horror of such a use of liberty in government would perhaps have determined them to choose blindfolded, or leave it to the decision of the most common lot—the cast of a die, cross or pile <note>heads or tails</note>, or whatever else might best enable them to clear themselves of the heinous charge of using even the least foresight, choice, or prudence in such an affair.

I would think it a great misfortune if my reader were among those who, in a kind of Cappadocian spirit, could easily be terrified by the proposal of being given their liberty,

and making him his own judge. My endeavor, I must confess, has been to show him his just prerogative in this respect, and to give him the sharpest eye over his author, inviting him to criticize honestly, without favor or affection, and with the utmost exertion of his talents and judgment. On this account it may be objected to me, perhaps, “that I am not a little vain and presumptuous in my own as well as in my author’s behalf, who can thus, as it were, challenge my reader to a trial of his keenest wit.”

But to this I answer, that should I have the good fortune to raise the masterly spirit of just criticism in my readers and exalt them ever so little above the lazy, timid, over-modest, or resigned state in which the majority of them remain—though by this very spirit I myself might possibly meet my doom—I should, however, abundantly congratulate myself on these my low flights. I would be proud of having feathered the arrows of better wits, and furnished artillery or ammunition of any kind to those powers to which I myself had fallen a victim.

->*Fungar vice cotis.*<sup>1</sup><-

I could reconcile my ambition in this respect to what I call my loyalty to the reader, and say of his elevation in criticism and judgment what a Roman princess said of her son’s advancement to empire, “let him kill me, so long as he reigns.” <sup>2</sup>

Had I been a Spanish Cervantes, and with success equal to that comic author, had destroyed the reigning taste of Gothic or Moorish chivalry, I could afterwards contentedly have seen my burlesque work itself despised and set aside, once it had wrought its intended effect and destroyed those giants and monsters of the brain, against which it was originally designed. Without regard, therefore, to the prevailing relish or taste which, in my own person, I may unhappily experience, when

<meta>This page continues the author’s defense of critical thinking, shifting the focus from the general duty of the reader to the specific need for improving the English stage and public taste.</meta>

As these miscellaneous works of mine are leisurely examined, I shall continue in my endeavor to refine my reader’s palate, honing and sharpening it as best I can for use and practice on minor subjects. I hope that through this exercise, it may acquire a greater sharpness and be much more effective regarding subjects of a higher kind that relate to his chief happiness, his liberty, and his manhood.

Supposing me, therefore, to be merely a comic humorist regarding those inferior subjects which I presume to criticize in the style of my familiar prose satire; may I not be allowed to ask, “whether there does not still remain among us noble Britons something of that original, barbarous, and Gothic taste, not yet completely purged away, when, even now, romances and similar gallantries—along with other works just as monstrous—are popular and fashionable, even among the people who make up our supposedly polite society?” Do I need, for this reason, to refer again to our author,<note>¹ Namely, in his *Advice to Authors*, Treatise iii.</note> where he treats generally the style and manner of our modern writers, from the theologian to the comedian? Who is there with the slightest judgment or understanding who cannot easily observe, without the help of a clergyman or a rigid moralist, the sorry state of our English stage? This stage is nevertheless the meeting place and chief entertainment of our best society, and from it, in all probability, our youth will continue to derive their notions of manners and their taste for life more directly and naturally than from the rehearsals and declamations of a more serious theater.

Let those whose business it is promote, as best they can, the benefit of that sacred oratory which we have recently seen—and are likely to continue seeing—employed for various purposes and further designs than those of instructing us in religion or manners. Let them, in that elevated setting, endeavor to refine our taste and judgment in sacred matters. It is the good critic’s task to improve our common stage, nor should this dramatic art be decried or condemned by those critics from a higher sphere.

The practice and art are honest in themselves. Our foundations are well-laid. And on the whole, our English stage (as has been remarked <margin>^1 Treatise III. part ii. §§ 1, 2, 3.</margin>) is capable of the highest improvement, due both to the current genius of our nation and the rich material provided by our early poets in this genre. But faults are more easily imitated than beauties.

We find, indeed, that our theater has lately become the subject of growing criticism. We hear it openly complained “that in our newer plays as well as in our older ones—in comedy as well as tragedy—the stage presents a literal scene of uproar: duels fought, swords drawn with many people on each side, wounds inflicted and sometimes even dressed, the surgeon called, and the patient examined and treated with a medical probe on the spot. In our tragedies, nothing is so common as wheels, racks, and gallows appropriately decorated, executions decently performed, headless bodies and bodiless heads exposed to view, battles fought, murders committed, and the dead carried off in great numbers.” Such is our refined society!

<margin>^2 Treatise III. part ii. § 3.</margin>
Nor are these plays, for this reason, any less frequented by either sex, which inclines me to favor the idea our author <margin>^2 Treatise III. part ii. § 3.</margin> has suggested regarding the mutual correspondence and relationship between our royal theater and the popular circus or bear-garden. For in the former of these assemblies, it is undeniable that at least the two upper regions or galleries contain spectators who frequent each place of entertainment indifferently. So it is no wonder we hear such applause resounding for the victories of an *Almanzor*, when the same people had possibly, no later than the day before, bestowed their applause just as freely on a victorious butcher, the hero of another stage. There, amidst various fights, animal and human blood, indiscriminate wounds and slaughter, one sex is observed to be as frequent and as pleased as spectators as the other—and sometimes not merely spectators, but actors in the gladiator-like roles. The chief of ancient critics [Aristotle], we know, extols Homer above all things for understanding how “to lie in perfection,” as shown in the passage we cited above in Treatise III, part iii, § 3. His lies, according to that master’s opinion and the judgment of many of the most serious and venerable writers, were in themselves the most just moral truths, and displayed the best doctrine and instruction for life and manners. It may be asked, perhaps, “how does the poet, then, come to draw no single pattern of this kind—no perfect character—in either of his heroic pieces?” I answer that should he attempt to do it, he would, as a poet, be preposterous and false. It is not the *possible* but the *probable* and likely which must be the poet’s guide in manners. By this, he wins attention and moves the conscious reader or spectator, who judges best from within, by what he naturally feels and experiences in his own heart. The perfection of virtue results from long practice and management, self-control, and, as it were, a force upon nature. But the common listener or spectator, who seeks pleasure only and loves to engage his passions by the view of other passions and emotions, understands little of the restraints, moderations, and corrections that form this new and artificial creature. For such indeed is the truly virtuous man, whose art—though ever so natural in itself or justly founded in reason and nature—is an improvement far beyond the common stamp or known character of humankind. And thus, the completely virtuous and perfect character is unpoetical and false. Effects must not appear where causes must necessarily remain unknown and incomprehensible. A hero without passion is in poetry as absurd as a hero without life or action. Now, if passion is allowed, passionate action must follow. The same heroic genius and seeming magnanimity which transport us when observed are naturally transporting in the lives and manners of the great who are described to us. And thus, the skilled designer who invents on behalf of truth and draws his characters according to the moral rule, does not fail to discover Nature’s propensity; he assigns to these high spirits their proper excess and inclination to overreach in that tone or type of passion which constitutes the eminent or shining part of each poetic character. The passion of *Achilles* is toward that glory which is acquired by arms and personal valor. In favor of this character, we forgive the generous youth his excess of ardor in the field, and his resentment when injured and provoked in council and by his allies. The passion of a *Ulysses* is toward that glory which is acquired by prudence, wisdom, and ability in affairs. It is in favor of this character that we forgive him his subtle, crafty, and deceitful air; since the intriguing spirit, the over-reaching manner, and over-refinement of art and policy are as naturally incident to the experienced and thorough politician as sudden resentment, and indiscreet and rash behavior, are to the open, undesigning character of a warlike youth. The gigantic force and military toil of an *Ajax* would not be so easily credible or engaging, if not for the honest simplicity of his nature and the heaviness of his mind and genius. For strength of body is so often noted by us as being unattended by equal faculties and strength of mind; when we see this natural effect expressed and find our secret and malicious kind of reasoning confirmed in this instance, we yield to any hyperbole of our poet on the other hand. He afterwards has full scope and liberty to enlarge and exceed in the peculiar virtue and excellence of his hero. He may lie splendidly, raise wonder, and be as astonishing as he pleases. Everything will be allowed him in return for this frank allowance. Thus the tongue of a *Nestor* may work prodigies, while the accompanying mixtures of a rhetorical fluency and aged experience are kept in view. An *Agamemnon* may be admired as a noble and wise chief, while a certain princely haughtiness, a stiffness and stately carriage natural to the character, are represented in his person and noted in their ill effects. For in this way, the excesses of every character are redressed by the poet. And since the misfortunes naturally attending such excesses are justly applied, our passions—while engaged and moved in the strongest manner—are corrected and purged in the healthiest and most effective way. Were a man to form himself by one single pattern or original, however perfect, he would himself be a mere copy. But while he draws from various models, he is original, natural, and unaffected. We see in outward carriage and behavior how ridiculous anyone becomes who imitates another, however graceful that person may be. They are mean spirits who love merely to copy; nothing is agreeable or natural but what is original. Our manners, like our faces, though ever so beautiful, must differ in their beauty. An over-regularity is next to a deformity. And in a poem (whether *epic* or *dramatic*) a com-

Art too seems to do this in imitation of nature. For painting, by combining the natures of black and white, yellow and red, makes its representations correspond with their types. Music, uniting sharp and deep notes, and long and short syllables, creates one harmony among different sounds. Grammar too, bringing together vowels and consonants, builds its whole art upon them. They have of late, it is true, reformed in some measure the "gouty joints" and patchwork of *whereuntos*, *wherebys*, *thereofs*, *therewiths*, and the rest of this kind, by which complex periods are so oddly strung or hooked together after the wordy manner of the legal bar or the pulpit. But to take into consideration no real accent or cadence of words, no sound or measure of syllables—to put together, at one time, a set of compounds of the longest Greek or Latin endings, and at another to let whole verses, and those too of our heroic and longest kind, pass commonly in monosyllables—is, I think, no small negligence. If single verses at the beginning, or in the most emphatic places of the most significant works, can admit such a structure and pass for truly harmonious and poetic in this negligent form, I see no reason why more verses than one or two of the same formation should not be just as well admitted. Nor do I see why an uninterrupted succession of these well-strung monosyllables might not be allowed to clatter after one another, like the hammers of a paper mill, without any breach of music or prejudice to the harmony of our language. But if persons who have gone no further than a blacksmith’s anvil to train their ears are yet likely, on a fair trial, to find a plain defect in these ten-monosyllable heroic lines, it would follow, I think, that even a prose author who attempts to write elegantly should endeavor to confine himself within those bounds which can never be exceeded in any proper meter or pleasing pronunciation without a breach of harmony.

Thus have I ventured to challenge the authority of those self-privileged writers who would exempt themselves from criticism and save their ill-acquired reputations by denouncing an art on which the cause and interest of wit and letters absolutely depend. Be it they themselves, or their great patrons

# MISCELLANEOUS REFLECTIONS

On behalf of those who would thus arbitrarily support the credit of bad writing, the attempt, I hope, will prove unsuccessful. Whether they are moderns or ancients, foreigners or natives, ponderous and austere writers or light and humorous ones, whoever takes refuge here or seeks protection from this, whoever joins their party or interest to this cause, it appears from the very fact and effort alone that there is just ground to suspect some inadequacy or fraud at the bottom. And for this reason the reader, if they are wise, will instead redouble their application and industry to examine the merit of this arrogant author. If, as reader and judge, they dare once assert that liberty to which we have shown them to be justly entitled, they will not easily be threatened or ridiculed out of the use of their analytical capacity and native privilege of criticism.

> It was to this art, so well understood and practiced in the past, that the wise ancients owed whatever was consummate and perfect in their productions. It is to the same art we owe the recovery of literature in these recent ages. To this alone we must attribute the recognition of ancient manuscripts, the discovery of what is fake, and the discernment of whatever is genuine among those venerable remains which have passed through such dark periods of ignorance and raised us to the improvements we now make in every science. It is to this art that even the sacred authors themselves owe their highest purity and correctness. The art itself ought to be esteemed as so sacred, since from its resources alone is formed that judicious and learned strength by which the defenders of our holy religion are able so successfully to refute the heathens, Jews, sectarians, heretics, and other enemies or opponents of our primitive and ancient faith.

But having thus, following our author’s example, asserted the use of criticism in all literary works—from the main structure or plan of every writing down to the smallest particle—we may now proceed to exercise this art upon our author himself. By his own rules, we shall examine him in this, his last treatise, while still reserving for ourselves the same privilege of variation and digression.

### CHAPTER II

->The generation and succession of our national and modern wit—The manners of the proprietors—Corporations and joint stock—A statute against criticism—A coffee-house committee—Mr. Bays—Other "Bays" in divinity—A censure of our author's dialogue piece, and of the manner of dialogue writing used by reverend wits.<-

According to the common practice of our age, we seldom see the characters of writer and critic united in the same person. There is, I know, a certain species of authors who subsist entirely by the practice of criticizing or commenting upon others, and can appear in no other form besides what this employment authorizes them to assume. They have no original character or primary role, but wait for something that may be called a work in order to graft onto it, and come in for shares second-hand.

Writers of this capacity and rank are, because of their function and employment, distinguished by the title of *answerers*. For it happens in the world that there are readers of a talent and stature just suited to these answering authors. If these authors teach them nothing else, they believe they will teach them how to criticize. And though these newly practicing critics are of a sort unlikely ever to understand any original book or writing, they can understand—or at least remember and quote—the subsequent reflections, insults, and jeers which may accidentally be made against such a piece. Whenever a gentleman of this sort happens to be in company, you shall no sooner hear a new book mentioned than it will be asked, “Who has answered it?” or, “When is an answer coming out?” Now the answer, as our gentleman knows, must necessarily be newer than the book; and the newer a thing is, the more fashionable it remains, and

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "answering wits"—writers who survive by critiquing others—and explores why the roles of "writer" and "critic" have become so separated in the modern literary world.</meta>

<page-num>325</page-num>
# MISCELLANEOUS REFLECTIONS

...the more refined the subject of discourse. For this, the bookseller knows how to satisfy our gentleman perfectly, for he usually has an answer already prepared, and perhaps finished by the time his new book is published. And it is likely that our fashionable gentleman, who takes both together, may read the latter first and drop the other for good.

But regarding these answering wits, and the manner of rejoinders and repeated replies, we have said enough in a previous Miscellany.<note>See above, *Misc.* i. ch. ii.</note> We need only remark in general, "that it is necessary a writing critic should understand how to write. And though every writer is not bound to show himself in the capacity of a critic, every writing critic is bound to show himself capable of being a writer. For if he is clearly incompetent in the latter kind, he is to be denied all title or reputation in the other."

To merely criticize what another person writes; to twitch, snap, snub, or mock; to torture sentences and phrases, turn a few expressions into ridicule, or write what is nowadays called an "answer" to any piece, is not sufficient to constitute what is properly considered a writer or author in due form. For this reason, though there are many answerers seen in public, there are few or no critics or satirists. But whatever the state of controversy may be in our religious or political concerns, it is certain that in the purely literary world, affairs are managed with a better understanding between the principal parties involved. The established writers or authors have an easier time than any government or religious party in power. They have found a way, by decrying all criticism in general, to get rid of their dissenters, and prevent all claims to further reformation in their state. The critic is made to appear distinct and of another species, wholly different from the writer. No one who has a talent for writing and can perform with any success is presumed to be so ill-natured or ill-bred as to try to distinguish themselves in criticism.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the separation of the roles of writer and critic, exploring how the current political climate allows mediocre talents to dominate the literary scene.</meta>

<page-num>326</page-num>
SHAFTESBURY'S CHARACTERISTICS

The difference between the writer and the critic has been so generally established among us that their fields seem entirely distinct and irreconcilable. The presumptuous wits who—without waiting for their proper time or completing their required studies—emerge in the world as authors, having acquired a reputation among mankind with little effort or judgment and merely by the power of imagination, can under no circumstances afterward submit to a rejection or disparagement of those immature works to which they owe their early status and distinction. Indeed, it would go poorly for them if, on these stubborn terms, they should venture into criticism, or attempt to stir that spirit which would inevitably disturb their established reputation.

Now we may consider that in our nation, and especially in our present age, while wars, debates, and public upheavals turn our minds so entirely toward business and public affairs, the better geniuses are in a sense necessarily involved in the active sphere, upon which the general eye of humanity is so strongly fixed. Consequently, there must remain a significant vacancy in the theater of wit, and the status of an actor upon that stage must be very easily attainable, and at a low cost of talent or understanding.

Therefore, the people who are in possession of the lead roles in this deserted theater, being allowed to maintain their ranks and positions in complete ease, naturally have a good agreement and understanding with their fellow-wits. Being indebted to the times for this good fortune—that with so little industry or ability they have been able to serve the nation with wit and take the place of the real dispensers and ministers of the muses’ treasures—they must necessarily (as they have any self-love or fatherly affection for their works) conspire with one another to preserve their common interest in laziness and justify their negligence, inaccuracy, dullness, and outright ignorance of all literary art or true poetic beauty.

->*Magna inter molles concordia.*<sup>1</sup><-

For this reason, you see them mutually courteous and benevolent, gracious and obliging beyond measure; complimenting one another reciprocally at the beginning of their works, in recommendatory verses, or in separate panegyrics, essays, and fragments of poetry. We see these in the *Miscellaneous Collections* (our yearly retail of wit), curiously assembled and adapted to the taste of the world. Here, the *tyrocinium* of geniuses is annually displayed. Here, if you see fit, you may make the acquaintance of the young offspring of wits as they gradually rise under the old ones, paying due courtship and homage to those great predecessors of fame in the hope of being one day admitted, in their turn, into the noble order and made wits by patent and authority.

This is the young crowd which you may see busily surrounding the grown poet or chief playhouse author,¹ at a coffee-house. They are his guards, ready to take up arms for him if he is at any time attacked by some presumptuous critic. They are indeed the very shadows of their immediate predecessor and represent the same features, perhaps with some small alteration for the worse. They are sure to aim at nothing above or beyond their master, and would on no account give him the least jealousy of their aspiring to any degree or order of writing above him. From this comes that harmony and reciprocal esteem which, on such a foundation as this, cannot fail of being perfectly well established among our poets: the age, meanwhile, being in this manner hopefully provided for and secure in a constant and similar succession of meritorious wits in every genre!

If by chance a man of sense, unaware of the authority of these high powers, should venture to accost the gentlemen of this fraternity at some coffee-house committee while they were occupied with mutual admiration and the usual praise of their

<meta>This page continues the dialogue regarding the merit of critics versus authors, moving from a defense of the critic's role to a historical justification of criticism by citing ancient philosophers and rhetoricians.</meta>

<header>SHAFTESBURY'S CHARACTERISTICS</header>

“No, sir. But you are a critic. And we know by certain experience that, when a critic writes according to rule and method, he is sure never to hit the English taste. Did not *Mr. Rymer*, who criticized our English tragedy, write a sorry one of his own? If he did, gentlemen, it was his own fault for not knowing his genius better. But is his criticism any less just on this account? If a musician performs his part well in the hardest symphonies, he must necessarily know the notes and understand the rules of harmony and music. But must a man, therefore, who has an ear and has studied the rules of music, necessarily have a voice or skill with his hands? Can no one possibly judge a fiddle except someone who is himself a fiddler? Can no one judge a picture except someone who is himself a painter?”

Thus far our rational gentleman might perhaps venture before his coffee-house audience. Had I been at his elbow to prompt him as a friend, I would hardly have thought it fit to remind him of anything further. On the contrary, I would have rather taken him aside to inform him of this clique and established corporation of wit, of their declared aversion to criticism, and of their known laws and statutes created and provided for that case. I should have told him, in short, that learned arguments would be wasted on people like these, and that he would find little success, even though he should ever so plainly demonstrate to the gentlemen of this caliber of wit and understanding, “that the greatest masters of art, in every kind of writing, were eminent in critical practice.” But that they really were so, witness, among the ancients, their greatest philosophers, <note>Namely *Plato* and *Aristotle*. Among the moderns, Boileau and Corneille are sufficient precedents for the case before us. They applied their criticism with just severity, even to their own works. This, indeed, is a method hardly practicable for the poets of our own nation. It would be unreasonable to expect them to use such standards that, when applied to their works, would reveal them to be completely deformed and disproportionate. It is no wonder, therefore, if we have so little of this critical genius surviving to guide us in our taste. forced to find a difficult way to devise how, or with what probability, he might introduce men of any status or fashion reasoning seriously and deliberately,¹ without joking or triviality, for two or three hours together on nothing but philosophy and morals. He finds these subjects (as he confesses) so far removed from common conversation, and by long custom so restricted to the school, the university chair, or the pulpit, that he thinks it hardly safe or practical to discuss them elsewhere or in a different tone. He is forced, therefore, to create specific literary devices and constrain his principal characters in order to present a better appearance and justify himself against the accusation of being pedantic. Thus, his gentleman philosopher, Theocles, before he reveals his real character, becomes a feigned preacher. And even when his real character appears, he hardly dares to maintain it; instead, to better handle his skeptical friend, he returns to role-playing and adopts the mood of the poet and the enthusiast. Palemon, the man of high social standing who is first introduced as a speaker in the work, must, for the sake of fashion, appear to be in love and suffering from a kind of melancholy caused by some misfortunes in the world. How else could he be expected to be so serious? Philocles, his friend (a lighthearted gentleman of the world and a thorough *railleur*²), must be directly confronted and feel the anger of his serious friend before he can be expected to be serious himself. He only needed to have brought his first speakers immediately into action and spared the narrative or descriptive part from Philocles to Palemon by presenting them as speaking characters upon his stage. The scene throughout could have been the park. From early evening until the late hour of night when the two gentlemen retired to their town apartments, there was enough time for the narrator, Philocles, to have recounted the entire transaction of the second and third parts, which would have remained exactly as they are now; only at the conclusion, when the narrative or descriptive part had ended, would the simple and direct dialogue have returned to conclude the scene. By this means, both the unity of time and the unity of place in the piece would have been preserved. Nor would our author have been forced to commit that anachronism of making his first part the last in chronological order.

It is with the same view that we miscellaneous authors, fearing the natural weariness and boredom of our lazy reader, have prudently adopted the method of chapters and tables of contents; so that as the reader proceeds, through frequent intervals of rest designed specifically for him, he may from time to time be informed of what is yet to come, and thus be tempted to renew his attention.

Thus, in our modern plays, we see descriptions or illustrations of the action on almost every other page—not in the poem itself, or spoken by the actors, but by the poet in his own voice. This appears to be done to compensate for a defect in the text with a kind of marginal note or comment, which makes these pieces a mix of narrative and drama. It is in this fashionable style or manner of "dumb show" that the reader finds the action of the piece expressed more vividly than he possibly could through the lines of the drama itself, where only the characters are allowed to speak.

It is out of the same concern for ease, for both the writer and the reader, that we see long descriptions of characters at the beginning of most dramatic pieces, to inform us of the relationships, family ties, interests, and goals of the *dramatis personae*; this being of the highest importance to the reader, so that he may better understand the plot and identify the principal characters and incidents of the work, which otherwise could not possibly reveal themselves when read in their proper order. And to do justice to our play-readers, they seldom fail to humor our poets in this regard, reading through the character descriptions with strict attention, as a sort of grammar or key, before they begin the play itself. I do not know whether they would do as much for any philosophical work in the world. Our author seems

Our author <sup>1</sup> gives more reasons himself for avoiding the direct method of dialogue, which is currently held in such low regard and is used only occasionally in our political pamphlets or modern theological essays. For lately, it seems, this style has been introduced into Church controversy, using mockery and humor as a supposedly more successful way to deal with heresy and unbelief. This "burlesque divinity" is becoming very fashionable. And the highly praised responses to unorthodox writings are generally those written with drollery or in a style that mimics the witty and humorous language of conversation.

Good for the reverend authors who can afford to be so cheerful, and who condescend to correct us using this worldly wit. The progress they make on behalf of piety and good manners through such a popular style is, no doubt, found through experience to be quite significant. Since these reformers are well-qualified to mimic the tone of good breeding and gentility, they will no doubt refine their style in time and improve this joking method for the education of the polite world, which has been led astray for so long by mockery and wit. They may perform wonders with their comic muse, and might even find a way to laugh gentlemen back into their religion.

At present, it must be admitted, the characters or personages employed by our new orthodox writers of dialogue carry with them little proportion or coherence, and in this respect may be said to suit perfectly with that figurative, metaphorical style and rhetorical manner in which their logic and arguments are generally expressed. Nothing can be more complex or varied than their moral drafts or sketches of humanity. These, indeed, are so far from representing any particular man or group of men, that they scarcely resemble anything of the kind. It is by their names only that these characters are identified. Though they bear different titles and are set up to maintain opposing viewpoints, they are found, at the bottom, to be all on the same side; and, despite their seeming disagreement, they cooperate in the most obliging manner with the author to display his own particular wit and the establishment of his private opinions and principles. They are indeed his very legitimate and submissive puppets, as much like real men in voice, action, and behavior as those wooden or wire machines of the puppet theater. Philotheus and Philatheus, Philautus and Philalethes are all of one and the same type: mere matches for one another; questioning and answering in harmony, and with the kind of turn-taking known in a common game, where one person lies down blindfolded and offers himself, as fairly as can be, to another, who—by favor of the company or the assistance of his good fortune—deals his companion many a hard blow, without ever being challenged or forced to take his own turn lying down.

There is the same strange mixture of chance and elegant variation in the style of these mock characters of our new theological drama; with this difference only: that after the poor phantom or shadow of an adversary has said as little for his cause as can be imagined, and provided as many openings and

I think it will hardly be objected to our moralist (the author of the philosophic dialogue *above*) “that the characters who sustain the skeptical or objecting roles are overly tame and manageable in their disposition.” If I perceived any such foul play in his work, I would hardly think it worthy of the criticism bestowed here. For in this kind of writing, where characters are exhibited and *natural* conversation is displayed, if the characters are not reasonably consistent and their manners are not described with some realistic likeness, there remains nothing but what is *too coarse and absurd for criticism or examination.*

It will perhaps be alleged, in answer to what is proposed here, “that if a dialogue were written according to the exactness of these rules, it should be condemned as a *worse* work for showing the infidel or skeptic such mercy and giving him the *full advantage of his argument and wit.*”

But to this I reply: either dialogue should never be attempted, or, if it is, the parties should appear natural and as they really are. If we paint at all, we should endeavor to paint from life and depict creatures as they are recognizable—in their proper shapes and better features—*not* as transformations, *not* as mangled, lame, distorted, awkward forms, and powerless chimeras. Atheists have their senses and wits like other men; otherwise, why is atheism so often challenged in those of the *higher* social rank? Why is it so often attributed to wit and subtle *reasoning*?

If I were to advise these authors—toward whom I am very well-disposed on account of their good-natured zeal and the apparent sociability of their religion—I would say to them, “*Gentlemen!* Do *not* be so cautious about providing your representative skeptic with arguments that are too good, or with too shrewd a turn of wit or humor. Do *not* be so afraid of showing mercy. Allow your adversary his full reason, his ingenuity, sense, and

<meta>This page continues the critique of religious and philosophical dialogues, specifically advising authors on how to properly characterize their protagonists and opponents to ensure the work is convincing and respectful of the reader's intelligence.</meta>

He will undoubtedly overcome the utmost force of his opponent, and dispel the darkness or cloud which the adversary may unluckily have raised. But if, when you have fairly developed your antagonist to his proper strength and recognizable proportions, your main character cannot afterwards prove a match for him or shine with a superior brightness; whose fault is it? The subject’s? This, I hope, you will never allow. Whose, therefore, besides your own? Beware then, and consider well your strength and mastery in this manner of writing, and in the qualifying practice of the polite world, before you attempt these accurate and refined <term>limnings</term> or portraits of mankind, or offer to bring gentlemen onto the stage. For if real gentlemen—seduced, as you pretend, and led into error in their religion or philosophy—do not discover even the slightest feature of their real faces in your looking-glass, nor know themselves in the least by your description, they will hardly be likely to think they are refuted. No matter how wittily your comedy may be written, they will scarcely realize that any of that wit applies to themselves. They may laugh indeed at the diversion you are pleased to give them, but the laugh perhaps may be different from what you intend. They may smile secretly to see themselves thus encountered; when they find, at last, your authority laid aside and your scholastic weapons abandoned, in favor of this weak attempt to master them by their own weapons and natural ability.”

Thus we have performed our critical task, and tested our strength both on our author and those of his order who attempt to write in dialogue after the active dramatic,¹ imitative, or personating way, according to which a writer is properly poetical.

What remains, we shall examine in our succeeding and last chapter.

## CHAPTER III

Of the extent or latitude of thought—Free-thinkers—Their cause and character—Dishonesty as a half-thought—Short-thinking as the cause of vice and bigotry—The agreement between slavery and superstition—Liberty: civil, moral, and spiritual—Free-thinking theologians—Representatives incognito—Ambassadors from the moon—The effective resolution of Christian controversy and religious belief.

HAVING now reached the conclusion of my work, after defending the cause of critics in general and applying what strength I had in that field to our adventurous author in particular, I may, with fairness and better grace, attempt a line or two in defense of that freedom of thought which our author has used, particularly through one of the characters in his last dialogue treatise.

There is good reason to believe that, however similarly formed or alike the human race may appear in other respects, they are not always equal thinkers, nor do they possess a similar ability in managing this natural talent we call thought. For this reason, the human race may justly be distinguished, as they often are, by the labels of the thinking and the unthinking. The purely unthinking are those who have not yet arrived at that fortunate realization by which they should observe “how necessary thinking is, and how fatal the lack of it must prove to them.” The thinking part of mankind, on the other hand, having discovered the diligence and effort required for right thinking, and having already begun as thinkers upon this foundation, are convinced as they progress of the necessity of thinking for a good purpose and carrying the work to a thorough conclusion. They know that if they hesitate or stop once on this road, they might as well have never set out. They are not so passive as to be held back by mere laziness when nothing stands in the way to interrupt the free course and progress of their thoughts.

The author argues that once the process of thinking has begun, it must be pursued to its logical conclusion to be effective.</summary>

--- Page 354 ---
<meta>This page continues the defense of free inquiry, arguing that once the habit of reasoning is established, it cannot be arbitrarily halted by external boundaries or authority without the thinker's own consent.</meta>

<header>SHAFTESBURY'S CHARACTERISTICS</header>
<page-num>342</page-num>

Some obstacles, it is true, may be claimed on this occasion. Specters may cross our path, and shadows of reason may rise up against reason itself. But if men have once heartily embraced the habit of reasoning or thinking, they will not easily be persuaded to give up the practice; they will not be instantly arrested or made to stand and surrender when they reach a certain boundary, landmark, post, or pillar, erected here or there (for reasons that can probably be guessed) with the inscription of a *ne plus ultra* <note>Latin for "nothing further beyond," indicating a finished state or an impassable limit.</note>.

Indeed, no authority on earth, as we are well aware, can stop us on this road unless we choose to impose the arrest or restriction ourselves. It is our own thought which must restrain our thinking. And how shall we ever judge whether the restraining thought is just, without examining it freely and without any constraint? How shall we be sure that we have rightly abandoned reason as too lofty and dangerous, too ambitious or presumptuous, if—through fear of any kind or by submitting to mere command—we abandon our very habit of examination and stop short in that moment, putting an end to further thinking on the matter? Is there much difference between this case and that of obedient beasts of burden, who stop exactly at their appointed inn, or at whatever point the driver or controller of the reins sees fit to signal for a halt?

From this, I cannot help but conclude that of all the species of creatures commonly said to have brains, the most dull, wretched, and absurd are those whom, in proper speech, we call <term>half-thinkers</term>.

I have often known those who pretend to be witty burst into admiration at the sight of some unrefined, heedless, unthinking gentleman, declaring on such occasions that they considered it the happiest situation in the world "never to think or trouble one's head with study or reflection." I have always looked upon this as one of the greatest airs of distinction that self-admiring wits are accustomed to adopt in public company. Now, the echo or response which these elegant exclaimers hope for, by this

If, for example, they overlooked the chief enjoyments of life, which are founded in honesty and a good mind; if they presumed mere life to be fully worth what its tenacious lovers are pleased to rate it at; if they thought public distinction, fame, power, an estate or title to be of the same value as is commonly conceived, or as they concluded on a first thought without further skepticism or later deliberation; it is no wonder if, having in time become such mature dogmatists and well-practiced dealers in the affairs of what they call a settlement or fortune, they are so hard-pressed to find ease or rest within themselves.

These are the deeply-loaded and over-pensive gentlemen, who, considering it the truest wit to pursue what they call their interest, wonder to find they are still as little at ease when they have succeeded as when they first attempted to advance.

There can never be less self-enjoyment than in these supposedly wise characters, these selfish <term>calculators of happiness</term> and private good, whose pursuits of interest, whether for this world or another, are attended with the same steady vein of cunning and low thought, sordid deliberations, perverse and crooked fancies, ill dispositions and false tastes of life and manners. The most negligent, undesigning, thoughtless <term>rake</term> <note>A person who lives a dissolute or immoral life; a profligate.</note> has not only more sociability, ease, tranquility and freedom from worldly cares, but in reality more worth, virtue, and merit than such grave plodders and thoughtful gentlemen as these.

If it happens, therefore, that these more serious, more cautious, and deeply self-interested gentlemen have, for the sake of their souls and through careful preparation for the afterlife, engaged in certain religious speculations, their taste for virtue and enjoyment of life is not improved because of it. Their thoughts on these new subjects of theology are so biased and confused by those half-formed thoughts and crude imaginings of personal interest and worldly affairs, that they are still hindered in the rational pursuit of happiness and the good; and being forced to remain shallow thinkers, they can go no further than they are led by those to whom, in their state of distress and confusion, they turn for a remedy and comfort.

It has been the main goal and principal purpose of these volumes, “to assert the reality of a beauty and charm in moral as well as natural subjects, and to demonstrate the reasonableness of a balanced taste and a decisive choice in life and conduct.” The standard of this kind and the well-known character of moral truth appear so firmly established in Nature itself, and so widely displayed throughout the intelligent world, that there is no spirit, mind, or thinking being that is not (if I may say so) actually conscious of it. Even the most stubborn and obstinate minds are convinced of this reality by certain recurring thoughts on every occasion, and are forced, like everyone else, to acknowledge actual right and wrong.

It is evident that whenever the mind, influenced by passion or mood, consents to any action, measure, or rule of life contrary to this governing standard and primary measure of intellect, it can only be because of weak thinking, a lack of judgment, and a failure to apply that unavoidable impression and primary natural rule of honesty and worth, against which whatever is proposed will serve no purpose other than to make a life distracted, incoherent, and full of indecision, regret, and self-disapproval.

For instance, when the eye or appetite is eagerly fixed on treasure and the monetary bliss of bags and money-chests, it is plain there is a kind of fascination in the case. The sight is instantly diverted from all other views of excellence or worth. And here, even the common people, as well as the more educated part of mankind, recognize the restricted spirit and acknowledge the narrowness of such a mind.

In luxury and intemperance, we easily understand how far thought is oppressed and the mind barred from just reflection, and from the free examination and criticism of its own opinions or maxims, upon which the conduct of a life is formed.

Even in that complicated good of the common kind which we usually call self-interest—in which we include pleasure, riches, power, and other external advantages—we may discern how a captivated sight restricts a spirit, and by shortening the view even of that very interest which it seeks, betrays the knave, and forces the most able and witty convert to such a lifestyle to expose himself in every emergency and sudden turn.

But above all other enslaving vices and restraints of reason and just thought, the most evidently ruinous and fatal to the understanding is that of superstition, bigotry, and common fanaticism. This passion, not contented like other vices to deceive and secretly undermine our reason, professes open war, holds up the intended chains and fetters, and declares its resolution to enslave.

The artificial managers of this human frailty speak out against free-thought and breadth of understanding. To go beyond those bounds of thinking which they have prescribed is declared by them to be a sacrilege. To them, freedom of mind, a mastery of sense, and a liberty in thought and action imply debauchery, corruption, and depravity.

# SHAFTESBURY'S CHARACTERISTICS

346

As a result of their moral maxims and political systems, they can indeed suggest no better notion of human happiness and enjoyment than that which is in every respect the most opposite to liberty. It is to them, undoubtedly, that we owe the disgrace and abuse of those naturally honest names of "free-livers," "free-thinkers," "latitudinarians," or whatever other label implies a breadth of mind and a noble use of the understanding. They would gladly confuse licentiousness in morals with liberty in thought and action, and make the libertine—who has the least mastery of himself—resemble his direct opposite. For such a man is indeed the person of resolute purpose and unshakeable adherence to reason against everything which passion, prejudice, cunning, or fashion can argue in favor of anything else. But here, it seems, lies the grievance. It is thought dangerous for us to be overly rational or too much the masters of ourselves in the conclusions we draw from reason alone. Therefore, these commentators rarely fail to bring the concept of liberty into disgrace. Even at the expense of virtue and of that very idea of goodness upon which they build the mysteries of their profitable science, they disparage morals and reverse all true philosophy. They refine on selfishness and reject generosity, promote a slavish obedience in the place of voluntary duty and free service, exalt blind ignorance as devotion, recommend petty thinking, decry reason, praise sensuality,¹ stubbornness, vengefulness, whimsy, vanity, and even deify those weak passions which are the disgrace rather than the ornament of human nature.²

But it is so far from the nature of liberty to indulge such passions as these,³ that whoever acts at any time under the power of any single one may be said to have already provided himself with an absolute master. And he who lives under the power of a whole set of them (since it is hardly possible to obey one without the others) must necessarily undergo the worst

That this is no paradox even the writers of entertainment can inform us, however others may moralize who discourse or write (as they claim) for profit and instruction. Even poets of the licentious sort give ample testimony of this slavery and the wretchedness of vice. They may extol sensual pleasure to the skies and point their wit as sharply as they can against a virtuous state. But when they later come to pay the necessary price to their commanding pleasures, we hear their pitiful moans and find the inward discord and calamity of their lives. Their example is the best of lessons, since they conceal nothing, are sincere, and speak their passions aloud. And it is in this that the very worst of poets may justly be preferred to the majority of modern philosophers or other formal writers with even more impressive-sounding names. The muses' pupils never fail to express their passions and write exactly as they feel. It is not, indeed, in their nature to do otherwise, while they indulge their creative vein and are under the power of that natural enthusiasm which leads them to what is highest in their work. They follow Nature. They move chiefly as she moves in them, without any thought of disguising her free motions and genuine operations for the sake of some scheme or hypothesis they have formed at leisure and from narrow perspectives. On this account, though at one time they may perhaps quarrel with virtue for restraining them in their forbidden loves, they can at another time make her sufficient amends when they indignantly complain "that merit is neglected, and their worthless rival is preferred over them." ¹

There was no fear in this fiction that their boyish nature would be misinterpreted as innocent and gentle. For my own part, I have complete confidence in the positive powers of reason, "that liberty and freedom shall never, through any trickery or delusion, be made to seem like frightening sounds to me, or be seen as shameful or hateful in any sense."

I can no more allow that to be *free living* where unlimited passion and unexamined whim govern, than I can allow that to be a *free government* where the common people govern instead of the laws. For no people in a civil state can possibly be free when they are governed by anything other than the laws they themselves have established, or to which they have freely given their consent. This was to be the effective means of union! This was to do the work, or nothing could! If we follow any one translation, or any one man's commentary, what rule or direction shall we have by which to choose that one correctly? Or is there any one man who has translated perfectly, or interpreted infallibly? If we resolve to follow any one only as far as we like or fancy, we shall then only do wrong or right by chance. If we resolve absolutely to follow any one wherever he leads, we shall probably arrive at last where, if we have any eyes left, we shall see ourselves become quite ridiculous."

The first holy messengers (for I take that to be the highest apostolic name) brought with them their proper testimonials in their lives, their manners, and behavior, as well as in powerful works, miracles, and signs from heaven. And though, indeed, it might well be considered a miracle of sorts if our present messengers were to represent their predecessors in any part of their demeanor or conduct, yet there are further miracles remaining for them to perform before they can modestly plead apostolic or messenger authority. For although in the flow of a sublime and figurative style a holy apostle may have perhaps used such a phrase as "embassy" or "ambassador" to express the dignity of his mission, it would be desirable if some who were never sent on any mission or message at all from God himself would use a humbler title to describe their voluntary negotiation between us and heaven.

I must confess, for my own part, that I think the notion of an embassy from there to be at best somewhat strained as a metaphor. But I am certain that if there is any such residency or agency now established, it is not immediately from God himself, but through the magistrate and by the prince or sovereign power here on earth that these gentlemen agents are appointed, distinguished, and set over us. They undoubtedly have a legal charter <gloss>1</gloss> and status, legal titles and precedence, legal garments, coats of arms, colors, and badges. But they would do well to consider that a thousand badges or liveries bestowed merely by men can never be sufficient to entitle them to the same authority as those who carried the immediate testimony and miraculous signs of power from above. A certain Indian in the retinue of the ambassador princes recently sent to us from some of those pagan nations, being occupied one Sunday in visiting our churches and happening to ask his interpreter "who the eminent persons were whom he observed haranguing so long, with such authority from a high place," was answered that "they were ambassadors from the Almighty, or (according to the Indian language) from the sun." Whether the Indian took this seriously or as a jest did not appear. But having afterward stopped in, as he went along, at the chapels of some of his fellow-ambassadors of the Roman Catholic religion, and at some other Christian dissenting congregations, where matters—as he perceived—were conducted with greater privacy and less ceremony, he asked "whether these also were ambassadors from the same place." He was answered "that they had indeed previously been part of the embassy and had possessed the same chief positions he had seen, but they were now succeeded there by others." "If those, therefore," replied the Indian, "were ambassadors from the sun, these, I take for granted, are from the moon."

Supposing, indeed, that one were not a pagan but a good Christian, well-versed in the original Holy Scriptures but unacquainted with the rites, titles, garments, and ceremonies of which there is no mention in those writings—might one not have inquired, with humble submission, into this affair? Might one not have quietly and from a distance applied for information concerning this high embassy, perhaps addressing some

# MISCELLANEOUS REFLECTIONS
<page-num>367</page-num>

An inferior officer or servant in uniform of the retinue asked modestly, "How and from where did they come? In whose carriage and gear did they appear? At whose expense were they maintained? And by whose vote or command were they appointed and authorized? Is it true, pray sirs, that their Excellencies of the current establishment are the only ones commissioned? Or are there as many real commissioners as there are claimants? If so, there can be no great danger for us, whichever path we take. We have a wide choice and may stick to whichever commission we like best. If there is only one single true one, we then have, it seems, good reason to look around us, search the matter closely, be careful in our choice, and (as current medical advertisements warn us) 'beware of counterfeits,' since there are so many of these out there with earthly powers and worldly commissions to support their spiritual claims."

It is to be feared, in all earnestness, that making a distinction of this kind will prove quite difficult, especially amidst this universal conflict, strife, and fury of religious challengers—these high defiances between opposing believers, this zealous opposition of one commission against another, and this din of hell, curses, and damnations raised everywhere by one religious party against another.

The allegedly commissioned parties are so far from showing their commission openly, or proving it from the original records or official rolls of heaven, that they deny us the right to inspect those very records they cite, and they refuse to submit their claim to human judgment or examination.

A poet of our nation suggests indeed on their behalf that they are fair enough in this respect. For when the murmuring people, speaking through their chosen orator or spokesman to the priests, say to them:

> With ease you take what we provide with care,
> And we who your legation must maintain,
> Find all your tribe are in the commission,
> And none but Heaven could send so large a train,

<summary>The author highlights the confusion and danger caused by various religious sects all claiming exclusive divine authority while refusing to provide verifiable evidence of their "commission." He uses the perspective of a skeptical observer to suggest that if many claim authority without proof, one might as well choose whichever one seems best.</summary>

<keywords>religious authority, divine commission, clergy, skepticism, religious conflict, credentials, priesthood, legation</keywords>

the apologist, afterwards excusing this boldness of the people and soothing the incensed priests with gentler words, says to them, on a footing of moderation, which he presumes to be their character:—

> You with such composure their intemperance bear,
> To show your solid science does rely
> So on itself that you no trial fear:
> For arts are weak that are of skeptics shy.<sup>1</sup>

The poet, it seems, never dreamed of a time when the very appearance of moderation should be out of fashion with the gentlemen of this order, and the word itself rejected as unworthy of their profession. And, indeed, so far are they at present from putting up with any skeptic or inquirer, however modest or discreet, that to hear an argument on a side contrary to theirs, or read whatever may be written in answer to their particular assertions, is made the highest crime. While they have among themselves such differences and sharp debates about their heavenly commission, and are even in one and the same community or establishment divided into different sects and leaderships, they will allow no detailed survey or inspection into the foundations of their disputed title. They would have us inferior passive mortals—amazed as we are, and beholding with astonishment from afar these tremendous subjects of dispute—wait blindfolded for the outcome and final decision of the controversy. Nor is it enough that we are merely passive. It is required of us that, in the midst of this irreconcilable debate concerning heavenly authorities and powers, we should be as confident of the truthfulness of some one, as of the imposture and fraud of all the other pretenders; and that, believing firmly there is still a real commission at the bottom, we should endure the misery of these conflicts and engage on one side or the other as we happen to have been born or educated, until by fire and sword, execution, massacre, and a kind of depopulation of this
